questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For a female patient planned for laparoscopic surgery, what is the most appropriate pre- operative instruction that should be given?
options: Drink plenty of water before surgery
Enema on the night before surgery
NPO for specific hours before surgery
questions.explanation: The most critical pre-operative instruction for a patient undergoing general anesthesia for laparoscopic surgery is to remain NPO (nil per os), meaning nothing by mouth, for a specific period (Option D). Standard guidelines usually mandate fasting from solids for at least 6–8 hours and clear liquids for 2 hours before the procedure. This is essential to minimize the volume of gastric contents, thereby reducing the risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction and the procedure itself. Instructions to eat fully (Option A) or drink plenty of water (Option B) just before surgery are dangerous and would lead to cancellation of the case. While bowel preparation or an enema (Option C) was historically routine, it is no longer standard for all laparoscopic surgeries unless specifically indicated for bowel-involved procedures. Therefore, adhering to strict fasting protocols is the primary safety requirement for pre-anesthetic preparation
questions.learning: The most critical pre-operative instruction for a patient undergoing general anesthesia for laparoscopic surgery is to remain NPO (nil per os), meaning nothing by mouth, for a specific period (Option D).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old male complained of fatigue for the past 1 year. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly. His blood workup shows the following findings. Which of the following is the most sensitive investigation in this case?

• Anemia
• Total leucocyte count - 1,50,000/microL
• Peripheral blood smear -

• Neutrophils- 60%
• Basophils- 6%
• Eosinophils - 4%
• Myeloblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes

• Myeloid to erythroid ratio- 18:1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FISH and PCR

The clinical presentation with fatigue, splenomegaly, and the peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML). The BCR-ABL gene which is specific for CML is detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization(FISH) or polymerase chain reaction(PCR) based tests.

Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Clinical features:

Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism, fatigability, weakness, weight loss, and anorexia. Dragging sensation in the abdomen caused by splenomegaly, or the acute onset of left upper quadrant pain due to splenic infarction. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral blood:

• Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.
• Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells.
• Platelet count is usually increased

Bone Marrow:

• Markedly hypercellular marrow because of massively increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors. There is usually an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.
• There is also an increase in megakaryocytes and usually include small, dysplastic forms and erythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers. Typically there is an increased reticulin deposition, but overt marrow fibrosis is rare early in the course.
• Sea-blue histiocytes - These are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled,green-blue cytoplasm.

Other options:

Immunophenotyping and flow cytometry: Flow cytometry refers to the measurement of cellular antigens as they flow in a fluid stream. Immunophenotyping is employed using labeled antibodies against specific epitopes of cellular antigens. The technique that is usually used in immunophenotyping is flow cytometry. It has a limited role in the diagnosis of CML. It is mainly used in identifying CML blast transformation.

LAP score: Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase(LAP) score is decreased in cases of CML. It is only a first-line test in the diagnosis of CML and the diagnosis needs to be confirmed by other tests including bone marrow biopsy, molecular diagnostics, and cytogenetic analysis.
questions.learning: FISH and PCR — The clinical presentation with fatigue, splenomegaly, and the peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A skeletal muscle biopsy is examined under an electron microscope before and during contraction. As actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, which of the following changes is expected in the sarcomere?
options: A band shortens while the I band remains unchanged
H zone and I band decrease in length, while the A band remains constant
A band decreases in length, while the H zone remains unchanged
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. H zone and I band decrease in length, while the A band remains constant

According to the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction occurs because thin (actin) filaments slide inward over thick (myosin) filaments. The filaments themselves do not shorten; instead, the degree of overlap between them increases.

As contraction occurs:

• H zone decreases or disappears because the region containing only myosin becomes smaller.
• I band decreases because the region containing only actin shortens.
• A band remains constant because the length of the myosin thick filament does not change.
• Z lines move closer together, resulting in shortening of the sarcomere.

Why not the other options?

• A. A band shortens while the I band remains unchanged: Incorrect. The A band remains constant, while the I band shortens.
• B. H zone and I band decrease in length, while the A band remains constant✅: Correct.
• C. A band decreases in length, while the H zone remains unchanged: Incorrect. The opposite occurs: A band remains unchanged, whereas the H zone decreases.
• D. Z lines move farther apart: Incorrect. During contraction, Z lines move closer together, shortening the sarcomere.
questions.learning: H zone and I band decrease in length, while the — A band remains constant According to the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction occurs because thin (actin) filaments slide inward over thick (myosin) filaments.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Acute liver failure is a clinical feature of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Amanita phalloides, commonly known as the "death cap" mushroom, is a highly toxic fungus. Its primary toxins, amatoxins, are potent inhibitors of RNA polymerase II, which stops protein synthesis in cells. This leads to severe, irreversible tissue damage, with the liver being the primary target due to high metabolic activity and first-pass exposure. Acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis) is the classic and often fatal clinical feature of this poisoning. Organophosphate (OP) poisoning (Option A) causes a cholinergic crisis but not primary liver failure. Belladonna (Option C) leads to an anticholinergic syndrome. Morphine (Option D) causes opioid toxicity (respiratory depression/coma). Mushroom poisoning often starts with a latent period, followed by severe gastrointestinal symptoms, and finally catastrophic hepatic and renal failure. There is no specific antidote for amatoxins, making early recognition and supportive care, including potential liver transplantation, the only management options
questions.learning: Amanita phalloides, commonly known as the "death cap" mushroom, is a highly toxic fungus. Its primary toxins, amatoxins, are potent inhibitors of RNA polymerase II, which stops protein synthesis in cells.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not included in MMR?
questions.explanation: The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) tracks the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management. Direct obstetric causes, such as death due to preeclampsia (Option B) or complications of an ectopic pregnancy (Option C), are included. Similarly, a death on the 14th day postpartum (Option D) falls well within the 42-day window and is included if it resulted from obstetric causes. However, deaths resulting from accidental or incidental causes, such as a Road Traffic Accident (RTA) (Option A), are not included in the calculation of MMR. MMR is a key indicator of a nation's reproductive health status and the quality of its obstetric care system. India has made significant progress in reducing its MMR through improved access to institutional deliveries and high-quality antenatal care
questions.learning: The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) tracks the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which organization should an official refer to for complete and regularly updated demographic data that includes records of vital events?
questions.explanation: The Sample Registration System (SRS) is the organization an official should refer to for complete and regularly updated demographic data including records of vital events. SRS provides continuous and reliable data on vital events through its dual record system combining continuous enumeration and periodic retrospective surveys. Why other options are wrong: (A) AIIMS is incorrect because AIIMS is purely a medical research and teaching institution with no mandate for maintaining national demographic databases or vital event registration systems. (B) National Sample Survey is incorrect because NSSO conducts broader socioeconomic surveys covering morbidity, family planning, health expenditure etc. It does not specifically focus on continuously updated demographic data and vital event registration. (D) Central Bureau of Health is incorrect because CBHI primarily compiles and publishes health statistics sourced from other agencies rather than independently maintaining continuous vital event registration systems at national level
questions.learning: The Sample Registration System (SRS) is the organization an official should refer to for complete and regularly updated demographic data including records of vital events.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An unknown disease of suspected infectious origin has come up in your town. As a microbiologist, you collect the relevant samples and detect the etiological cause. Which of the following types of PCR would you do?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Multiplex PCR

Multiplex PCR can be used to identify an unknown infectious agent.

Types of PCR:

* Multiplex PCR: Primers to more than one pathogen are used simultaneously and hence multiple products are obtained.

* Nested PCR: It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. The first primer set is used for amplification and the amplicon obtained is then used as a target sequence for second amplification. This ensures specificity. Used in GeneXpert to detect Mycobacterium TB and resistance to rifampicin.

* Quantitative PCR: Apart from just detecting the target sequences, it also tells the number of such target sequences. We can quantify the HIV viral load with this technique.

* Reverse transcriptase PCR: The enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complimentary copy of DNA (cDNA) from RNA and this cDNA is then used as a template for PCR. Unlike conventional PCR which can only amplify DNA, this one can even amplify RNA. It is used to detect H1N1 from the Nasopharyngeal swab.

* Real-time PCR: This helps quantify the PCR and gives an estimate of the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. It uses fluorescent dyes or specific DNA probes. It is also known as qPCR (Quantitative PCR).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Efferent arteriolar constriction causes all except:
options: Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries
Increases hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries

Efferent arteriolar constriction increases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries.

Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic response on GFR depending on the severity of resistance.

Moderate efferent arteriolar constriction causes increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure and slightly increased GFR.

However, in cases of severe efferent arteriolar constriction (more than threefold increase in efferent arteriolar resistance), the renal blood flow is significantly reduced. This results in increased plasma protein concentration, thereby increasing the glomerular colloid oncotic pressure. As the increase in colloid oncotic pressure exceeds the increase in hydrostatic pressure, the net force for filtration decreases, resulting in decreased GFR.
questions.learning: Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries Efferent arteriolar constriction increases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries. Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic response on GFR depending on the severity of resistance.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old female with 6 years of infertility, has a BMI of 33 and facial hair. Investigations reveal she has (PCOS) and spills from bilateral tubes. She and her husband are trying to conceive, what would be the best plan of management for this lady?
options: Weight loss + Metformin + induction of ovulation with urinary gonadotrophins
Weight loss + folic acid, Try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction of ovulation
Weight loss + Metformin + Induction of ovulation with clomiphene
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Weight loss + folic acid, Try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction of ovulation

In the given clinical scenario the most appropriate management would be weight loss + folic acid, try for spontaneous induction, if failed move to induction of ovulation. In obese PCOS patients, even modest weight loss (5% of body weight) can help in the restoration of ovulatory cycles in some cases. Hence spontaneous induction is tried. Folic acid is normally administered as prophylaxis before conception to prevent neural tube defects.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)/ Polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD)/ Stein-Leventhal syndrome is a multisystem disorder. It involves metabolic and endocrine dysfunctions that commonly occur among women in the reproductive age group. It has multifactorial causation, such as lifestyle changes, stress, diet, obesity, and hyperinsulinemic states.

Important clinical features of PCOS are Menstrual abnormalities (70%) - oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, obesity, hirsutism, acne, and alopecia due to hyperandrogenism, acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance, and infertility.

Rotterdam criterion is used to diagnose PCOS. The presence of any two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis of PCOS.

•  Oligo/ amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility
• Hirsutism/ acne
• Ultrasound findings-

•

Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mL

•

12 or more small follicles each of 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally.

Investigations

• Hormonal studies
• USG is diagnostic of PCOS - it shows enlarged ovaries with multiple follicles in the periphery. It also rules out other pathologies like ovarian tumors, endometrial hyperplasia.
• Laparoscopy (therapeutic). It reveals bilateral enlarged ovarian cysts.

The ultrasound image below shows an enlarged ovary with multiple follicles in the periphery.

Management of PCOD is individualized. Weight reduction and lifestyle changes are the first-line therapy for PCOD. Oral contraceptive pills (OCP), preferably fourth-generation pills with 30 mcg E2 and 2-3 mg drospirenone are used to treat menstrual abnormalities. Hirsutism and acne are managed with OCP with cyproterone acetate and topical agents such as epiornithine, clindamycin lotion 1%, erythromycin gel 2%, and isotretinoin.

Patients with PCOD are more prone to developing insulin resistance which can be controlled with metformin(Option A, C and D) and acarbose. Patients presenting with infertility are treated by inducing ovulation using clomiphene as a first-line drug, along with dexamethasone and letrozole.

Surgical management includes laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary.

Note:

PCOS in association with diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular disease presenting in reproductive age group is known as "X syndrome".

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly woman underwent surgical resection of her bowel. After a few months, she presents with easy fatiguability and tiredness. Blood smear evaluation shows macrocytic anemia. Resection of all the following can cause this, except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Duodenum

The given clinical vignette indicates a diagnosis of macrocytic anemia due to either vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) and/or vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency. The resection of the duodenum is least likely to cause this condition.

The duodenum is involved in iron absorption and hence its resection causes iron deficiency anemia which shows a microcytic hypochromic picture on peripheral blood smear.

The stomach and ileum are involved in the absorption of vitamin B12, and the jejunum is mainly used in folic acid absorption. Hence, a resection of these segments will result in a deficiency of the vitamins which in turn causes megaloblastic anemia with a peripheral smear showing macro-ovalocytes and a hypersegmented neutrophil.

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin), is a water-soluble vitamin derived from animal products such as red meat, dairy, and eggs. Absorption of vitamin B12 begins when pepsin in the stomach releases vitamin B12 from the binding proteins in the food. The released B12 binds to haptocorrin (R-factor), which is a salivary protein. In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases release B12 from haptocorrin, which then binds to intrinsic factors to form the IF- B12 complex. Intrinsic factor (IF) is a glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach. In the terminal ileum, this complex is absorbed by the enterocytes.

Pernicious anemia is a specific form of megaloblastic anemia caused by autoimmune gastritis. It is due to impaired production of the intrinsic factor from the parietal cells.It is a common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency. The other causes of vitamin B12 deficiency are gastrectomy, gastric bypass surgery, inflammatory bowel disease, pancreatic insufficiency and so on.

Vitamin B9 (folate) is a water-soluble vitamin, and its active form is tetrahydrofolate (THFA). They are mainly derived from liver, yeast, spinach, other greens, and nuts. Its deficiency results in megaloblastic anemia, homocysteinemia, and neural tube defects (spina bifida, Anencephaly) in the fetus.

Absorption of vitamin B9 is mainly from the upper small intestine, specifically the proximal jejunum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which filter is used in a colposcope?
questions.explanation: A colposcope is a specialized low-power microscope used to examine the cervix. A fundamental component of a colposcopic examination is the use of the green filter (Option C). The green filter (or blue-green filter) is specifically used to enhance the visualization of vascular patterns. It works by making red structures like blood vessels appear dark or black, providing sharp contrast against the surrounding lighter-colored epithelium. This is critical for identifying "atypical vessels," punctation, and mosaicism, which are hallmarks of high-grade cervical dysplasia and invasive cancer. Black (Option A), Red (Option B), and Yellow (Option D) filters do not provide this specific vascular contrast and are not standard components of the colposcopic diagnostic procedure. Therefore, the green filter is the definitive answer for the tool used to increase diagnostic accuracy during a colposcopy. Mastering its use is essential for any practitioner involved in cervical cancer screening and management

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding STEP criteria of drugs?
options: It is related to the various steps in clinical trial.
It lists out steps of drug metabolism
It helps to calculate volume of distribution of drugs
It helps to choose P drugs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It helps to choose P drugs

STEP criteria is mainly used to select P drugs.

P drugs or Physician's drugs or Personal drugs are those drugs that a physician is very familiar with and routinely prescribes for a specific disease. This concept includes the name, dosage form, schedule, and duration for a specific illness.

STEP here stands for

* Safety of the drug

* Tolerability of the drug

* Efficacy of the drug

* Price of the drug

Selecting P drugs

*  Define the diagnosis

*  Specify the therapeutic objective

*  Make an inventory of effective groups of drugs

*  Choose an effective group according to criteria

*  Choose a P-drug

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following tests would a surgeon advise first in a patient with a large thyroid swelling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroid function tests

Assessing the biochemical function of the thyroid i.e. thyroid function test (TFT) is the first investigation done in any thyroid condition.

Evaluation of any thyroid disease should begin with the assessment of TSH, T3, and T4. TSH is the only test necessary in most patients with thyroid nodules that clinically appear to be euthyroid.

If a discrete swelling is associated with hyperthyroidism, it indicates a toxic adenoma. This is followed by an ultrasound of the neck or radioiodine uptake. Findings in thyroid swelling associated with thyroid neoplasia include microcalcification and increased vascularity. FNAC should be used under ultrasound guidance, on all nodules that fall outside a fully benign category.

Modalities for evaluation of thyroid swelling include:

* Laboratory evaluation

* TSH

* T3

* T4

* Thyroid imaging

* Ultrasound

* Radioisotope scanning

* CT/MRI

* Biopsy techniques

* Fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNA)

* Tru-cut/core-needle biopsy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which cranial nerve provides sensory innervation to the orbit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trigeminal nerve

The sensory innervation of the orbit is provided by the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

• Trigeminal nerve (CN V) → main sensory nerve of the face

• Ophthalmic division (V1) supplies:

• Cornea (highly sensitive)
• Conjunctiva
• Eyelids
• Lacrimal gland
• Orbit and surrounding structures

Important branches of V1:

• Nasociliary nerve → corneal sensation (afferent limb of corneal reflex)
• Frontal nerve
• Lacrimal nerve

Why not others:

• Vagus nerve (CN X): Visceral functions, no orbital sensory role
• Oculomotor nerve (CN III): Motor to extraocular muscles + parasympathetic to pupil
• Facial nerve (CN VII): Motor to facial muscles; lacrimation (parasympathetic), but no sensory supply to orbit

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about heat exhaustion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of thermoregulatory mechanism

Heat exhaustion is due to fluid and electrolyte depletion with intact thermoregulation, making option A (loss of thermoregulatory mechanism) incorrect.

• Core temperature: Usually < 40°C (104–105°F)
• Mechanism: Thermoregulatory system is still functioning (sweating present)
• Clinical features:

• Profuse sweating
• Orthostatic hypotension
• Weakness, dizziness
• May have mild confusion but no severe CNS dysfunction

Differentiation from heat stroke:

• Heat exhaustion:

• Thermoregulation intact
• Sweating present
• Mild/no altered consciousness

• Heat stroke:

• Failure of thermoregulation
• Core temp > 40°C
• Severe CNS symptoms (delirium, coma)
• Often dry skin

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The railway police has brought a person with suspected poisoning. On examination, he was confused with slurred speech, hot skin, dry mouth, and dilated pupils. What is the probable poisoning?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Datura

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Datura poisoning.

Datura has two main types: Datura alba with white flowers and Datura nigra with purple flowers. The fruit is spiny and contains many small, yellowish-brown seeds. All parts of the plant are toxic, especially the seeds and fruits. Datura contains alkaloids like atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine, which are potent anticholinergic agents. They block muscarinic receptors both peripherally and centrally, resulting in the classical anticholinergic toxidrome.

This typical presentation is seen in children who accidentally ingest datura seeds, especially from roadside or railway plants, where datura often grows wild—hence known as "railway poison". Signs of poisoning include 8 D's:

* Dryness of mouth

* Dysphagia

* Dilated pupils

* Drunken gait

* Delirium

* Dry-hot skin

* Drowsiness

* Death due to respiratory failure.

Gastric emptying is often delayed, and the small, plentiful seeds can become trapped among the gastrointestinal folds after ingestion. Thus gastric decontamination can be an important therapy.

Physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist, is an effective treatment for severe anticholinergic poisoning.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient is told about the benefits and complications of hysterectomy and she agrees to the procedure. What kind of consent is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Informed consent

This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

Informed consent is one given by the patient after understanding the nature of the condition, proposed treatment, outcomes of the recommended treatment, alternative options to treatment, and the risks and benefits involved. The patient can accept or reject the procedure. This is also called the rule of full disclosure.

Consent refers to a voluntary agreement, compliance, or permission. It can be expressed or implied.

Implied consent (option B) is that which is not written or expressly stated. It is implied that the patient is giving consent to examination in a general sense. For example, when a patient visits the hospital with an illness, it implies that he has given consent to a physical examination to find out the nature of his illness. Another example of implied consent is when a patient exposes his arm for injection. It is legally effective.

Expressed consent can be oral or written and refers to consent in which the terms are clearly stated in distinct and explicit language.

Opt out (Option C) refers to a patient's refusal of the procedure, test, or treatment. It is the physician's duty to disclose the risks or consequences of refusal adequately and appropriately to the patient.

Passive consent (Option D) is not commonly described. However, in regard to research, it refers to parents signing and returning a form if they do not want to allow their child to participate in research.
questions.learning: Informed consent — This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: While doing a lumbar puncture, the following structures are pierced: 1. Ligamentum flavum 2. Supraspinous ligament 3. Interspinous ligament 4. Dura mater 5. Arachnoid mater 6. Epidural space 7. Subdural space Arrange them in the sequence in which they are pierced.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2–3–1–6–4–7–5

Lumbar puncture is performed by advancing the needle through the midline structures of the lumbar spine until it reaches the subarachnoid space to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Knowledge of the anatomical layers traversed is essential for safe and accurate needle placement.

The structures are pierced in the following sequence:

1. Supraspinous ligament
2. Interspinous ligament
3. Ligamentum flavum
4. Epidural space
5. Dura mater
6. Subdural space (potential space)
7. Arachnoid mater → Needle enters the subarachnoid space containing CSF.

Hence, the correct sequence is: 2 → 3 → 1 → 6 → 4 → 7 → 5

Why not the other options?

• The other sequences incorrectly place the arachnoid before the dura, omit the epidural space, or reverse the order of the ligaments.
questions.learning: 2–3–1–6–4–7–5 Lumbar puncture is performed by advancing the needle through the midline structures of the lumbar spine until it reaches the subarachnoid space to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Pacemaker generating the rhythm for breathing is ________
options: Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pre-Bőtzinger complex

Pre-Botzinger complex generates the rhythm for automated breathing.

• These are also known as pacemaker cells located in the medulla.
• These are the first set of neurons that initiate inspiration.
• These neurons discharge rhythmically, and they produce rhythmic discharges in the phrenic motor neurons.

Breathing is under the control of both the following:

• Voluntary control: Located in the cerebral cortex (via corticospinal tract)
• Automatic control: Driven by pacemaker cells in the medulla (Pre-Botzinger complex). These activate motor neurons via cervical (Phrenic nerve innervating diaphragm) and thoracic spinal cord (external intercostal muscle).

There is a reciprocal innervation to expiratory and inspiratory muscles in that motor neurons supplying expiratory muscles are inactive when motor neurons supplying inspiratory muscles are active, and vice versa.

Inspiration

Initiation
Pre-Botzinger complex (Pacemaker cells) in Medulla

Maintenance
Apneustic center in lower Pons stimulates Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla

Termination
Apneustic center inhibited by Vagus and Pneumotaxic center

Regulation of expiration: During quiet breathing, expiration is a passive process; there is no firing of neurons. Ventral respiratory group of neurons are involved in forceful expiration like during exercise.

Mnemonic DIVE: Dorsal respiratory group for Inspiration and Ventral respiratory group for Expiration.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Where is the electrode placed in cochlear implant procedures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Scala tympani

The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani. It allows for the electrodes to be in close proximity to the ganglion cells and their dendrites which are located in the modiolus and bony spiral lamina of the cochlea.

A cochlear implant is an electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from a hearing aid. It converts sound to an electrical signal (transduction) and delivers this to the auditory nerve. Prerequisites include an intact cochlear nerve and higher auditory pathway.

In the auditory brainstem implant, the site of the implant is the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle. It is used when the cochlear nerve is not intact.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Under which one of the following conditions, the HPA axis suppression is likely to result in crisis due to adrenal insufficiency following withdrawal of glucocorticoids?
options: If glucocorticoids have been given by intravenous route for five days
If glucocorticoids have been administered orally for one week
If glucocorticoids have been prescribed repeatedly for short courses within the previous year
If the dose is less than equivalent of 5 mg prednisolone per day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. If glucocorticoids have been prescribed repeatedly for short courses within the previous year

Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis suppression occurs when exogenous glucocorticoids suppress endogenous CRH → ACTH → cortisol production. Abrupt withdrawal in patients with significant suppression can precipitate adrenal insufficiency or adrenal crisis, especially during physiological stress.

Repeated short courses of glucocorticoids within the previous year can cumulatively suppress the HPA axis. Even if each course is brief, repeated exposure may impair adrenal responsiveness, increasing the risk of adrenal crisis after withdrawal.

Factors Increasing Risk of HPA Axis Suppression

• Long duration of glucocorticoid therapy (>3–4 weeks)
• High-dose glucocorticoid therapy
• Evening/night-time dosing
• Repeated courses of systemic steroids
• Recent glucocorticoid exposure within the previous year

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. IV glucocorticoids for 5 days → Usually insufficient to cause significant HPA suppression.
• B. Oral glucocorticoids for 1 week → Generally do not cause clinically significant adrenal suppression.
• D. <5 mg prednisolone/day → Considered a physiologic or low dose with minimal risk of HPA axis suppression.
questions.learning: If glucocorticoids have been prescribed repeatedly for short courses within the previous year Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis suppression occurs when exogenous glucocorticoids suppress endogenous CRH → ACTH → cortisol production.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is most likely to be released from the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hexokinase IV

Hexokinase type IV/ glucokinase is most likely to be released from the hypothalamus (ventromedial hypothalamus)

Glucokinase, also known as hexokinase IV, catalyses the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, which constitutes the first step of glycolysis.

The hypothalamus is an important centre for the regulation of glucose homeostasis. It contains glucokinase/hexokinase IV which plays a central role in the counterregulatory response, which is a feedback system to counteract hypoglycemia by increasing the production of glucose and limiting its utilization.

There are four isoforms of hexokinase:

* Hexokinase type I: major isoform in the brain but also ubiquitously expressed

* Hexokinase type II: predominant in insulin-sensitive tissues such as adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and cardiac muscle.

* Hexokinase type III: not predominant in any tissue.

* Hexokinase type IV: primarily in the liver, pancreas, hypothalamus, small intestine and other neuroendocrine tissue.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A lady who is 38 weeks pregnant comes to the OPD for a routine checkup. She has a history of normal twin delivery at term 4 years ago. What is her gravida and para score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. G2P1

The woman has had two pregnancies in total - the previous twin pregnancy and the current pregnancy, hence the gravida score is 2. The first pregnancy resulted in delivery at term (crossed viable period), hence her para score is 1 (parity doesn't include current pregnancy).  Hence, her obstetric score would be G2P1 (Gravida - 2, Para - 1).

Multifetal pregnancies count as one for both gravida and para. A pregnant woman who delivers twins for the first time is expressed as primipara.

The obstetric score is used to summarise the past obstetric history as follows:

• G - Gravidity, denoting the total number of pregnancies, including the present one
• P - Parity, denoting the total number of pregnancies crossing the period of viability. This includes both live births and stillbirths. The current pregnancy is not included.
• A - Abortion is the termination of pregnancy, either spontaneous or induced, before fetal viability.
• L - Living children.

The GTPAL system includes the following:

• Gravida
• Term (>37 weeks)
• Preterm (20w - 36w 6d)
• Abortions (<20 weeks)
• Number of living children

Note: The period of viability is when the fetus is capable of independent existence. The WHO defines it to be 24 weeks while the Indian definition is 28 weeks.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the role of caffeine in wakefulness?
options: Blocks adenosine action and causes wakefulness
Activates locus coeruleus and cause wakefulness
No role in maintaining wakefulness if taken 1hr before sleep
Activates histamine release and prevents sleep
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blocks adenosine action and causes wakefulness

Caffeine = adenosine receptor antagonist → removes “sleep pressure” → promotes wakefulness

Caffeine promotes wakefulness by blocking adenosine receptors, particularly A₁ and A₂A, in the brain. Adenosine normally accumulates during wakefulness and induces sleepiness; its blockade reduces sleep drive.

Thus, caffeine causes increased alertness and delayed sleep onset.

| Time awake | Adenosine level | Effect

| ---------- | --------------- | ------

| Morning | Low | Alert

| Afternoon | Moderate | Slight fatigue

| Night | High | Sleep drive ↑

Caffeine does NOT reduce adenosine, it just blocks its effect

| Neurotransmitter | Source | Role

| ---------------- | ------ | ----

| Adenosine | ATP metabolism | Promotes sleep

| Norepinephrine | Locus coeruleus | Arousal

| Histamine | Tuberomammillary nucleus | Wakefulness

| Dopamine | VTA | Alertness

| Orexin | Hypothalamus | Stabilizes wakefulness

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with secondary amenorrhea for 9 months and infertility. She has a history of dilatation and curettage, with both the progesterone and estrogen-progesterone challenge tests negative and normal LH and FSH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis? PCOS - Polycystic ovarian syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Asherman syndrome

A history of dilatation and curettage followed by secondary amenorrhea and infertility, in the presence of normal LH and FSH levels and negative progesterone as well as estrogen-progesterone challenge tests, is highly indicative of Asherman’s syndrome.

Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of uterine synechiae, due to the destruction of the endometrium. It can occur as a result of trauma to the endometrium following vigorous curettages for elective abortion, tuberculous endometritis, and uterine surgeries. Depending on the degree of scarring, patients may have amenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, or recurrent pregnancy loss because of inadequate placentation.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is used to evaluate the uterine cavity and tubal patency, where intrauterine adhesions typically appear as irregular, angulated filling defects with a characteristic “moth-eaten” appearance. The gold standard for definitive diagnosis and treatment is hysteroscopy, with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis being the preferred surgical approach.

Hormonal assays also aid in the diagnosis of Asherman syndrome. All women with amenorrhea in the reproductive age group are considered pregnant unless proven otherwise by negative urinary or serum β-HCG levels. Once negative for pregnancy, further testing is done by a progesterone challenge test.

This test is done by administering medroxyprogesterone acetate as a 10-mg daily oral dose for 10 days. If the woman bleeds, then she is assumed to produce estrogen and to have a developed endometrium, and the presence of a patent outflow tract is confirmed. If she does not bleed, then she is given estrogen followed by progesterone treatment in the form of combined OCPs. If she fails to bleed after completing the 21 hormone-containing pills, then an anatomic abnormality is diagnosed such as Asherman syndrome.

Below is the HSG showing moth-eaten appearance in asherman syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Sheehan's syndrome/ pituitary apoplexy is hemorrhagic infarction of large pituitary adenomas or pituitary infarction due to traumatic major blood loss. If this blood loss occurs during delivery, it's called Sheehan's syndrome. Affected women may present with panhypopituitarism and may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to the deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to the deficiency of gonadotropins).

Option B: PCOS is a multisystem, metabolic, endocrine dysfunction that commonly occurs among women in the reproductive age group. LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls. Estrone(E1) levels are elevated but estradiol level in PCOS is low in comparison to Estrone (E1).

Option C: Premature Ovarian failure or premature menopause is the development of menopause before the age of 40 years. It is diagnosed when at least 2 serum FSH levels are elevated (>40 mIU/l) when measured at least 1 month apart in a woman <40 years. The other findings consistent with POF include low estradiol and an elevated FSH/LH ratio.

Condition

Lab markers

1. Sheehan's syndrome

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Spread of prostate cancer to lumbar vertebra is via?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer characteristically metastasizes to the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis through venous spread. This occurs via Batson’s venous plexus, which is a system of valveless veins connecting the prostatic venous plexus to the internal vertebral venous system. Because these veins lack valves, changes in intra-abdominal pressure can cause retrograde blood flow, allowing malignant cells to travel directly from the prostate to the spine. Regarding the distractors, arterial spread (Option A) is less common and usually occurs late in the disease. Local spread (Option B) involves direct invasion of the bladder or seminal vesicles. Lymphatic spread (Option C) primarily affects the pelvic lymph nodes, such as the obturator and internal iliac nodes. Therefore, the unique valveless venous communication is the primary anatomical route responsible for the classic osteoblastic vertebral metastases seen in prostate cancer patients

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the duration of abstinence post vasectomy?
questions.explanation: Post-vasectomy, a man is not considered sterile until all stored sperm in the reproductive tract are cleared. The standard medical advice is to use alternative contraception or practice abstinence for a duration of 3 months. This timeframe typically corresponds to roughly 20 ejaculations, which is the volume required to flush out remaining viable sperm. Confirmation of success must be obtained via a semen analysis showing zero sperm count before discontinuing protection. Options B (7 months), C (8 months), and D (5 months) are all significantly longer than the standard 12-week guideline. While individual clearance rates can vary, 3 months is the universally accepted clinical benchmark for initial follow-up testing. Relying on the procedure immediately after surgery can lead to unwanted pregnancy, making the 3-month buffer period critical for patient safety
questions.learning: Post-vasectomy, a man is not considered sterile until all stored sperm in the reproductive tract are cleared. The standard medical advice is to use alternative contraception or practice abstinence for a duration of 3 months.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness, and episodes of syncope. On examination, the pulse is irregularly irregular. What finding is most likely to be observed on jugular venous pressure (JVP) examination?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of an irregularly irregular pulse in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of atrial fibrillation (AF), often referred to as "Holiday Heart Syndrome" in this context. The jugular venous pulse (JVP) reflects pressure changes in the right atrium; specifically, the 'a' wave is produced by active atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract effectively in a coordinated manner; instead, they undergo rapid, disorganized electrical activity. Consequently, there is a complete loss of the organized atrial systole required to produce the 'a' wave, leading to its disappearance on the JVP tracing. Large 'a' waves (Option B) occur during resistance to atrial emptying, such as in tricuspid stenosis. Cannon 'a' waves (Option C) are seen when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block. A steep 'y' descent (Option D) is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis. Thus, the absent 'a' wave is the definitive JVP finding for AF
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of an irregularly irregular pulse in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of atrial fibrillation (AF), often referred to as "Holiday Heart Syndrome" in this context.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after choking on a bone while eating. He is conscious but unable to speak. What should be the immediate next step in management?
options: Deliver 5 back slaps and 5 chest compressions
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits a complete airway obstruction, indicated by the inability to speak or cough while remaining responsive. For a responsive adult or adolescent with a foreign body airway obstruction, the "Heimlich maneuver" (subdiaphragmatic abdominal thrusts) is the recommended immediate intervention to expel the object. Back slaps and chest compressions (Option A) are used for infants under one year of age, not adults. Endoscopic removal (Option B) is a definitive treatment for objects in the esophagus or bronchus but is not the first-line emergency step for a choking patient in respiratory distress. Bag and mask ventilation (Option C) will not work because the airway is mechanically blocked; it may actually push the object deeper. If the patient becomes unresponsive, the provider should start CPR, beginning with chest compressions, to relieve the obstruction

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the name of the pregnancy test kit introduced by the Indian government?
questions.explanation: The Indian government introduced the NISHCHAY kit to provide accessible and reliable pregnancy testing at the community level, primarily through ASHA workers. This initiative aims to ensure early detection of pregnancy, facilitating timely antenatal care and informed reproductive choices. It is a simple urine-based test kit. Understanding the distractors is crucial for public health literacy: NIKSHAY (Option B) is the unified ICT portal for Tuberculosis (TB) patient management and tracking in India. NIKUSTH (Option C) is a similar digital platform specifically designed for the surveillance and management of Leprosy cases. AXSHYA (Option D) refers to a civil society project aimed at improving the reach and quality of TB services. Therefore, while these programs are all vital components of India's health infrastructure, NISHCHAY is the only one dedicated to pregnancy diagnosis. This kit plays a significant role in reducing maternal mortality by bringing diagnostic services directly to the doorsteps of rural and underserved populations
questions.learning: The Indian government introduced the NISHCHAY kit to provide accessible and reliable pregnancy testing at the community level, primarily through ASHA workers.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Lignocaine is used in a loading dose for the treatment of arrhythmias. The loading dose of this drug depends upon which of the following factors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Volume of distribution

Goal: Achieve target plasma concentration

↓

Drug distributes in body compartments

↓

Extent depends on Vd

↓

Higher Vd → higher loading dose

Loading dose is determined by the amount of drug needed to rapidly achieve the target plasma concentration. It depends primarily on the volume of distribution, which reflects how extensively the drug distributes into tissues. Clearance and half-life influence maintenance dosing, not the loading dose. Hence Vd is the key determinant.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with a fever of 38.5°C and retinal spots noted on fundoscopic examination. His complete blood count shows leukocytosis (20,000/cu mm), and blood cultures have been sent. With infective endocarditis suspected, how many minor Duke’s criteria are fulfilled in this case?
questions.explanation: The Modified Duke Criteria are used to diagnose Infective Endocarditis (IE). In this patient, three minor criteria are clearly satisfied based on the provided information: 1. Predisposition: The patient is an intravenous (IV) drug user, which is a significant predisposing factor for IE. 2. Fever: The documented temperature of meets the threshold for a minor criterion. 3. Immunological Phenomena: The "spots noted over the fundus" are classic Roth spots, which are classified as an immunological phenomenon under the Duke criteria. The elevated leukocyte count (leukocytosis) and suspected IE are clinical clues but do not themselves constitute specific Duke criteria. Major criteria would require positive blood cultures (with typical organisms) or echocardiographic evidence of vegetation. Since the patient currently meets three minor criteria, the diagnosis is "Possible IE" (requires 1 major + 1 minor OR 3 minor). He does not meet the "Definite IE" threshold yet (requires 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor). Thus, exactly three minor criteria are satisfied at this stage

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the appropriate treatment for cryptorchidism (undescended testis)?
options: Manually bringing the testis down to the bottom of the scrotum
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism is the most common congenital anomaly of the male genitalia. While surgical orchidopexy is the definitive gold standard for management (ideally performed by age 1), hormonal therapy is sometimes used as a preliminary or adjunctive measure. GnRH analogues (Option A) or human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) can be administered to stimulate endogenous testosterone production, which may encourage the descent of a "high scrotal" or "inguinal" testis. However, the success rate for hormonal therapy is generally low, around 10-20%. Testosterone (Option B) is not the primary hormonal treatment. Cold compressions (Option C) have no therapeutic role and may actually cause reflex retraction of the testis. "Manually bringing the testis down" (Option D) describes the diagnosis of a "retractile testis," which is a normal variant that does not require treatment, rather than a management strategy for true cryptorchidism. When hormonal therapy fails, surgical intervention is mandatory to preserve germ cell function and allow for cancer screening
questions.learning: Cryptorchidism is the most common congenital anomaly of the male genitalia. While surgical orchidopexy is the definitive gold standard for management (ideally performed by age 1), hormonal therapy is sometimes used as a preliminary or adjunctive measure.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 58-year-old female patient presents with a pathological fracture of the hip and femur. Her serum calcium and phosphate are increased. DEXA scan confirms decreased bone density. Which of the following parameters will increase in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tartrate resistant acid phosphatase

In this patient, the pathological fracture and elevated serum calcium and phosphate suggest a possible metabolic bone disease such as Paget’s disease of bone. The parameter likely to be increased is TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase), which is a marker of osteoclast activity.

TRAP is an enzyme produced by osteoclasts, which are cells responsible for bone resorption. Elevated levels of TRAP are often seen in conditions with increased bone turnover, such as Paget’s disease, hyperparathyroidism, and certain bone malignancies.
questions.learning: Tartrate resistant acid phosphatase — In this patient, the pathological fracture and elevated serum calcium and phosphate suggest a possible metabolic bone disease such as Paget’s disease of bone.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Perioperative benefit from transfusion is with a haemoglobin level of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6–8 g/dL

Current perioperative transfusion practice follows a restrictive transfusion strategy. Patients with hemoglobin <6 g/dL almost always require transfusion, while those with Hb 6–8 g/dL are the group most likely to benefit, depending on symptoms, ongoing blood loss, and comorbidities.

Why not the other options?

• A. <6 g/dL: Transfusion is generally mandatory, not merely a range where benefit is assessed.
• C. 8–10 g/dL: Routine transfusion is not recommended; consider only in selected high-risk patients.
• D. >10 g/dL: Transfusion is generally not indicated.
questions.learning: 6–8 g/dL Current perioperative transfusion practice follows a restrictive transfusion strategy. Patients with hemoglobin 10 g/dL: Transfusion is generally not indicated.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A posterior staphyloma was observed on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia (outpouching) of the posterior sclera. It is most commonly seen in pathological or high myopia. Progressive elongation of the globe in myopia leads to mechanical stretching and thinning of the posterior pole, resulting in this structural deformity. Hypermetropia (Option B) involves a shorter axial length and is not associated with scleral ectasia. Primary open-angle glaucoma (Option C) causes optic nerve cupping but not global scleral thinning. Retinitis pigmentosa (Option D) is characterized by "bone-spicule" pigmentation and vessel attenuation, not staphylomas. Therefore, posterior staphyloma is a hallmark diagnostic feature of degenerative high axial myopia
questions.learning: A posterior staphyloma is an ectasia (outpouching) of the posterior sclera. It is most commonly seen in pathological or high myopia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which one among the following terms best fits the description “the entire gamut of preventive, therapeutic and rehabilitative services for the protection of society from antisocial, criminal or deviant conduct of man”?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Social defence

Social defence refers to the entire range of preventive, therapeutic and rehabilitative measures aimed at protecting society from antisocial, criminal or deviant behaviour.

• A. Social delinquency: Refers to antisocial or delinquent behaviour itself.
• B. Social defence — Correct: Encompasses prevention, treatment and rehabilitation of individuals exhibiting antisocial or deviant behaviour.
• C. Social pathology: Study of social problems and dysfunctional social behaviour.
• D. Social survey: Systematic collection of information about a population or social group.
questions.learning: Social defence Social defence refers to the entire range of preventive, therapeutic and rehabilitative measures aimed at protecting society from antisocial, criminal or deviant behaviour. • A.

questions.text: Identify the heart chamber marked in the given CT image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left atrium

The structure marked in the above CT image is the left atrium.

Transverse CT images are to be observed from the foot end of the supine patient, as if we are sitting at the patient's feet. So the right-hand side of the observer corresponds to the left-hand side in the CT.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with easy fatigability, back pain, and radiological evidence of multiple lytic lesions in the skull. Bone marrow biopsy findings point toward a hematological malignancy. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of bone pain, "multiple lytic lesions" in the skull (punched-out lesions), and anemia (fatigability) in an older adult is classic for Multiple Myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by the malignant proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells. The provided bone marrow histology confirms this by showing a "sheet-like proliferation of plasma cells" with eccentric nuclei and a perinuclear halo (Hoff). CML (Option A) and CLL (Option B) are leukemias involving mature myeloid and lymphoid cells, respectively, and do not typically cause lytic bone lesions. Hairy cell leukemia (Option D) is characterized by splenomegaly and B-cells with hair-like projections, not bone destruction. Common laboratory findings in myeloma include the "M-spike" on serum protein electrophoresis, hypercalcemia, and renal insufficiency (the CRAB criteria). Treatment involves proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulators, and potentially autologous stem cell transplantation
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of bone pain, "multiple lytic lesions" in the skull (punched-out lesions), and anemia (fatigability) in an older adult is classic for Multiple Myeloma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following methods is not effective against preventing the spread of COVID 19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1% glutaraldehyde

1% glutaraldehyde is not effective against preventing the spread of COVID 19.

Effective everyday practices that prevent the spread include actions like keeping a social distance (at least 6 feet) from others, washing your hands with soap and water for 20 seconds or using a hand sanitizer with at least 70% alcohol, and wearing a face mask when you have to go out in public.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following can be prescribed in case of an open angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Latanoprost

Latanoprost can be given in a case of open-angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma.

Latanoprost is a PGF2α analog and it is not associated with systemic side effects like bronchospasm and hence can be given for asthmatic patients. Prostaglandin analogs are the first choice drugs for open-angle glaucoma.

Mechanism of action: It reduces intraocular pressure by altering the ciliary muscle tension and improving the outflow of the aqueous humor.

Advantages of latanoprost:

• Good efficacy
• Once-daily application
• Absence of systemic side effects

Disadvantage: High cost

Adverse effects:

• Blurring of vision
• Iris pigmentation
• Thickening and darkening of eyelashes
• Macular edema can occur especially in aphakic patients.

Other options:

Option A- Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker used topically in glaucoma. It is associated with systemic effects by absorption through the nasolacrimal duct and can cause life-threatening bronchospasm in asthmatics and COPD patients. Hence they are not given in in this case.

Option B- Gemeprost is a PGE1 analog used for the termination of early pregnancy.

Option D- Mannitol infusion is given for acute congestive glaucoma and not for open-angle glaucoma. It causes decongestion of the eye by its osmotic action.
questions.learning: Latanoprost Latanoprost can be given in a case of open-angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma. Latanoprost is a PGF2α analog and it is not associated with systemic side effects like bronchospasm and hence can be given for asthmatic patients.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy who was started on treatment for Burkitt lymphoma develops acute onset respiratory distress and decreased urine output. Investigations reveal: Hb 8 g/dL TLC 15000/mm³ Platelet count 1 lakh/mm³ Serum potassium 6.5 mEq/L Corrected serum calcium 6.7 mg/dL Serum creatinine 2 mg/dL The most important drug for emergency management is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rasburicase

This child has tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) following treatment of Burkitt lymphoma, a highly proliferative tumor with a high tumor burden.

The findings strongly support TLS:

• Hyperkalemia: K⁺ 6.5 mEq/L
• Hypocalcemia: corrected Ca²⁺ 6.7 mg/dL
• Acute kidney injury: creatinine 2 mg/dL
• Respiratory distress may result from severe metabolic disturbances/fluid overload.

Rasburicase rapidly converts uric acid → allantoin, which is much more soluble, thereby rapidly reducing uric acid and preventing/worsening uric acid nephropathy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Dexamethasone: Used in ALL/lymphoma treatment but does not provide the rapid metabolic correction required in established TLS.
• B. Broad-spectrum antibiotics: No evidence of bacterial sepsis is provided.
• D. Folinic acid rescue: Used to reduce methotrexate toxicity, not TLS.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a criteria for severe acute malnutrition?
options: Weight for height less than -3 SD
Weight for age less than -3 SD
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight for age less than -3 SD

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) according to the WHO criteria is the weight for height (not age) less than minus -3 SD.

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children of ages 6 to 59 months is defined by the WHO as any of the following:

• Weight-for-length (or height) below −3 SD of the WHO child growth standards
• Presence of bipedal edema
• Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) <11.5 cm.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not done before drawing blood for arterial blood gas analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flexion of wrist

Flexion of the wrist is not done just before drawing blood for ABG analysis.

During arterial blood gas analysis, the ideal position for drawing arterial blood from the radial artery is to maintain the wrist in extension. This provides stability to the artery and prevents it from slipping away during the puncture. To draw blood for ABG analysis, the skin is pierced at a 45° angle.

Allen's test is done prior to radial cannulation to identify the adequacy of radial and ulnar collateral blood flow to the hand.

The syringe used to draw blood for ABG analysis is rinsed with heparin prior to the procedure. Prior to collecting blood, 0.1 ml heparin is drawn into the syringe and then flushed out. The residue that lubricates the inner wall of the syringe is sufficient to prevent the blood from clotting.
questions.learning: Flexion of wrist Flexion of the wrist is not done just before drawing blood for ABG analysis. During arterial blood gas analysis, the ideal position for drawing arterial blood from the radial artery is to maintain the wrist in extension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A renal biopsy of a patient is shown below. Identify the cell marked in the given histological image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Macula Densa

The structure in the histological image is the macula densa cells in the distal convoluted tubule.

Specialized cells at the start of the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) form the macula densa. They detect sodium and chloride concentrations of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium and chloride, the macula densa cells trigger the contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing the flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate.

This happens as follows: When there is increased sodium, there is increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity which leads to increased ATP hydrolysis causing more adenosine formation. The adenosine receptors on the macula densa cells stimulate it to release more calcium, so that there is vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole, thereby decreasing the GFR.

Other options:

The given image constitutes the juxtaglomerular apparatus and has the following parts:

Option B: Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole.

Option C: Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole, they secrete renin. Fall in pressure in afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

Option D:  Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes (pedicels) as shown below.
questions.learning: Macula Densa — The structure in the histological image is the macula densa cells in the distal convoluted tubule. Specialized cells at the start of the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) form the macula densa.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the appropriate timing for taking a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 72 hours after delivery

The appropriate time for taking a blood sample to diagnose neonatal hypothyroidism is 72 hours after delivery.

After birth, there is a temporary elevation in TSH levels due to physiological neonatal surge, which remains elevated for the first 2-3 days of life. If sampling is done during this period, falsely elevated TSH values may be obtained. Therefore, the ideal time for sampling through a heel prick is after 72 hours of life.

Screening for children for congenital hypothyroidism is very important, as early diagnosis and treatment can help in normal intellectual development. Otherwise, congenital hypothyroidism is known as the most common preventable cause of mental retardation. Children diagnosed beyond the neonatal period have a poor outcome.

The most commonly used strategy is to screen for TSH first as that has have higher sensitivity compared to the T4-based approach. Although the TSH-based approach is better, it doesn't identify central hypothyroidism, which can be identified by the T4-first approach. However, the T4-based approach misses out on the cases of compensated hypothyroidism.

The incidence of congenital hypothyroidism seems to be 4 times higher in India compared to Western countries. Thyroid dysgenesis has emerged as the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism in India accounting for about 75% of all cases. Interestingly, an Increased incidence of thyroid dysgenesis is noted in Down syndrome.

Clinical features of hypothyroidism:

Congenital
Acquired

Open posterior fontanel
Growth retardation

Umbilical hernia
Delayed skeletal maturation

Characteristic edematous facies
Delayed dental development

Constipation
Delayed puberty

Pallor
Myopathy and pseudohypertrophy

Hypothermia
Enlarged sella

Large tongue
Pseudotumor cerebri

Rough dry skin

Hypotonia

Large abdomen

Management: Thyroid replacement soon after the diagnosis. Thyroxine of dose 10-15 μg/kg/day should be started and adjusted to achieve normal free T4 range. TSH may be elevated up to 2 years of age with reset of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
