questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old female patient underwent surgery on her middle ear and a nerve was injured intraoperatively. She came a week later to OPD with difficulty in closing her eyes on the same side. Ocular examination reveals decreased corneal sensation and dryness of the cornea. Which of the following cranial nerves was most likely injured during the surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VII

This patient with a past history of intra-op nerve injury during middle ear surgery presented with dry eye, decreased corneal sensation, and incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos) due to injury to cranial nerve (CN)VII.

Lagophthalmos can be caused by conditions such as facial nerve injury, parkinsonism (reduced muscle tone), lid scarring, and proptosis. The facial nerve runs horizontally in the medial wall and vertically in the posterior wall of the middle ear. Hence, they can be injured due to surgery of the middle ear.  Clinical features include dry eyes, decreased corneal sensation which can eventually lead to  mild punctate epithelial changes and epithelial breakdown.

CN VII lies in proximity to the middle ear. Hence there are chances of nerve injury during middle ear surgery.
The given image shows the course of the facial nerve within the middle ear cavity.

Treatment depends on whether the exposure is reversible or permanent. Reversible exposure can be treated with artificial tears and eye ointments. The eyelid can be taped closed at night or external barriers like bandage silicone hydrogel or scleral contact lenses can be used. Permanent exposure requires permanent tarsorrhaphy.

Other options:

Option B - CN IV palsy leads to paralysis of superior oblique muscles.

Option C - CN VI palsy leads to lateral rectus palsy and lateral gaze palsy.

Option D - CN III injury leads to injury of levator palpebrae superioris and ptosis.

None of these nerves pass through the middle ear.
questions.learning: VII — This patient with a past history of intra-op nerve injury during middle ear surgery presented with dry eye, decreased corneal sensation, and incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos) due to injury to cranial nerve (CN)VII.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, which of the following are the end products?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments

When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, the end products are 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments.

If an antibody molecule is digested with papain, cleavage occurs above the disulfide bonds that hold the heavy chains together. This generates 3 separate fragments, two of which are called Fab (fragment antigen binding), and one of which is called Fc (fragment crystallizable).

The image given below shows the cleavage of immunoglobulin by papain.

Cleavage of the antibody molecule with pepsin generates one large fragment called F(ab´)2 and a digested Fc fragment.

The image given below shows the cleavage of immunoglobulin by pepsin.
questions.learning: 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments When papain acts on a molecule of immunoglobulin, the end products are 1 Fc and 2 Fab fragments. If an antibody molecule is digested with papain, cleavage occurs above the disulfide bonds that hold the heavy chains together.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old man is reported deceased, and relatives state that he had a tattoo. However, no tattoo is visible on external examination during autopsy. To confirm its presence, further evaluation is required. What is the most appropriate site to examine to locate the tattoo?
questions.explanation: Tattooing involves injecting insoluble pigment granules into the dermal layer of the skin. Over time, macrophages and other immune cells phagocytose these pigment particles. Because these particles are often too large or chemically stable to be broken down, they are transported via the lymphatic system to the regional draining lymph nodes. In cases where a body is decomposed, charred, or if an attempt was made to surgically remove or chemically bleach a tattoo, the skin may no longer show visible ink. However, the pigment remains permanently sequestered within the regional lymph nodes, often staining them the same color as the original tattoo ink. This makes lymph node examination a vital forensic tool for identifying individuals with known tattoos when the skin is compromised. The spleen (Option A), liver (Option D), and arteries (Option B) are not part of the primary lymphatic drainage pathway for dermal pigments and would not reliably contain concentrated tattoo ink for identification purposes
questions.learning: Tattooing involves injecting insoluble pigment granules into the dermal layer of the skin. Over time, macrophages and other immune cells phagocytose these pigment particles.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs should be avoided in the first-line ART regimens because of its well-recognized metabolic toxicities?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stavudine (d4T)

Stavudine (d4T) is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that is no longer recommended as part of first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) because of its significant metabolic and mitochondrial toxicities. WHO and the National AIDS Control Programme (NACO) have replaced stavudine with Tenofovir (TDF) due to its better safety profile.

• A. Zidovudine (AZT) ✗

• Can cause bone marrow suppression (anemia, neutropenia) and myopathy, but is not primarily avoided because of metabolic toxicity.

• B. Stavudine (d4T) ✓

• Causes severe metabolic toxicities and has been phased out from first-line ART.

• C. Tenofovir (TDF) ✗

• Preferred first-line NRTI.
• Main adverse effects are renal toxicity and reduced bone mineral density, not metabolic toxicity.

• D. Lamivudine (3TC) ✗

• Well tolerated and routinely used in first-line ART regimens.
questions.learning: Stavudine (d4T) Stavudine (d4T) is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that is no longer recommended as part of first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) because of its significant metabolic and mitochondrial toxicities.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 60-year-old man presented with acute onset of chest pain radiating to the left arm and diaphoresis. His ECG and cardiac biomarkers show non-ST elevation myocardial infarction. Which of the following will be used in the treatment of this patient?

1. Atorvastatin
2. Aspirin
3. Clopidogrel
4. Low molecular weight heparin
5. Alteplase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 4

While atorvastatin, aspirin, clopidogrel, and low molecular weight heparin all have a role in the management of a patient with NSTEMI, there is no role of alteplase.

Initial management of a patient with NSTEMI includes bed rest to decrease the load on the heart. Oxygen is administered only if the patient has hypoxemia (SpO2 <90%) or heart failure. Further management includes the following medical therapy:

Nitrates (such as nitroglycerine given sublingually) reduce the venous return to the heart, thus reducing the cardiac output and the oxygen demand. Nitrates are contraindicated if the patient has hypotension.

β-blockers also reduce the myocardial oxygen demand predominantly by their negative chronotropic effect. Diltiazem or verapamil are given to reduce the heart rate if the patient doesn't respond to β-blockers.

Morphine is given if the patient continues to have severe chest pain despite the administration of the abovementioned anti-ischemic drugs.

Antithrombotic therapy, which includes:

• Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and a P2Y12 blocker such as clopidogrel. DAPT is continued for a minimum of 3 months, but preferably for 12 months.
• Anticoagulants such as low molecular weight heparin and bivalirudin

Clot formation and fibrinolysis is a dynamic process occurring in the coronary arteries. Antithrombotic therapy is given to prevent new clot formation while fibrinolysis is occurring by intrinsic or extrinsic mechanisms.

Statins, such as atorvastatin are started because they reduce the risk of recurrence of NSTEMI and stabilize the atherosclerotic plaque in the coronary arteries.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4 While atorvastatin, aspirin, clopidogrel, and low molecular weight heparin all have a role in the management of a patient with NSTEMI, there is no role of alteplase.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following biologic agents used in the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease acts by inhibiting the enzyme 'Janus Kinase'?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tofacitinib

Tofacitinib is an oral targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (tsDMARD) that acts by inhibiting Janus kinase (JAK) enzymes, primarily JAK1 and JAK3. This blocks the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, thereby reducing the production of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines involved in immune-mediated diseases.

In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), tofacitinib is approved for the treatment of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis in patients who have had an inadequate response or intolerance to conventional therapy or anti-TNF agents.

Why not the other options?

• A. Infliximab: A chimeric monoclonal antibody against TNF-α; used in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis.
• B. Adalimumab: A fully human monoclonal antibody against TNF-α.
• C. Vedolizumab: A monoclonal antibody against α4β7 integrin, preventing lymphocyte migration specifically into the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.learning: Tofacitinib Tofacitinib is an oral targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (tsDMARD) that acts by inhibiting Janus kinase (JAK) enzymes, primarily JAK1 and JAK3.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Miss Uma presents with a six-month history of a mass descending through her vagina. Examination reveals a grade 3 uterovaginal prolapse with an associated pressure ulcer on the prolapsed tissue. What is the likely cause of this pressure ulcer, and what are the appropriate treatment options?
options: Venous congestion and reduction of the pro- lapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine
questions.explanation: Venous congestion and reduction of the prolapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine. A pressure ulcer occurring on a prolapsed uterus or vagina is known as a decubitus ulcer. This ulcer is primarily caused by venous congestion (Option B), as the downward displacement of the organs stretches the veins, leading to edema and tissue breakdown . Infection (Option C), trauma (Option D), and malignancy (Option A) are not the primary causes, although the ulcer can become secondarily infected. The standard and most effective treatment is to reduce the prolapsed part back into the vagina to restore circulation, followed by daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine. Glycerine acts as a hygroscopic agent to reduce tissue edema, while acriflavine serves as an antiseptic. This treatment is mandatory to heal the ulcer before any definitive surgical repair (like a vaginal hysterectomy) can be performed safely. Therefore, restoring local blood flow and managing edema is the definitive management strategy for decubitus ulcers. .
questions.learning: Venous congestion and reduction of the prolapsed part into the vagina and daily packing with glycerine and acriflavine. A pressure ulcer occurring on a prolapsed uterus or vagina is known as a decubitus ulcer.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In which intracellular structures are lysosomal enzymes normally found?
questions.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes (hydrolases) are synthesized by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and undergo initial glycosylation within the ER lumen. They are then transported to the Golgi apparatus, where they receive the mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag — the critical signal that directs them to lysosomes rather than being secreted extracellularly. This entire process follows the classical secretory pathway, meaning these enzymes are always kept within membrane-bound compartments from the moment of synthesis. Why other options are wrong: (A) Cytosol is incorrect because the cytosol lacks a membrane boundary. If lysosomal enzymes were released freely into the cytosol, they would cause catastrophic self-digestion of cellular proteins. They must always remain membrane-enclosed to protect the cell. (B) Mitochondria is incorrect because mitochondria have their own distinct enzyme sets dedicated to oxidative phosphorylation and the TCA cycle. They play absolutely no role in lysosomal enzyme synthesis or storage. (D) Nucleus is incorrect because the nucleus houses genetic material and transcription machinery. Lysosomal enzymes are never trafficked there, as they exclusively follow the ER → Golgi → Lysosome secretory pathway from the point of synthesis onward
questions.learning: Lysosomal enzymes (hydrolases) are synthesized by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and undergo initial glycosylation within the ER lumen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which lymph node is most commonly involved in prostate cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pelvic

The most common lymph node of metastatic disease in prostate cancer is the pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the pelvic, obturator, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels may be useful to assist with the diagnosis and management.
questions.learning: Pelvic — The most common lymph node of metastatic disease in prostate cancer is the pelvic or retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following are extra-esophageal complications associated with GERD?

1. Asthma
2. Laryngitis
3. Pulmonary fibrosis
4. Cough
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2,3,4

Asthma, laryngitis, pulmonary fibrosis, and cough are all extra esophageal complications in gastroesophageal reflux disease(GERD)

Extraoesophageal symptoms of GERD are:

• Chronic cough
• Laryngitis,
• Asthma
• Dental erosions (especially on the lingual and palatal tooth
surfaces).
• Pulmonary fibrosis
• Sinusitis
• Pharyngitis
• Recurrent otitis media

Extraesophageal symptoms of GERD originate from the respiratory tract and include both laryngeal and pulmonary issues These symptoms can arise through two mechanisms. The first and most common mechanism involves proximal esophageal reflux and microaspiration of gastroduodenal contents, which cause direct injury to the larynx and lower respiratory tract. The second mechanism involves distal esophageal acid exposure triggering a vagal nerve reflex, leading to bronchospasm and cough, due to the shared vagal innervation of the trachea and esophagus.

The incidence of Barrett's esophagus is also more in patients with long term GERD, which in turn increases the risk of adenocarcinoma of esophagus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child with a history of perianal pain is brought to the OPD. On subjecting the specimen from the perianal region to a test, it produces yellow rhombic crystals of spermine picrate. What is the test done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Barberio test

The test done in the scenario is the Barberio test.

It is used to detect seminal fluid. When saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid is added to the spermatic fluid, yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate are produced.

Florence test:

• Used to detect: semen
• Stain used: 10% hydrochloric acid and Florence solution (potassium iodide, iodine, and water)
• Finding: If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately

Takayama test (Haemochromogen crystal test):

• Used to detect: bloodstains
• Stain used: Takayama reagent
• Finding: If bloodstain is present, pink feathery crystals of haemochromogen or reduced alkaline haematin appear in a few minutes

Teichmann test (Haemin Crystal Test):

• Used to detect: bloodstains
• Stain used: glacial acetic acid and a small crystal of sodium chloride
• Finding: If bloodstain is present, faint yellowish-red to brownish-black rhombic crystals of haemin or haematin chloride appear. When hydrogen peroxide is added, the haematin crystals give bubbles of gas
questions.learning: Barberio test — The test done in the scenario is the Barberio test. It is used to detect seminal fluid.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is admitted to the ICU and is receiving oxygen at 2 L/min. Arterial blood gas analysis shows hypoventilation with a pH of 7.33 and a pCO₂ of 64 mmHg. Based on these findings, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (PPV) should be given
Invasive positive pressure ventilation (PPV) should be given
Intubate and start on a ventilator
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD with acute respiratory acidosis (pH 7.33 and high ). For COPD patients with respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35), Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV), such as BiPAP, is the first-line intervention. NIPPV reduces the work of breathing, improves gas exchange, and significantly decreases the need for endotracheal intubation. Invasive ventilation (Option B and D) is reserved for patients who fail NIPPV or have contraindications like coma or severe hemodynamics. Increasing the oxygen flow rate (Option C) without providing ventilatory support can dangerously worsen hypercapnia in COPD patients by reducing their hypoxic respiratory drive. NIPPV should be initiated promptly while continuing medical therapies like bronchodilators and steroids. Successful management is indicated by an improvement in pH and a decrease in the within the first few hours
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD with acute respiratory acidosis (pH 7.33 and high ). For COPD patients with respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35), Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV), such as BiPAP, is the first-line…

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient underwent the following investigation for suspected malignancy. Which of the following compounds is used in this investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluorodeoxyglucose

The image shows a positron-emission tomography (PET) scan. PET involves the use of a radiolabeled bio-compound such as 2-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (FDG), which is injected intravenously.

It is based on the principle that tumor cells have a high metabolic rate and can metabolize FDG. However, tumor cells can metabolize FDG only to FDG-6-phosphate, and no further. Hence, it accumulates in tumor cells and can be detected and quantified.

Applications of PET:

* Oncologic:

* Detection, staging, drug response

* Differentiation between radiation necrosis and recurrence

* Neurologic:

* Early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease

* Localization of seizure focus in the interictal phase

* Localizing eloquent areas (e.g. speech, motor function)

* Cardiac:

* Identification of hibernating myocardium

The combination of PET imaging with CT (PET-CT) combines the metabolic information (PET) with the cross-sectional anatomic information (CT). PET-CT is used in oncology imaging to detect malignant cells as they demonstrate increased glucose metabolism relative to normal tissues.
questions.learning: Fluorodeoxyglucose — The image shows a positron-emission tomography (PET) scan. PET involves the use of a radiolabeled bio-compound such as 2-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (FDG), which is injected intravenously.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a rabies free area ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lakshadweep

In the following options, Lakshadweep is a rabies-free state as water is a natural barrier to rabies.

Rabies occurs in more than 150 countries and territories. A number of carnivorous and bat species serve as natural reservoirs and dogs are the primary sources of infection.

While some countries have achieved "rabies-free" status by vigorous campaigns of elimination, in others the disease has never been introduced. A "Rabies-free"
area has been defined as one in which no case of indigenously acquired rabies has occurred in man or any animal species for 2 years.

Geographic boundaries seem to play an important role here. Water appears to be the most effective natural barrier to rabies.

In India, the Union Territory of Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar islands are free of the disease. Other areas of the world include Australia, China, Taiwan, Cyprus, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Malta, New Zealand, the U.K., and the islands of the Western Pacific.

Note: A recent initiative by the Worldwide Veterinary Services called the  'Mission Rabies Project' is ongoing in the state of Goa and other parts of India to eradicate the disease. On June 23, 2021 the state of Goa declared that they have not reported a single case of rabies in the past 3 years.
questions.learning: Lakshadweep — In the following options, Lakshadweep is a rabies-free state as water is a natural barrier to rabies. Rabies occurs in more than 150 countries and territories.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: As a senior resident in the OBG department, You would consider uterine artery embolization as a treatment option in all of the following cases except ________
options: Prior to the removal of Placenta accreta in Multiparous woman
Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids

Uterine artery embolization is indicated in all the above-given cases except in a patient with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids.

A calcified fibroid does not shrink with the procedure. The pedunculated fibroids can fall off after the procedure resulting in intrauterine or peritoneal infections.

Hence, the calcified, submucous, and subserous types of fibroids are contraindications for this procedure.

Other indications for Uterine artery embolization(UAE) include,

* Postpartum hemorrhage.

* Placenta accreta to reduce bleeding prior to placental removal, or caesarean delivery.

* This technique is most suited for menorrhagia in a multiparous woman

Technique:

* Under local sedation, bilateral UAE is approached through percutaneous femoral catheterization.

* It is done using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), gel foam particles or metal coils.

Embolization reduces vascularity and the size of the fibroid in 3–4 months

Advantages of UAE:

* No major surgery.

* No intraoperative bleeding.

* Short hospital stay.

* Less abdominal adhesions.

Pearl PF1535: Contraindications to Uterine artery embolization

Absolute contraindications:

* GnRH agonist use

* Asymptomatic fibroids

* Pregnancy

* Pelvic inflammatory disease

* Uterine malignancy

* Calcified fibroid

Relative contraindications:

* A desire for future pregnancy: Poor uterine perfusion and pelvic adhesions following UAE would negatively impact fertility, and result in obstetric complications or adverse fetal effects.

* Postmenopausal status: The procedure is indicated primarily for premenopausal women since fibroids tend to decrease in size and symptoms improve or resolve after menopause. An enlarging uterus after menopause should raise the suspicion of malignancy and careful follow-up is warranted.

* Subserosal or submucosal fibroids: They are pedunculated and may detach either intraperitoneally or within the uterine cavity. Detachment may be associated with sterile peritonitis or intrauterine infection.

* Size or number of fibroids: The volume of necrosis after UAE in a large fibroid uterus can be substantial with a proportionate level of postprocedural pain and risk of infection.

* Contraindications to radiologic contrast agents.
questions.learning: Patient diagnosed with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids Uterine artery embolization is indicated in all the above-given cases except in a patient with calcified and pedunculated submucous fibroids.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What does the given pedigree chart indicate?
questions.explanation: The pedigree shows a pattern where an affected mother transmits the condition to all her children, regardless of sex. In the first generation, the affected female has multiple children, and all of them are affected. This is a hallmark feature of mitochondrial inheritance, as mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the mother. In the next generation, an affected male does not transmit the disease to any of his children, which further confirms mitochondrial inheritance, since fathers do not pass mitochondrial DNA to offspring. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Autosomal Dominant (AD): Would show transmission from both males and females equally, including father-to-child transmission. (B) Autosomal Recessive (AR): Typically skips generations and affects both sexes equally without strict maternal inheritance. (D) X-linked Recessive (XLR): More common in males and shows no male-to-male transmission, but does not show transmission to all children of affected females. The strict maternal transmission pattern confirms a mitochondrial disorder
questions.learning: The pedigree shows a pattern where an affected mother transmits the condition to all her children, regardless of sex. In the first generation, the affected female has multiple children, and all of them are affected.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient comes to you with fears of becoming pregnant and presents a history of unprotected sex five days ago. Which of the following emergency contraceptives can be used in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intra uterine contraceptive device (IUCD)

Since the patient had unprotected sex 5 days ago, an intrauterine contraceptive device(IUCD) can be used for emergency contraception in this case. It can be inserted within 5 days (120 hours) of coitus as a method of emergency contraception. All other methods of emergency contraception mentioned above need to be administered within 72 hours.

The administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy is known as the emergency contraception method. They are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse.

IUCD (Intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

Emergency contraceptives, also known as postcoital contraceptives are used to prevent conception after unprotected intercourse. They are interceptives. Their main action is to make the endometrium unsuitable for implantation. They can also delay or inhibit ovulation, and prevent fertilization of the egg by sperm.

They include:

* RU 486 (Mifepristone): 25 mg single dose is effective in 99.1% as a postcoital drug.

* Prostaglandins

* Copper T

* Yuzpe method: Combined high-dose estrogen-progestin pills are used as post-coitus contraceptives.
questions.learning: Intra uterine contraceptive device (IUCD) Since the patient had unprotected sex 5 days ago, an intrauterine contraceptive device(IUCD) can be used for emergency contraception in this case.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
In which of the following conditions is live vaccination not contraindicated?

1. DiGeorge syndrome
2. Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome
3. Ataxia telengiectasia
4. Complement deficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4 only

Live vaccination is not contraindicated in complement deficiency. In DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and Ataxia telangiectasia, live vaccines are contraindicated.

In patients with DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and Ataxia telangiectasia, there is a risk of severe or fatal infections due to live vaccines because of their impaired T-cell immunity. In contrast, a patient with a complement deficiency has an intact T-cell and B-cell immunity, which are crucial for building an immune response against live vaccines. These patients have an increased susceptibility to certain bacterial infections, especially those caused by Neisseria species, due to defects in the complement system, which is part of the innate immune system. But their adaptive immune system, which is primarily responsible for responding to vaccinations, is generally intact. Therefore, live vaccinations are not typically contraindicated in these patients.

DiGeorge syndrome is due to a developmental defect involving the endodermal derivatives of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches. Cell-mediated immunity is defective due to decreased T-cells. Affected individuals also have depressed graft rejection, hypocalcemia, and cardiac defects. For severe T cell deficiencies (e.g. severe combined immunodeficiency disease [SCID], complete DiGeorge syndrome), no live viral or live bacterial vaccines should be given.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome(WAS) is an X-linked recessive immunodeficiency disorder. It is caused by mutations in the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) that primarily affects the T lymphocytes. In patients with partial T cell deficiencies (e.g., partial DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome), all live viral vaccines are avoided.

Ataxia telangiectasia is caused due to mutation of the ATM gene. This gene is involved in the repair of double-strand DNA breaks. This defect in DNA repair leads to impaired Ig isotype switching and the formation of antigen receptors. As a result, the patient is immunodeficient with partial T cell deficiency, and hence live vaccines are avoided.
questions.learning: 4 only Live vaccination is not contraindicated in complement deficiency. In DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, and Ataxia telangiectasia, live vaccines are contraindicated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are true? 1. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT 2. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles 3. It is an autosomal recessive condition 4. Extra-intestinal manifestations of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome include hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome caused by a mutation of the STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 19p13.3.

1. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT — TRUE

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is characterized by:

• Multiple hamartomatous polyps
• Mainly in the small intestine (especially jejunum), but can occur throughout GIT.

2. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles — TRUE

This is the classic histological hallmark of Peutz-Jeghers polyps.

Histology:

• Tree-like (“arborizing”) branching smooth muscle extending into the polyp.

3. It is an autosomal recessive condition — FALSE

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is:

• Autosomal dominant
• Usually due to mutation in STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene.

4. Extra-intestinal manifestations include hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium — FALSE

Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) is associated with:

Familial adenomatous polyposis

—not Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Important Differential Diagnosis

| Syndrome | Polyp Type | Gene | Key Feature

| -------- | ---------- | ---- | -----------

| PJS | Hamartomatous | STK11 | Mucocutaneous pigmentation

| Juvenile polyposis | Hamartomatous | SMAD4/BMPR1A | Juvenile retention polyps

| FAP | Adenomatous | APC | CHRPE, colon cancer

| Cowden syndrome | Hamartomatous | PTEN | Trichilemmomas, breast/thyroid cancer
questions.learning: 1, 2 Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome caused by a mutation of the STK11/LKB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 19p13.3.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the smallest diameter of the true pelvis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sacrocotyloid diameter

The sacrocotyloid diameter is the shortest oblique diameter of the pelvic inlet and extends from the sacral promontory to the iliopectineal eminence (cotyloid region) on one side.

Important pelvic diameters:

• Diagonal conjugate → measured clinically from sacral promontory to inferior pubic symphysis
• True conjugate (obstetric conjugate) → narrowest anteroposterior diameter through which the fetal head passes
• Interspinous diameter → narrowest transverse diameter of the midpelvis
• Sacrocotyloid diameter → smallest diameter of the true pelvis

| Diameter | Measurement

| -------- | -----------

| Interspinous (bispinous) | 10.5 cm

| Diagonal conjugate | 12.5 cm

| True (obstetric) conjugate | 10 cm

| Obstetric conjugate | 10 cm

| Sacrocotyloid diameter | 9–9.5 cm ← smallest

Sacrocotyloid diameter = distance from sacral promontory → iliopectineal eminence (cotyloid notch) bilaterally

• Represents the posterior sagittal diameter of the pelvic brim
• At 9–9.5 cm, it is the smallest diameter of the true pelvis
• Clinically significant in flat/platypelloid pelvis — head engagement affected
questions.learning: Sacrocotyloid diameter — The sacrocotyloid diameter is the shortest oblique diameter of the pelvic inlet and extends from the sacral promontory to the iliopectineal eminence (cotyloid region) on one side.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Based on Globocan 2020 data, which cancer type is the most prevalent among males in India?
questions.explanation: According to the Globocan 2020 report, lip and oral cavity cancer is identified as the most prevalent malignancy among the male population in India. This high incidence is largely attributed to cultural habits involving the consumption of tobacco, areca nut, and betel quid, particularly in smokeless forms like gutka and khaini. While lung cancer (Option A) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality globally and is highly significant in India, its overall incidence ranks below oral cancers in this specific demographic. Colorectal cancer (Option C) and liver cancer (Option D) are increasing due to changing lifestyles and viral hepatitis prevalence, respectively, but they have not yet surpassed the burden of oral cavity lesions. Public health strategies in India focus heavily on tobacco cessation and early screening for oral lesions to reduce this significant disease burden. Understanding these localized epidemiological trends is essential for clinical practice and resource planning within the Indian healthcare context
questions.learning: According to the Globocan 2020 report, lip and oral cavity cancer is identified as the most prevalent malignancy among the male population in India. This high incidence is largely attributed to cultural habits involving the consumption of tobacco, areca…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Most appropriate choice for administering intravenous regional anesthesia?
questions.explanation: Intravenous Regional Anesthesia (IVRA), also known as a Bier block, involves injecting a local anesthetic into the venous system of an isolated limb (using a double-tourniquet). Lidocaine (0.5% preservative-free, Option D) is the most appropriate and commonly used drug for this technique. It provides a rapid onset of anesthesia and has a relatively high safety profile. Bupivacaine (Option A) is strictly contraindicated in Bier blocks because it is highly cardiotoxic; if the tourniquet fails and the drug enters the systemic circulation, it can cause fatal cardiac arrest that is difficult to resuscitate. Mepivacaine (Option B) and Procaine (Option C) are not the standard agents used for this specific procedure due to differences in toxicity or efficacy profiles. Therefore, for a Bier block, Lidocaine remains the standard of care due to its balance of effectiveness and lower risk of lethal cardiotoxicity upon systemic release
questions.learning: Intravenous Regional Anesthesia (IVRA), also known as a Bier block, involves injecting a local anesthetic into the venous system of an isolated limb (using a double-tourniquet).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a triage system, highest priority and dead patients are respectively colour coded by
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Red and black

Highest priority patients are coded red and dead patients are coded black.

* Triage consists of rapidly classifying the injured on the basis of the severity of their injuries and the likelihood of their survival with prompt medical intervention.

* Triage is the only approach that can provide maximum benefit to the greatest number of injured in a major disaster situation.

Pearl PF1015: Triage Colour Coding

Triage system consists of four colour codes:

Color code
Priority
Type of patients

Red
High
Need for immediate resuscitation or surgery in the next 6 hours or transfer (Eg. massive hemorrhage, tension pneumothorax)

Yellow
Medium
Possible resuscitation or surgery in next 24 hours (Eg. Isolated simple fracture)

Green
Low
Ambulatory patients or minor illness (Eg. Isolated abrasions, contusions, sprains)

Black
Least
Dead or moribund patients (Eg. massive head injuries, 95% third degree burns)
questions.learning: Red and black Highest priority patients are coded red and dead patients are coded black. * Triage consists of rapidly classifying the injured on the basis of the severity of their injuries and the likelihood of their survival with prompt medical…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the murmur of Patent Ductus Arteriosus: 1. It is a continuous ‘machinery’ murmur. 2. There is a late diastolic accentuation. 3. It is maximal in the second left intercostal space below the clavicle. 4. With the development of Eisenmenger Syndrome, the murmur becomes louder and rumbling in character. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

• 1. Continuous “machinery” murmur: Correct

• PDA produces a continuous murmur because blood flows from the aorta to the pulmonary artery during both systole and diastole.
• It is classically described as a machinery murmur.

• 2. Late diastolic accentuation: Incorrect

• The murmur is generally continuous with systolic accentuation, rather than specifically late-diastolic accentuation.

• 3. Maximal at the second left intercostal space below the clavicle: Correct

• The murmur is best heard at the left upper sternal border / second left intercostal space, beneath the left clavicle.

• 4. Becomes louder and rumbling with Eisenmenger syndrome: Incorrect

• As pulmonary vascular resistance rises and the shunt decreases or reverses, the PDA murmur becomes softer and may eventually disappear.
• A prominent continuous murmur requires a significant left-to-right pressure gradient.
questions.learning: Continuous “machinery” murmur: Correct • PDA produces a continuous murmur because blood flows from the aorta to the pulmonary artery during both systole and diastole. • It is classically described as a machinery murmur. • 2.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following eye signs can be appreciated in the image?
questions.explanation: The image shows a dark brown–black horizontal band on the exposed sclera, with surrounding dryness. This is characteristic of tache noire, a postmortem change seen in eyes that remain partially open after death. It occurs due to drying of the sclera, leading to discoloration, typically appearing as two triangular patches or a horizontal band. Key feature: 1. Drying and pigmentation of exposed sclera 2. Seen in postmortem eyes, especially when eyelids are not fully closed Why other options are incorrect: (B) Kevorkian sign: Refers to retinal vessel segmentation (trucking), not visible externally (C) Corneal changes: Include opacity or clouding, not localized dark patches (D) Vitreous humour changes: Internal eye changes, not visible on external inspection The visible dark scleral band clearly indicates tache noire, a classic postmortem ocular sign

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A lesion in which lobe will lead to impairment of hand-eye coordination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Parietal lobe

A lesion in the parietal lobe will lead to impairment of hand-eye coordination.

The somatic sensory area and related parts of the posterior parietal lobe project to the premotor cortex. Some of these neurons are concerned with aiming and manipulating the hands at an object, whereas other neurons are concerned with hand-eye coordination. Neurons in this posterior parietal cortex contribute to the descending pathways involved in motor control.

There are two parietal lobes, the dominant side, and the non-dominant side.

• The functions of the dominant side of the parietal lobe are calculation, language, planned movement, appreciation of size, shape, weight, and texture. A lesion here causes dyscalculia, dysphasia, dyslexia, apraxia, agnosia, homonymous hemianopia.
• The function of the non-dominant side is spatial orientation and constructional skills. Its lesion causes spatial disorientation, constructional apraxia, neglect of the non-dominant side, dressing apraxia, and homonymous hemianopia.

Other options:

Option B: The frontal lobe is responsible for personality, emotional response, social behavior. Any lesion in the frontal lobe causes disinhibition, antisocial behavior, impaired memory, incontinence, anosmia.

Option C: The temporal lobe has two lobes and is divided as dominant and non-dominant.

• The dominant temporal lobe has important functions like auditory perception, speech, language, verbal memory, smell. Lesions lead to dysphasia, dyslexia, poor memory, complex hallucinations (smell, sound, vision), impaired face recognition (Prosopagnosia) and homonymous hemianopia.
• The nondominant temporal lobe auditory perception, music, tone sequences, non-verbal memory (faces, shapes, music). Lesions here leads to poor non-verbal memory, loss of musical skills, complex hallucinations, and homonymous hemianopia.

Option D: The occipital lobe is responsible for the analysis of vision. A lesion in occipital lobe mainly affects vision leading to homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia, impaired face recognition (prosopagnosia), visual hallucinations (lights, lines and zigzags).
questions.learning: Parietal lobe — A lesion in the parietal lobe will lead to impairment of hand-eye coordination. The somatic sensory area and related parts of the posterior parietal lobe project to the premotor cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which anatomical structure is represented by the label “C” in the given image?.
questions.explanation: The label “C” in the CT scan corresponds to the lentiform nucleus, which is a wedge-shaped structure located lateral to the internal capsule. The lentiform nucleus is composed of two parts: the putamen (laterally) and the globus pallidus (medially). On axial CT images, it appears as a relatively dense, lens-shaped gray matter structure in the basal ganglia region, matching the position indicated by label “C”. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Globus pallidus : This is only the medial component of the lentiform nucleus. It lies closer to the internal capsule and appears smaller and more medial than the structure marked “C”. Since “C” points to the entire lens-shaped area, it cannot represent just the globus pallidus. (B) Putamen : The putamen is the lateral part of the lentiform nucleus. While it forms a major portion, the label “C” includes both medial and lateral parts, indicating the complete structure rather than just the putamen. (D) None : This is incorrect because the labeled structure clearly corresponds anatomically to the lentiform nucleus. Thus, the correct answer is (C) Lentiform nucleus
questions.learning: The label “C” in the CT scan corresponds to the lentiform nucleus, which is a wedge-shaped structure located lateral to the internal capsule. The lentiform nucleus is composed of two parts: the putamen (laterally) and the globus pallidus (medially).

questions.text: Which one of the following is correct regarding obesity and infertility?

It is associated with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
There is no change in HPO axis
It is always associated with endometrial atrophy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is associated with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

Obesity is an important cause of subfertility/infertility. It alters the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis, leading to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, ovulatory dysfunction, and menstrual irregularities.

Why not the other options?

• B. It is associated with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism is seen in primary ovarian failure, not obesity.
• C. There is no change in HPO axis: Obesity disrupts the HPO axis and impairs ovulation.
• D. It is always associated with endometrial atrophy: Obesity is associated with unopposed estrogen exposure, leading to endometrial hyperplasia and an increased risk of endometrial carcinoma, not atrophy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The Trapezoid of Disaster includes: (NEET PG 2015)
options: Triangle of death and circle of death
Triangle of doom and circle of death
Triangle of doom medially and triangle of pain laterally
Triangle of doom laterally and triangle of pain medially
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triangle of doom medially and triangle of pain laterally

During laparoscopic hernia repair, the surgeon must navigate important anatomical landmarks in the inguinal region. The "Trapezoid of Disaster" contains two important triangles that require careful attention during mesh placement. The Triangle of Doom is bounded medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the testicular vessels, containing the external iliac vessels and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve. The Triangle of Pain is located lateral to this, bounded medially by testicular vessels and laterally by the iliopubic tract, containing the femoral nerve, anterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, and lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with chronic liver disease develops hyperammonemia, presenting with asterixis and somnolence. Brain imaging reveals cerebral edema. Which sequence of biochemical events directly links elevated ammonia to both the cerebral edema and the disruption of cerebral energy metabolism, tracing through two distinct downstream pathways from a single shared precursor?
options: NH3 directly damages the blood-brain barrier, causing edema; separately, NH3 inhibits glycolysis directly, causing energy failure — two unrelated mechanisms

NH3 combines with α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, then glutamine; glutamine causes osmotic cerebral edema, while the consumption of α-ketoglutarate for this reaction depletes the TCA cycle intermediate, impairing oxidative energy metabolism
NH3 directly forms urea in the brain, and urea accumulation causes both osmotic edema and TCA cycle inhibition simultaneously
NH3 is converted to GABA directly without intermediate steps, causing both sedation and cerebral edema through GABA receptor overactivation alone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NH3 combines with α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, then glutamine; glutamine causes osmotic cerebral edema, while the consumption of α-ketoglutarate for this reaction depletes the TCA cycle intermediate, impairing oxidative energy metabolism

Excess NH3 combines with α-ketoglutarate (forming glutamate, then glutamine via glutamine synthetase) — this serves two simultaneous pathologic purposes: (1) glutamine accumulation causes osmotic cerebral edema (glutamine draws water into astrocytes), and (2) the consumption of α-ketoglutarate for this detoxification reaction depletes a critical TCA cycle intermediate, inhibiting the TCA cycle and impairing cellular energy metabolism in the brain — both consequences trace back to the same nitrogen-disposal reaction, explaining the dual toxicity from a single shared precursor.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Identify the incorrect statement in rapid sequence intubation?
options: Preoxygenation with 100% oxygen for 3 min is done.
It is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patient.
Induction agent and muscle relaxant are given simultaneously.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patient.

The incorrect statement regarding rapid sequence intubation (RSI) is that it is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patients.

RSI is a technique of anesthesia induction in patients who are at an increased risk of gastric regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents. Common cases include pregnancy, full stomach, intestinal obstruction, poorly controlled gastroesophageal reflux disease, morbid obesity, and diabetic gastroparesis. The goal is to intubate rapidly to minimize the time between the loss of consciousness and securing of the airway with a cuffed endotracheal tube.

It is achieved by pre-oxygenating the patient with 100% oxygen for 2-3 minutes. An inducing agent is administered, which is immediately followed by a muscle relaxant succinylcholine or rocuronium. The trachea is intubated without any prior bag and mask ventilation using a high-volume and low-pressure cuff which adequately cuffs the airway and prevents aspiration.

Cardiac arrest is an emergency condition with importance given to start chest compressions, defibrillation, or drugs to restore perfusion. The airway is commonly blocked by posterior displacement of the tongue which can be managed by head tilt and chin lift or giving jaw thrust. In case of airway blockade or to prevent aspiration, the airway is maintained by emergency tracheal tube intubation and does not involve the procedure that is followed in RSI. Endotracheal tube placement is commonly done during post-cardiac arrest care.
questions.learning: It is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patient. The incorrect statement regarding rapid sequence intubation (RSI) is that it is the method of choice in cardiac arrest patients.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presented with cough for 15 days. On examination, cervical lymphadenopathy was noted and the lymph node biopsy showed the following features. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis

The histopathological findings and clinical history are suggestive of tuberculosis.

Once Mycobacterium tuberculosis enters the macrophage, it inhibits the formation of the phagolysosome. This allows it to replicate unchecked. M. tuberculosis recruits a host protein coronin to block the fusion of phagosome and lysosome. Th1 response to M. tuberculosis is mounted about three weeks following the infection. The antigen-presenting cells (APCs) present mycobacterial antigens to the T-cells in the lymph nodes and release IL-12 and IL-18 to cause the differentiation of T-cells into Th1 cells. Th1 cells produce IFN-γ. IFN-γ is the critical step in the body's defense against M. tuberculosis. It acts by activating macrophages, causing phagolysosome maturation, and inducing nitric oxide synthase enzyme to form more reactive nitrogen species. It also mobilizes anti-bacterial compounds like defensins and stimulates autophagy.

Th1 response leads to the formation of a granuloma and caseous necrosis. Macrophages that are activated by the action of IFN-γ differentiate into epithelioid histiocytes. These are the cells that actually aggregate to form a granuloma. Some epithelioid cells may also fuse to form a giant cell.

The microscopic picture shows the caseating granuloma. Eosinophilic necrotic debris known as caseation, bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhan giant cells and lymphocytes can be seen. Epitheloid cells merge to form Langhan's giant cell where nuclei are arranged in a horseshoe shape (a characteristic feature of tuberculosis).

Clinically, tuberculosis presents with chronic cough, breathing difficulty, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Chest radiograph shows tree-in-bud pattern, infiltrates, and cavity formation predominantly in the upper lobes.

Other options:

Option B: Leprosy presents with skin lesions and nerve involvement with loss of sensation. Histopathology shows noncaseating granulomas.

Option C: Sarcoidosis shows giant cells with cytoplasmic inclusions and noncaseating granuloma with fibroblastic proliferation at the periphery.

Option D: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection that shows hyperplasia of the capsule accompanied by fibrosis, perivascular inflammation, and infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells with caseating granulomas.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about indications of hysterosalpingography are correct? I. Tubal patency assessment following tuboplasty operation II. Diagnosis of uterine synechiae III. Detection of IUD IV. Diagnosis of subserosal fibroid Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a radiographic procedure in which a water-soluble contrast medium is injected through the cervix to visualize the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes under fluoroscopy. It is primarily used in the evaluation of infertility, especially to assess tubal patency and abnormalities of the uterine cavity. The following are appropriate uses of HSG:

• I. Tubal patency assessment following tuboplasty operation: HSG is used to evaluate the success of tubal reconstructive surgery (tuboplasty) by confirming tubal patency.
• II. Diagnosis of uterine synechiae: HSG can demonstrate intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) as irregular filling defects or partial obliteration of the uterine cavity.
• III. Detection of IUD: HSG can demonstrate the presence and position of an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUD) within the uterine cavity.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Diagnosis of subserosal fibroid: Subserosal fibroids lie on the outer surface of the uterus and do not distort the uterine cavity, so they are not detected by HSG. They are better evaluated by ultrasonography or MRI.
questions.learning: I, II and III Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is a radiographic procedure in which a water-soluble contrast medium is injected through the cervix to visualize the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes under fluoroscopy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to the outpatient department with spotting following IUD insertion. No pain or fever was reported. What is the next best step in this scenario? IUD - Intrauterine device
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give iron tablets and observe

In this scenario of a woman presenting to the outpatient department with spotting following an IUD insertion with no complaints of fever or pain, the next best step would be to give iron tablets and observe.

Spotting is a common side effect after IUD insertion and often resolves on its own without intervention. Since no other complications are present in this patient, there is no need to remove the IUD or prescribe any medications. The patient just needs to be under observation.

It's important to monitor the woman for any signs of heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or other unusual symptoms that could indicate complications such as infection or perforation.

Complications following an IUD insertion :

* Pain accounts for 15–40% of IUD removal, hence, it is the most common cause of IUD removal.

* However, bleeding is the most common side-effect reported after IUD insertion.

* Disturbances in menstrual bleeding are very commonly reported in the form of increased blood loss or irregular bleeding.

* Studies have shown that larger non-medicated IUDs cause greater incidences of bleeding than copper devices and hormone-releasing devices.

* Other side effects and complications are pain, pelvic infection, uterine perforation, and ectopic pregnancies.

Contraindications for IUD usage include:

Absolute contraindications
Relative contraindications

• Suspected pregnancy
• PID
• Vaginal bleeding of unknown etiology
• Carcinoma cervix/uterus/adnexa /other pelvic tumours

• Anemia
• Menorrhagia
• History of PID since the last pregnancy
• Purulent cervical discharge
• Distortions of the uterine cavity due to fibroids
• Uterine malformations
• An unmotivated person

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 45-year-old obese woman with diabetes, previously treated with oral hypoglycemic agents, presents to the emergency department with features of hypoglycemia. Based on her medication history, which drug is most likely responsible for this episode?
questions.explanation: Among the common oral anti-diabetic medications, sulfonylureas are the class most frequently associated with clinical hypoglycemia. Glimepiride is a second-generation sulfonylurea that works by stimulating pancreatic beta cells to secrete insulin regardless of current blood glucose levels. This "glucose-independent" mechanism can lead to severe and prolonged hypoglycemic episodes, especially if a meal is missed. Metformin (Option A) is a biguanide that does not stimulate insulin secretion and thus carries a negligible risk of hypoglycemia when used alone. Pioglitazone (Option B), a TZD, and Sitagliptin (Option C), a DPP-4 inhibitor, are both considered "weight-neutral" or "weight-friendly" drugs with low hypoglycemia risk because their actions are either insulin-sensitizing or glucose-dependent. Therefore, because of its direct insulinotropic effect, Glimepiride is the most likely pharmacological cause of this patient’s emergency presentation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is most suitable for treating diarrhea in a patient receiving 5-fluorouracil therapy for colorectal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Diarrhea is a frequent and potentially severe side effect of chemotherapy agents like 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or irinotecan. For the symptomatic management of this non-infectious, drug-induced diarrhea, Loperamide is the most appropriate and standard first-line treatment. Loperamide is an opioid-receptor agonist that acts directly on the circular and longitudinal muscles of the intestinal wall to slow down gut motility and increase fluid absorption. Ciprofloxacin (Option A) and Ornidazole (Option D) are antimicrobials used for infectious diarrhea and have no role in managing toxic chemotherapy side effects. Atropine (Option C) is an anticholinergic used specifically to prevent the acute early-onset diarrhea caused by irinotecan (which is cholinergic in nature), but it is not the standard choice for the more common, delayed secretory diarrhea of 5-FU. In oncology, "high-dose loperamide" protocols are often utilized to prevent life-threatening dehydration and electrolyte imbalances. Clinicians must educate patients to initiate loperamide immediately at the first sign of loose stools

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent cholecystectomy for gallstones over 2 years ago. She now presents with symptoms of obstructive jaundice. Investigation reveals a stone in the common bile duct. What is the stone most likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary

This patient has a history of cholecystectomy done for gallstones 2 years ago. Thus, in this patient with choledocholithiasis, the stones found in the common bile duct would most likely be primary stones.

Choledocholithiasis or common bile duct stones are classified based on their point of origin:

• Primary stones are brown pigment stones that arise de novo in the bile duct and are composed of bile pigments and cholesterol.
• Secondary stones (option B) are usually cholesterol stones, which originate in the gall bladder and pass down into the common bile duct. Since this patient has already undergone cholecystectomy more than 2 years ago, secondary stones are unlikely.
• When stones are found in the common bile duct within 2 years of history of cholecystectomy, they are termed retained stones (option D).
• If they are found more than 2 years after cholecystectomy, they are known as recurrent stones (which are mostly primary).

Clinical features: Mostly clinically silent, but may present with biliary colic and even obstructive jaundice. When there is fever, jaundice, and associated right upper quadrant abdominal pain, it is known as Charcot’s triad, seen in cholangitis.

Management of choledocholithiasis:
ERCP +/- sphincterotomy followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the most preferred management of choledocholithiasis.

If stones cannot be removed through ERCP and sphincterotomy, then common bile duct exploration is carried out intraoperatively either in an open procedure or via laparoscopy. A T-tube is left in place after choledochotomy.
questions.learning: Primary — This patient has a history of cholecystectomy done for gallstones 2 years ago. Thus, in this patient with choledocholithiasis, the stones found in the common bile duct would most likely be primary stones.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The virulence factor of Bacillus anthracis responsible for resistance to phagocytosis is its capsule. Which of the following is the correct biochemical composition?
options: pXO1 plasmid and poly-α-glutamic acid capsule
pXO2 plasmid and poly-γ-glutamic acid capsule
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. pXO2 plasmid and poly-γ-glutamic acid capsule

Bacillus anthracis is unique among bacteria because its antiphagocytic capsule is composed of poly-γ-D-glutamic acid, not polysaccharide. Capsule synthesis is encoded by the pXO2 plasmid, while the pXO1 plasmid encodes the anthrax toxin components.

Why is D correct?

• pXO2 plasmid → Encodes the poly-γ-D-glutamic acid capsule, which prevents phagocytosis.
• The capsule is an important virulence factor responsible for immune evasion.

Why not the other options?

• A. pXO2 plasmid and polysaccharide capsule: Incorrect; the capsule is poly-γ-D-glutamic acid, not polysaccharide.
• B. pXO1 plasmid and poly-α-glutamic acid capsule: Incorrect; pXO1 encodes toxins, not the capsule, and the capsule is γ, not α, glutamic acid.
• C. pXO1 plasmid and polysaccharide capsule: Incorrect for both the plasmid and capsule composition.
questions.learning: pXO2 plasmid and poly-γ-glutamic acid capsule Bacillus anthracis is unique among bacteria because its antiphagocytic capsule is composed of poly-γ-D-glutamic acid, not polysaccharide.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman visits an infertility clinic. She has a regular 28-day cycle. How should she be evaluated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum progesterone on day 21

Serum progesterone on day 21 should be evaluated in this woman to check for anovulatory cycles.

Anovulation is the major cause of female infertility. Therefore, tests are done to rule out anovulatory defects in a woman presenting with infertility.

After ovulation, the plasma concentration of progesterone increases and reaches its peak during the mid-luteal phase. Serum progesterone levels are assessed on day 8 and day 21 of a 28-day cycle. If the progesterone value increases from less than 1 ng/mL to greater than 6 ng/mL, it indicates ovulation. Subsequently, as the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone levels decline.

If the plasma progesterone level remains low during the mid-luteal phase, it suggests a corpus luteal phase defect and indicates the need for hormonal therapy.

Daily estimation of serum LH (options C and D) around the midcycle can detect the LH surge. Ovulation coincides about 10 to 12 hours after the LH peak.
questions.learning: Serum progesterone on day 21 Serum progesterone on day 21 should be evaluated in this woman to check for anovulatory cycles. Anovulation is the major cause of female infertility.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Calculate the ECF volume in a volunteer in whom 10 gm of mannitol was injected in venous blood. At equilibrium urinary excretion of mannitol was found to be 10% and the plasma concentration of mannitol was 65 mg/100 ml.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 14L

ECF volume of the above volunteer is calculated to be 14 L.

The ECF volume can be calculated using the formula:

Where,

• V = ECF volume
• Amount injected = 10 gm
• Amount of mannitol excreted = 10% of 10 gm = 1gm
• Plasma concentration of mannitol = 65 mg/100mL = 0.65 gm/L

Calculation:

ECF Volume = (10-1)/0.65

= 13.8 L = approximately 14 L

Mannitol cannot cross cell membranes, hence, it will be distributed in ECF but not in ICF. Thus mannitol is a marker for ECF volume and therefore calculating the volume of distribution of mannitol gives the value of ECF volume.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Under normal physiological conditions, why is hemoglobin unable to pass through the glomerular filtration barrier?
options: It is a large molecule bound with another protein
It gets attracted to the negative charge of the glomerular filtration barrier
questions.explanation: Under normal physiological conditions, hemoglobin is contained within red blood cells and does not reach the glomerular filtrate. However, if free hemoglobin is present in the plasma due to mild hemolysis, it is rapidly bound by a plasma protein called haptoglobin. This hemoglobin-haptoglobin complex is too large to pass through the pores of the glomerular filtration barrier, thus preventing hemoglobinuria and protecting the renal tubules from oxidative damage. Option B is incorrect because the glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged due to heparin sulfate proteoglycans, which "repels" rather than attracts negatively charged proteins like albumin or hemoglobin. Therefore, "Both A and B" (Option C) is incorrect as statement B is physiologically backwards. Hemoglobinuria only occurs when the hemolytic rate exceeds the binding capacity of haptoglobin (haptoglobin depletion), allowing free hemoglobin dimers to be filtered. This distinction is critical in hematology and nephrology for differentiating between various hemolytic anemias and mechanical trauma to red cells

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young male had a road traffic accident and was brought to emergency with stable vitals. Which wound is not expected:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chop wound

In road traffic accidents (RTA), injuries are typically due to blunt force trauma, not sharp weapons.

Common RTA injuries :

• Abrasions (especially graze/brush abrasions) → due to friction with road surface
• Contusions (bruises) → due to impact
• Lacerations → irregular tears from blunt force

Why chop wound is not expected:

• Chop wounds are caused by heavy sharp weapons (e.g., axe).
• Characterised by: Clean-cut margins + underlying bone injury
• Not seen in accidental blunt trauma like RTA.
