questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man from a tropical region presents with a history of recurrent episodes of fever and chills along with progressive swelling of the lower limbs over several months. Examination reveals marked non-pitting edema of both legs extending to the scrotum, with thickened, mildly erythematous skin. He reports similar episodic symptoms over the past few years, and laboratory investigations show eosinophilia. Involvement of which structure is responsible for the development of this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of recurrent fever, chills, and massive, thickened, non-pitting edema of the lower extremities and scrotum (elephantiasis) in a tropical resident is classic for Lymphatic Filariasis, caused by parasites like Wuchereria bancrofti. These filarial worms reside in and damage the lymphatic vessels, leading to chronic lymphatic obstruction and stasis. Unlike venous edema, lymphatic edema is "non-pitting" because of the accumulation of protein-rich fluid and subsequent subcutaneous fibrosis and skin thickening (hyperkeratosis). Eosinophilia is a common laboratory finding in parasitic infections. Arteries (Option A) and veins (Option B) are not the primary sites of filarial worm residence or the cause of this specific type of hard, fibrotic swelling. Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT, Option D) causes acute, painful, pitting edema, usually in one leg, and does not lead to the chronic, massive skin changes or scrotal involvement characteristic of filarial elephantiasis. Therefore, the involvement of the lymphatic system is the definitive cause of this condition
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of recurrent fever, chills, and massive, thickened, non-pitting edema of the lower extremities and scrotum (elephantiasis) in a tropical resident is classic for Lymphatic Filariasis, caused by parasites like Wuchereria bancrofti.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient after RTA had a renal shut down. Work-up shows: FeNa: < 1%, Urine osmolality: 300 mOsm/kg, Urinary sodium: 40 mEq/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s laboratory findings point toward intrinsic renal damage, specifically Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN). In ATN, damaged tubules lose the ability to concentrate urine and reabsorb sodium. The urinary sodium of 40 mEq/L is elevated, indicating sodium wasting, and the urine osmolality of ~300 mOsm/kg reflects "isosthenuria," where the kidney can no longer produce concentrated or dilute urine compared to plasma. Although a Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FeNa) < 1% is typically associated with pre-renal states, it can also be seen in early or non-oliguric ATN. Pre-renal AKI (Option B) is characterized by a lower urinary sodium (< 20 mEq/L) and a much higher urine osmolality (> 500 mOsm/kg). Post-renal AKI (Option C) requires evidence of obstruction on imaging. "Renal AKI" (Option D) is a broad category; ATN is the specific pathological diagnosis that matches the electrolyte wasting and osmolality findings
questions.learning: The patient’s laboratory findings point toward intrinsic renal damage, specifically Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN). In ATN, damaged tubules lose the ability to concentrate urine and reabsorb sodium.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An auxiliary nurse midwife has to conduct a vaccination camp in a village. She received 2 open vials, one of which is a pentavalent vaccine and the other is an MR vaccine. What can she do regarding the utilization of these vials?
options: Use MR vaccine and discard pentavalent vaccine
Use pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Use pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine

She can use the pentavalent vaccine and discard the MR vaccine.  According to the open vial policy, the pentavalent vaccine can be reused, whereas MR can not be reused.

Open vial policy was implemented to allow the reuse of partially used multidose vials under the Universal Immunization Program (UIP) for up to 28 days if certain conditions are met. This was implemented to reduce vaccine wastage.

It applies only to DPT, TT, hepatitis B, oral polio vaccine (OPV), liquid pentavalent, PCV, injectable IPV, inactivated Japanese encephalitis (JE) vaccine, and rotavirus vaccine. It does not apply to Measles/MR and BCG vaccines.

Note: Open vial policy does not apply to rotavirus vaccine with VVM on cap, it applies only to new rotavirus vaccine with VVM on label.
questions.learning: Use pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine She can use the pentavalent vaccine and discard the MR vaccine. According to the open vial policy, the pentavalent vaccine can be reused, whereas MR can not be reused.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is it called when a tour guide leads a group of tourists as they follow him through various attractions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herd

When a tourist guide directs a group of people who closely follow him at different tourist sites, it is referred to as herd behaviour.

A herd is a group of animals or people moving together, often following a leader or collective behaviour. In tourism, herd behaviour refers to a group of tourists following a guide, making collective decisions rather than acting independently.

Temporary social groups

* Crowd: It is a temporary group motivated by a common interest or curiosity. It lacks an internal organization and has no leader.

* Mob: The mob is a crowd with a leader, and is more emotional than a crowd. It is unstable and has no internal organization.

* Herd: This social group has a leader and the members have to follow his/her orders without question.

* A band is a permanent spatial group that constitutes a few families living together.

* Other permanent spatial groups are villages, cities towns and the state.
questions.learning: Herd When a tourist guide directs a group of people who closely follow him at different tourist sites, it is referred to as herd behaviour. A herd is a group of animals or people moving together, often following a leader or collective behaviour.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following are symptoms of Gradenigo syndrome?
options: Ear discharge, retro-orbital pain, and diplopia
Nasal discharge, retro-orbital pain, and diplopia
Ear discharge, retro-orbital pain, and headache
Retro-orbital pain, Diplopia, and hearing loss
questions.explanation: Gradenigo syndrome is a classic clinical triad caused by petrous apicitis, an infection of the apex of the petrous temporal bone, most often arising as a complication of otitis media. The triad consists of: 1. Ear discharge (otorrhea): Persistent discharge due to ongoing middle ear infection. 2. Retro-orbital pain: Deep pain behind the eye caused by irritation of the ophthalmic division (V₁) of the trigeminal nerve in Meckel’s cave. 3. Diplopia: Double vision due to abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) palsy, as the nerve passes through Dorello’s canal, leading to lateral rectus muscle paralysis. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Option B: Nasal discharge is incorrect; the infection is otogenic, not sinonasal. 2. Option C: Headache may occur but this option misses diplopia, a hallmark feature. 3. Option D: Hearing loss can be associated with otitis media, but ear discharge is essential to establish the otogenic origin. Diagnosis is confirmed with CT/MRI of the temporal bone, and management requires aggressive intravenous antibiotics, with surgical drainage if there is no response or complications develop
questions.learning: Gradenigo syndrome is a classic clinical triad caused by petrous apicitis, an infection of the apex of the petrous temporal bone, most often arising as a complication of otitis media.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study is carried out among nursing staff to assess the amount of time spent on various patient care activities, including bed preparation, monitoring vital signs, attending doctors’ rounds, blood sample collection, and drug administration. Which management technique is most suitable for this type of work analysis?
questions.explanation: The study aims to estimate the proportion of time nursing staff spend on various activities throughout the day. Work Sampling is the most appropriate statistical technique for this purpose because it involves making observations at random intervals to determine how time is distributed across different tasks. This method is efficient for assessing workload and providing data for staffing without the need for constant, intrusive monitoring. In contrast, the Critical Path Method (Option A) is a project management tool used for scheduling dependent tasks, not for measuring time proportions. System Analysis (Option B) is a broader study of entire organizational processes. A Time and Motion Study (Option D) involves continuous observation and timing of every single step in a task; while it provides high detail, it is more intrusive and often unnecessary for a general analysis of nursing care time distribution. Therefore, Work Sampling is the standard choice for this healthcare analysis
questions.learning: The study aims to estimate the proportion of time nursing staff spend on various activities throughout the day. Work Sampling is the most appropriate statistical technique for this purpose because it involves making observations at random intervals to…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient who engaged in strenuous exercise, skipped a meal, and later consumed alcohol at a party— which metabolic process is inhibited by alcohol intake in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Alcohol metabolism in the liver significantly increases the ratio of to . This high ratio shifts metabolic reactions away from producing glucose. Specifically, it diverts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, effectively inhibiting gluconeogenesis. In the scenario provided, the patient has already depleted their glycogen stores through strenuous exercise and fasting (starvation). Since they cannot perform gluconeogenesis due to alcohol, they are at a very high risk of developing severe, life-threatening fasting hypoglycemia. Alcohol does not primarily inhibit glycogenolysis (Option B); in fact, the body would have already used this process up during exercise. The HMP shunt (Option C) and ketone body formation (Option D) are not the primary targets of alcohol-induced metabolic inhibition. Clinical awareness of this "starvation + alcohol" interaction is vital for emergency room physicians, as these patients may present as unconscious or "drunk" when they are actually suffering from profound hypoglycemia that requires immediate intravenous glucose
questions.learning: Alcohol metabolism in the liver significantly increases the ratio of to . This high ratio shifts metabolic reactions away from producing glucose.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He was unable to pass urine and blood was seen at the tip of the urethra. A diagnosis of bulbar urethral injury was made. Where do you least expect the urine to get collected in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial portion of thigh

In bulbar urethral injury, the medial portion of the thigh is the least likely site for the collection of urine.

The rupture of the urethra below the urogenital diaphragm will result in extravasation of urine into the superficial perineal pouch, penis and scrotum in males and labia majora in females, and the anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial fascia of the abdomen is divided below the umbilicus into a superficial fatty layer (fascia of Camper) and a deep membranous layer (fascia of Scarpa). Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the membranous layer of the superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia).

Colles' fascia is attached to fascia lata (the deep fascia of the thigh) along the Holden's line that extends from the pubic tubercle laterally for 8 cm. Extravasated fluid cannot pass into the medial thigh below Holden's line due to the firm attachment of Colles' fascia to the fascia lata.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the lymphatic structure from the histology section given below?
questions.explanation: The histology section displays a distinct lobulated architecture, which is characteristic of the thymus. Each lobule is divided into a darker, peripheral outer cortex (rich in immature T-cells) and a lighter, central inner medulla. A pathognomonic feature found in the thymic medulla is Hassall’s corpuscles, which are concentric whorls of keratinized epithelial cells. In contrast, a tonsil (Option A) would show lymphoid follicles with germinal centers and an overlying stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. A lymph node (Option B) also contains follicles but is distinguished by its subcapsular sinus and distinct paracortical region. The spleen (Option C) is characterized by red and white pulp and does not have this lobular cortex-medulla arrangement. Therefore, the lobulated appearance and medullary characteristics confirm that the structure is the thymus
questions.learning: The histology section displays a distinct lobulated architecture, which is characteristic of the thymus. Each lobule is divided into a darker, peripheral outer cortex (rich in immature T-cells) and a lighter, central inner medulla.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following will increase the GFR?
options: Decrease in bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decrease in bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure

A decrease in Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure causes an increase in glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

A decrease in Bowman's Capsule Hydrostatic Pressure increases GFR because it reduces the opposing force to filtration, thus enhancing the net filtration pressure and increasing the amount of filtrate formed.

Factors that can increase the GFR are as follows:

* Increase in glomerular capillary filtration coefficient Kf: This coefficient depends on the hydraulic conductivity and surface area of the glomerular capillaries.

* Decrease in Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure: Conditions with urinary tract obstruction can lead to an increase in this pressure and a fall in GFR.

* Decrease in glomerular colloid osmotic pressure: Accumulation of plasma proteins that are not filtered from the blood contributes to this pressure, and an increase reduces further filtration and GFR. It is directly proportional to the following factors: Arterial plasma colloid osmotic pressure.

* Filtration fraction : An increase in filtration fraction concentrates the plasma proteins and raises the glomerular colloid osmotic pressure which in turn decreases the GFR.

Other options :

Option A: Efferent Arteriole Dilation reduces the resistance to blood leaving the glomerulus. This leads to a decrease in glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. A reduction in hydrostatic pressure lowers the driving force for filtration, resulting in a decreased GFR.

Option B: Afferent Arteriole Constriction decreases blood flow into the glomerulus. This lowers the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure. Lower pressure reduces the filtration rate across the glomerular capillary wall, leading to a decrease in GFR.

Option C: Increase in Glomerular Plasma Flow: If glomerular plasma flow increases but the efferent arteriole doesn't constrict, the extra blood flow is quickly carried away. This prevents a significant rise in the pressure inside the glomerular capillaries. As a result, the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) doesn't significantly increase, because the necessary increase in filtration pressure doesn't occur.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with carcinoma in pyriform Fossa. On laryngoscopy, the lesion is around 5cm and the right vocal folds are not mobile. There is no lymph Node involvement and no distant metastasis. What is the TNM staging for the malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T3N0M0

The patient has carcinoma hypopharynx as it is a tumor in the pyriform fossa and his staging of the disease is T3N0M0 as he has no nodal mets or involvement of vocal cords.

Staging of carcinoma hypopharynx:

1)Tumour

T1:

* Tumor involves only in one part of the hypopharynx

* is less than <2 cms

T2:

* Tumor involves more than one part of the hypopharynx

* has grown into a nearby area

*  > 2cm but < 4 cm across

* not affected the vocal cords

T3:

* Tumor is > 4 cm across

* Tumor is affecting the movement of the vocal cords

* Tumor has grown into the esophagus

T4a:

* The tumor has grown into thyroid or cricoid cartilage/ hyoid bone/ thyroid gland/nearby muscle or fat.

T4b:

* Tumor grows into Prevertebral Space

* Superior Mediastinum

* Encases carotid artery

2)Nodal staging:

* NX -cannot be assessed

* N0 No regional lymph node metastasis

* N1 Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, <3 cm

* N2a Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, >3cm but < 6 cm

* N2b Metastasis in multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes, <6 cm

* N2c Metastasis in bilateral or contralateral lymph nodes, < 6 cm

* N3 Metastasis in a lymph node > 6 cm

3)Systemic metastasis

* M0- no metastasis

* M1- metastasis present
questions.learning: T3N0M0 — The patient has carcinoma hypopharynx as it is a tumor in the pyriform fossa and his staging of the disease is T3N0M0 as he has no nodal mets or involvement of vocal cords.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient with a known history of asthmatic bronchitis presents to a peripheral hospital with severe breathlessness and palpitations. His oxygen saturation is 88%, and the facility does not have ventilator support. In the context of immediate management with the available resources, which of the following interventions should not be given?
options: Oxygen with an oxygen mask, and reservoir
questions.explanation: The patient is in acute severe asthma with hypoxia (SpO₂ 88%), which is a medical emergency. Management in such settings focuses on rapid-acting, safe, and effective therapies. Theophylline is NOT recommended in acute asthma management because it has a narrow therapeutic index and a high risk of serious adverse effects such as tachycardia, arrhythmias, seizures, and vomiting. This is especially dangerous in a resource-limited setting without ventilator support. Additionally, theophylline has a delayed onset of action and provides limited bronchodilation compared to inhaled β₂-agonists. Modern guidelines (e.g., GINA) have largely excluded theophylline from acute asthma treatment. Why other options are correct: (A) Hydrocortisone → Essential to reduce airway inflammation (C) Oxygen with reservoir mask → Crucial for hypoxia (D) Leukotriene antagonist → Not useful acutely but not harmful
questions.learning: The patient is in acute severe asthma with hypoxia (SpO₂ 88%), which is a medical emergency. Management in such settings focuses on rapid-acting, safe, and effective therapies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cholesterol is synthesized primarily from___.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. acetyl-CoA

Cholesterol is synthesized from acetyl-CoA mainly in the liver, adrenal cortex, testes, ovaries, and intestine.

The enzymes involved in cholesterol synthesis are partly located in the endoplasmic reticulum and partly in the cytoplasm. The enzyme HMG CoA reductase is the principal enzyme involved in the regulation of cholesterol synthesis in the body.

HMG-CoA is reduced to mevalonate by NADPH in a reaction catalyzed by HMG-CoA reductase which is the principal regulatory step in the pathway of cholesterol synthesis. It is the site of action of the cholesterol-lowering statins, which are HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors.

Long-term regulation of cholesterol synthesis involves regulating the transcription of the gene for HMG CoA reductase. When there is sufficient cholesterol in the cell, transcription of the gene for HMG CoA reductase is suppressed, and there is decreased synthesis of cholesterol.

Cholesterol regulates the expression of the gene for HMG CoA reductase. When cholesterol is less, proteases in the Golgi bodies cleave a sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP). The protein which is then formed binds to a sterol regulatory element (SRE) on the DNA. This activates transcription of the HMG CoA reductase gene which increases cholesterol synthesis.

Hormones that influence HMG reductase are:

* Insulin and thyroxine increase the activity of HMG CoA reductase

* Cortisol and glucagon decrease the activity of HMG CoA reductase

* Statins inhibit the activity of HMG CoA reductase
questions.learning: acetyl-CoA Cholesterol is synthesized from acetyl-CoA mainly in the liver, adrenal cortex, testes, ovaries, and intestine. The enzymes involved in cholesterol synthesis are partly located in the endoplasmic reticulum and partly in the cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely causative agent for a Tzanck smear showing multinucleated cells?
questions.explanation: A positive Tzanck smear is identified by the presence of multinucleated giant epithelial cells. This finding is classically associated with the herpesvirus family, most commonly Herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Varicella-zoster virus (VZV). While both can produce these giant cells, HSV is the most frequent clinical cause for localized herpetic lesions tested with this method. Human papillomavirus (Option C) causes warts and is characterized by koilocytosis rather than giant cells on Tzanck. Coxsackievirus A16 (Option D) causes Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease but does not result in a positive Tzanck smear. Therefore, when presented with this specific microscopic finding in a general diagnostic context, HSV remains the most likely causative agent for the observed multinucleation
questions.learning: A positive Tzanck smear is identified by the presence of multinucleated giant epithelial cells. This finding is classically associated with the herpesvirus family, most commonly Herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Isotype switching is seen in ____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Activated B cells

Isotype switching is seen in activated B cells.

Isotype switching: Conversion of one antibody class (isotype) to another resulting from the genetic rearrangement of heavy-chain constant-region genes in activated B cells.

Isotype switching is dependent on the presence of both antigens and cytokines secreted by T-cells.

Note: Defect in isotype switching can cause immunodeficiencies known as Hyper IgM syndrome.
questions.learning: Activated B cells Isotype switching is seen in activated B cells. Isotype switching: Conversion of one antibody class (isotype) to another resulting from the genetic rearrangement of heavy-chain constant-region genes in activated B cells.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with pain and swelling of his left arm after a fall from height. An upper arm X-ray was done. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

In the above clinical scenario, the history and radiograph suggest a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus. The radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition. This is because the radial nerve follows a superficial path around the humerus and can be stretched or compressed when there is significant trauma to the upper arm.

It manifests with wrist drop (inability to dorsiflex the wrist) and finger drop (inability to dorsiflex the digits). Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits.

Management of humerus shaft fractures:

* Conservative management using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks followed by functional bracing

* Surgical fixation by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins, or an external fixator is indicated in:

* Open fractures

* Pathological fractures

* Unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow)

* Radial nerve palsy

The below X-ray shows shaft of humerus fracture.

Other options:

* The axillary nerve is most commonly injured in shoulder dislocations or fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus.

* The ulnar nerve is more commonly injured in conditions like elbow dislocations, fractures of the medial epicondyle of the humerus, or entrapment at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome).

* The median nerve is more frequently associated with injuries in the forearm or wrist, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, or with certain systemic conditions like pronator teres syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is false regarding papillary thyroid cancer?
options: Most common age group is between 30- 50 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Calcitonin is the tumour marker

The wrong statement is option d. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma and not papillary carcinoma

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy with relatively good prognosis (option b) . It is more commonly seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50 (option a). Radiation exposure (option c) and a family history of thyroid malignancies are common etiologies. Genetic abnormalities in either the RET gene or the BRAF gene can be seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Clinical features include an asymptomatic thyroid swelling with cervical lymph node enlargement. In advanced disease, there may be features like hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.

An ultrasound scan accurately assesses the size and number of nodules, as well as categorizes the lesions as benign, indeterminate, or malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a diagnostic test, helpful in investigating an indeterminate or malignant lesion.

Histopathology shows the following features:

* Branching papillae

* Orphan Annie eye nuclei: optically clear nuclei with fine nuclear chromatin

* Pseudo inclusions: invaginations of the nuclear membrane

* Psammoma bodies: concentric calcifications in the core of the papillae.

Below is the histopathological image of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid with characteristic Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is known to spread via lymphatics, hence lymph node metastasis is commonly seen.

Treatment of Papillary thyroid carcinoma is as follows:

Total thyroidectomy is the treatment of choice. Routine central neck dissection is not recommended. Neck dissection is indicated in higher-risk situations, such as

* Tumor size > 4 cm (T3 stage) or gross extrathyroidal extension (T4 stage) or enlarged central lymph nodes - Total thyroidectomy + Central Neck Dissection

* Lateral Aberrant Thyroid - Total thyroidectomy + Modified Radical Neck Dissection + Central Neck Dissection

For occult papillary cancer (<1 cm tumor size, with no lymphatic, vascular or capsular invasion) - Lobectomy can be sufficient.

Radio-iodine ablation is undertaken when a whole-body iodine scan is positive after a total thyroidectomy for any differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary or follicular carcinoma).

The presence of any metastatic or residual thyroid tissue after total thyroidectomy can be detected by observing the uptake of radio-iodine in the entire body. To achieve effective uptake of radio-iodine, TSH levels need to be greatly increased, for example, by withdrawing thyroxine after the surgery for 4-6 weeks.

A positive whole-body iodine scan after total thyroidectomy indicates that there is either a metastatic or residual disease present. These patients are treated with I131 for radio-iodine ablation.

A negative scan means there is no metastasis or residual thyroid tissue. They are followed up regularly with serum thyroglobulin, TSH and USG-neck.
questions.learning: Calcitonin is the tumour marker — The wrong statement is option d. Calcitonin is the marker for medullary carcinoma and not papillary carcinoma Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy with relatively good prognosis (option b) .

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A diabetic patient was advised exercise by the treating physician. The glucose transporter which is insulin sensitive is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glut 4

GLUT-4 is the insulin-sensitive glucose transporter, primarily found in:

• Skeletal muscle
• Adipose tissue

Mechanism:

• In response to insulin, GLUT-4 translocates from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane
• This increases glucose uptake into cells
• Exercise can also stimulate GLUT-4 translocation independent of insulin

Clinical relevance in diabetes:

• Exercise improves glucose uptake even when insulin action is impaired
• Hence, exercise is beneficial in diabetes management

Why other options are incorrect:

• GLUT-1: RBCs, brain (insulin-independent)
• GLUT-2: Liver, pancreas (high Km, bidirectional)
• GLUT-3: Neurons (high affinity, insulin-independent)
questions.learning: Glut 4 GLUT-4 is the insulin-sensitive glucose transporter, primarily found in: • Skeletal muscle • Adipose tissue Mechanism: • In response to insulin, GLUT-4 translocates from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane • This increases glucose uptake…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presented with a lower abdominal mass and lower abdominal discomfort. On examination, the uterus appears uniformly enlarged and adnexa is free. MRI shows the presence of a myometrial cyst. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenomyosis

Multiparous women >40yrs, presenting with abdominal mass (free from adnexa) and myometrial cysts on MRI, point towards a diagnosis of adenomyosis.

Adenomyosis refers to the growth of the endometrium (both stromal and glandular components) directly into the myometrium. It is predominantly seen in multiparous women above the age of 40 years. Patients generally present with menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea, and sometimes dyspareunia. On examination, there is a gross symmetrical enlargement of the uterus corresponding to 12-14 weeks size. The uterus is soft and tender on bimanual examination.

Transvaginal ultrasonography (TVS) reveals a salt-and-pepper appearance of the myometrium and the presence of sub-endometrial striations producing the Venetian blind appearance. MRI can also be done for diagnosis. However, the only definitive mode of diagnosis is histopathological examination.

Since most women affected by the condition are past the childbearing age, total hysterectomy is the treatment of choice. Localized excision/Levonorgestrel containing IUCD can be tried in younger women.

Other options:

Option A: Endometriosis refers to the presence of endometrial tissue outside the endometrial lining (uterus). They usually present as dysmenorrhea and lower dull abdominal pain. Vaginal examination reveals a tender fixed retroverted uterus. They can be managed medically (oral contraceptives, aromatase inhibitors, etc)  and surgically (if failed medical management). Abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is performed in advanced cases.

Option C: Leiomyoma (fibroid) is the commonest benign tumor arising from the uterus. They present as abnormal uterine bleeding, infertility, and abdominal pain. On bimanual examination, the uterus is enlarged and the mass moves with the cervix. It can be managed medically (mifepristone or newer progesterone) and surgically. A myomectomy is performed for large fibroids with significant symptoms.

Option D: Endometrial hyperplasia can be simple, glandular, or atypical. They are seen in women with estrogen excess states like obesity, PCOD, or on tamoxifen therapy. They usually present as abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB).
questions.learning: Adenomyosis Multiparous women >40yrs, presenting with abdominal mass (free from adnexa) and myometrial cysts on MRI, point towards a diagnosis of adenomyosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All among the following are ionizing radiations except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MRI

MRI is a technique that produces topographic images by means of magnetic fields and radiofrequency waves.

The ionizing radiations

• Alpha

• Gamma
• X-Rays

The non-Ionizing radiations are:

• Radiofrequency waves
• UV rays
• Microwaves

Alpha and beta rays are particulate radiation (particles) whereas gamma and x-rays are electromagnetic rays. All electromagnetic waves have a constant velocity of 3×108 m/s and no mass. The electromagnetic spectrum, from low frequency to high frequency consists of:

Radiowaves < Microwaves < Infrared < Visible light < Ultraviolet < X-rays < Gamma rays

Note: W. C. Roentgen is the father of X-ray and the first medical X-ray by Roentgen was of his wife Anna Bertha's left hand. Physicists Peter Mansfield and Paul Lauterbur developed MRI-related imaging techniques in medicine and they were awarded the Nobel prize in 2003.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Advise HPV vaccine

The patient's 14-year-old daughter should be advised to take the HPV vaccine.

The patient's daughter is not at a higher risk for developing cervical cancer because it does not run in families. The etiology of cervical cancer is related to human papilloma virus (HPV) infection, and immunization against the virus is protective.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which pairing correctly matches the trauma patients brought to the casualty?
options: Penetrating injury to eustachian tube- CSF otorrhea
Penetrating injury to eye- Battle sign
questions.explanation: In clinical neurology and trauma assessment, specific physical signs are linked to localized brain injuries. A lesion in the midbrain (specifically the pretectal area or superior colliculi) characteristically results in vertical gaze palsy, a component of Parinaud's syndrome. Option A is incorrect because an extradural hemorrhage typically causes an ipsilateral dilated pupil (Hutchinson's pupil) due to uncal herniation compressing the oculomotor nerve, not a pinpoint pupil (which suggests pontine injury or opioid overdose). Option B is incorrect because CSF otorrhea results from a fracture of the petrous part of the temporal bone, not an isolated injury to the eustachian tube. Option C is incorrect as the Battle sign (ecchymosis over the mastoid) is a classic indicator of a base of skull fracture in the middle cranial fossa, not a direct eye injury. Therefore, the connection between gaze palsy and midbrain pathology is the only anatomically and clinically correct pairing provided in the list

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding the post mortem change shown in the image given below?
options: Due to sulphemoglobin accumulation and formation
Due to aseptic non bacterial cause
It is associated with a case of lightning
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Due to sulphemoglobin accumulation and formation

The postmortem change shown in the given image is marbling. It is seen when blood in the vessels is haemolysed to sulfmeth-hemoglobin, which stains the vessel walls and the adjacent tissues, giving rise to a marbled appearance.

Marbling:

The marbling of the skin begins at about 24 hours and becomes prominent in 36–48 hours after death. It is a visible postmortem change that is characterized by linear branching patterns on skin that correspond to the course of superficial veins. Intestinal bacteria infest the venous system and there is subsequent gas production and hemolysis which stains the vessel walls. This becomes prominent in the summer and is distinctly appreciable in the superficial veins of the abdomen, shoulders, chest, and inguinal region.

Lichtenberg's figures or filigree burns are pathognomonic for lightning injury. It is a superficial, thin, tortuous, fern-like pattern of erythema in the skin. It indicates the path taken by the electrical discharge and tends to follow skin creases and the long axis of the body. They are also known as arborescent burns or feathering as they have a resemblance to the branches of a tree. Lichtenberg's figures occur due to the rupture of small vessels. They are usually seen over the shoulder or flank within an hour of injury and disappear in 1-2 days.

Medico-legal aspect: Its recognition may be lifesaving in the unaccompanied comatose patient and is important because even delayed resuscitation of lightning victims can be very successful.

The image below shows the filigree burns seen in a case of lightning.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per the United Nations definition of a vital events registration system, vital events include which of the following? 1. Foetal deaths 2. School admissions 3. Legal separations 4. College graduations Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

A Vital Registration System (Civil Registration System) is defined by the United Nations as the continuous, permanent, compulsory, and universal recording of vital events occurring in a population. It provides the legal basis for vital statistics and demographic planning.

• 1. Foetal deaths ✓

• Fetal deaths (stillbirths) are recognized vital events and are included in the civil registration system.

• 2. School admissions ✗

• School admissions are administrative events, not vital events.

• 3. Legal separations ✓

• Legal separation is a vital event recognized by the UN because it affects civil status.

• 4. College graduations ✗

• Educational achievements are not vital events.
questions.learning: 1 and 3 A Vital Registration System (Civil Registration System) is defined by the United Nations as the continuous, permanent, compulsory, and universal recording of vital events occurring in a population.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In which phase of clinical trials is drug dosing done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phase I

The dosing of a new drug is tested in phase I of a clinical trial.

Phase I trials are usually performed on healthy volunteers to check the safety and pharmacokinetic properties of a drug. The participants in this phase do not gain any direct health benefits from taking part. They are generally paid a fee for their time, with the payments being regulated and not related to the risk involved.

In clinical trials, drug dosing typically occurs in Phase I, where researchers establish the optimal dose to achieve desired effects while minimizing side effects. In these phases, they focus on safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics.

Dose-ranging, primarily conducted in Phase II trials, involves testing multiple doses to identify the most effective and safe dose range. This phase helps determine the minimum effective dose and maximum tolerated dose, providing critical data for subsequent studies in Phase 3, where the chosen dose is tested for efficacy and safety in a larger population.
questions.learning: Phase I — The dosing of a new drug is tested in phase I of a clinical trial. Phase I trials are usually performed on healthy volunteers to check the safety and pharmacokinetic properties of a drug.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient complaining of vertigo without hearing loss has consulted an ENT surgeon. The surgeon performs a diagnostic maneuver and cautiously performs a therapeutic maneuver. What is the diagnostic maneuver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dix-Hallpike maneuver

The given clinical scenario of a patient with vertigo without hearing loss is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). The diagnostic maneuver used in BPPV is the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, the gold standard for diagnosing BPPV. The therapeutic maneuver is Epley's maneuver.

BPPV is characterized by vertigo, recurrent brief (<1 minute) episodes triggered by specific head movements, and is not associated with hearing loss or other neurological symptoms.

It is thought to be caused by the dislodgement of crystals of calcium carbonate from the degenerating macula of the utricle. When this crystal settles on the cupula of the posterior canal, it causes displacement of the cupula and vertigo.

A patient presenting with vertigo should be evaluated for ruling out the central lesions (like a tumor in the fourth ventricle, cerebellum, temporal lobe, or multiple sclerosis) before confirming the diagnosis of BPPV. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver helps to differentiate a peripheral from a central lesion.

Dix-Hallpike maneuver: The maneuver starts with the patient in a sitting position. Their head is turned 45 degrees towards the ear to be tested. Then the examiner quickly brings the patient to a supine position with their head 30 degrees below the horizontal. The 45-degree head rotation is maintained during the procedure. Now the examiner observes the patient for nystagmus.

The features of nystagmus differentiate between BPPV and central lesions:

Nystagmus
BPPV
Central lesions

Latency
2-20 seconds
No latency

Duration
<1 minute
>1 minute

Direction
fixed, towards the lower-placed ear
changing

The result on repetitions of the test
nystagmus is not seen (fatiguable)
nystagmus persists (nonfatiguable)

Symptoms during the test
severe vertigo
Absent/mild

The therapeutic maneuver is the Epley maneuver which displaces the otolith out of the posterior canal. This ends the sensation of vertigo with positional changes relieving the symptoms.
questions.learning: Dix-Hallpike maneuver — The given clinical scenario of a patient with vertigo without hearing loss is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with pruritic, hypopigmented macules and confluent patches on the chest. Skin scraping and KOH preparation show numerous yeast-like cells with short branching filaments, described as having a “spaghetti and meatballs” appearance. Which microorganism is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of hypopigmented macules on the chest (Pityriasis versicolor) and the pathognomonic "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on a KOH mount are diagnostic for Malassezia furfur. The "spaghetti" refers to the short, thick hyphae, and the "meatballs" refer to the clusters of round yeast cells. Trichophyton (Option B) causes dermatophytosis (ringworm) and would show long, branching septate hyphae. Candida (Option D) typically shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast on microscopy. Chlamydospores (Option C) are thick-walled resting spores seen in certain fungi but are not a causative agent. Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast that is part of the normal skin flora but overgrows in hot, humid conditions. Therefore, the unique visual pattern described and pictured definitively identifies Malassezia as the causative organism
questions.learning: The clinical description of hypopigmented macules on the chest (Pityriasis versicolor) and the pathognomonic "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on a KOH mount are diagnostic for Malassezia furfur.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following conditions are associated with oligohydramnios?
questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios is defined as an abnormally low volume of amniotic fluid. Since fetal urine is the primary source of amniotic fluid in the second and third trimesters, any condition that impairs fetal urine production leads to oligohydramnios. "Renal agenesis" (the absence of kidneys) is a classic cause, often resulting in Potter’s sequence due to compression of the fetus. Neural tube defects (Option B) and esophageal atresia (Option C) are characteristically associated with polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot effectively swallow the fluid (swallowing is the primary way amniotic fluid is removed). Premature birth (Option D) itself is not a primary cause, though preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) is a common clinical cause of low fluid. Other causes of oligohydramnios include placental insufficiency and posterior urethral valves. Monitoring via ultrasound is essential to prevent complications like pulmonary hypoplasia or limb deformities in the fetus
questions.learning: Oligohydramnios is defined as an abnormally low volume of amniotic fluid. Since fetal urine is the primary source of amniotic fluid in the second and third trimesters, any condition that impairs fetal urine production leads to oligohydramnios.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of colchicine?
options: Binds to tubulin and inhibits granulocyte migration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Binds to tubulin and inhibits granulocyte migration

Colchicine acts by binding to tubulin and inhibits granulocyte migration.

Colchicine produces its anti-inflammatory effects by binding to the intracellular protein tubulin. This prevents the polymerization of tubulin into microtubules which is necessary for leukocyte migration and phagocytosis. Inhibition of microtubule formation prevents granulocyte migration and also arrests cell division at G1 phase.
questions.learning: Binds to tubulin and inhibits granulocyte migration Colchicine acts by binding to tubulin and inhibits granulocyte migration. Colchicine produces its anti-inflammatory effects by binding to the intracellular protein tubulin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3

The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also know as common peroneal nerve)

The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve

Motor innervation

• Peroneus longus
• Peroneus brevis

• Extensor digitorum longus
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Tibialis anterior
• Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation

• Lateral aspect of the lower leg
• Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital web-space

• The first interdigital space

Injury to the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve) at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The ureter is safe in which type of hysterectomy?
questions.explanation: In vaginal hysterectomy, the ureter is considered to be at the lowest risk of injury compared to other surgical approaches. This is because the procedure is performed through the vaginal canal with minimal dissection near the ureters and fewer abdominal manipulations. In contrast, laparoscopic (Option B) and robotic (Option C) hysterectomies carry a higher risk of ureteric injury due to potential thermal damage from electrocautery and traction. Open laparotomy (Option A) also involves significant risk during the ligation of the uterine vessels or the cardinal ligaments where the ureter passes close by. While no surgery is entirely without risk, the anatomical approach used in vaginal hysterectomy provides the greatest degree of ureteric safety. Therefore, for patients without contraindications, the vaginal route is preferred for minimizing pelvic urinary tract complications

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Olfactory sensation is transmitted by all of the following nerves, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoglossal nerve

CN XII is a purely motor nerve supplying intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, with no sensory component.

Trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves contribute general sensory input (irritant, pungent stimuli) that modulates perceived olfactory sensation, but CN XII has no such role.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which type of graphical representation is most appropriate for demonstrating trends and variations over time in the incidence of diarrheal disease within a defined geographic area?
questions.explanation: A Line Graph is the best graphical tool for illustrating trends or changes over time for a single variable, such as the number of cases of diarrheal disease. By plotting the frequency of disease on the Y-axis against time (days, months, or years) on the X-axis, the line graph clearly shows seasonal patterns, outbreaks, or long-term declines resulting from public health interventions. A Histogram (Option B) is used to show the frequency distribution of a continuous variable at a single point in time but is less effective for showing a temporal trend. An Ogive (Option C) is a cumulative frequency graph. A Tree diagram (Option D) is used to show hierarchical relationships or decision-making paths. Therefore, because the question asks for "changes in occurrence," the line graph is the standard epidemiological choice for time-series data
questions.learning: A Line Graph is the best graphical tool for illustrating trends or changes over time for a single variable, such as the number of cases of diarrheal disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia undergoes prophylactic irradiation prior to autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Which of the following will be the least affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurons

Neurons are least susceptible to radiation. The radiosensitivity of biological tissue is directly proportional to its mitotic activity and inversely proportional to its degree of differentiation. This is known as the law of Bergonie and Tribondeau.

Hence, hematopoietic cells are the most radiosensitive, and the central nervous system is the least sensitive to radiation.

Acute Radiation Syndromes (ARS) is an acute illness that is caused by exposure of the entire body to a high dose of penetrating radiation in a very short period of time. It is also known as radiation toxicity or radiation sickness. It consists of three syndromes:

Syndrome
Radiation dose

Hematopoietic (Bone marrow)
>0.7 Gy

Gastrointestinal
>10 Gy

Cardiovascular/ Central nervous system
>50 Gy

Stages of ARS:

• Prodromal stage - This stage starts within minutes of exposure and may continue for a few days. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and anorexia.
• Latent stage - It begins within a few hours and continues up to a few weeks. The patient generally feels healthy.
• Manifest illness stage - This stage may continue up to months and symptoms vary according to the syndrome.
• Recovery/ death - The recovery process occurs over two years. Recovery cannot be expected in cardiovascular and central nervous system syndromes, which lead to death.
questions.learning: Neurons Neurons are least susceptible to radiation. The radiosensitivity of biological tissue is directly proportional to its mitotic activity and inversely proportional to its degree of differentiation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: True statement for oxytocin?
options: It can be given by oral route
It is secreted by anterior pituitary
In higher doses, it exerts diuretic like action
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone with several critical reproductive functions. The only true statement provided is that it is responsible for galactokinesis (Option A), which is the "milk let-down" or milk ejection reflex. It causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli. It is NOT given by the oral route (Option B) because it is a peptide and would be digested; it is given parenterally or intranasally. It is synthesized in the hypothalamus and stored/secreted by the posterior pituitary, not the anterior (Option C). Crucially, in high doses, oxytocin has an anti-diuretic effect (similar to ADH) due to cross-reactivity with V2 receptors, which can lead to water intoxication (Option D is the opposite). Therefore, its role in milk ejection is its definitive physiological hallmark
questions.learning: Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone with several critical reproductive functions. The only true statement provided is that it is responsible for galactokinesis (Option A), which is the "milk let-down" or milk ejection reflex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In malignant hyperthermia, a genetic mutation in the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) causes a potentially fatal reaction to certain anaesthetics. What is the primary ionic abnormality caused by this receptor?
options: Excessive calcium influx from extracellular fluid
Reduced ATP binding to actin-myosin complex
Excessive calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle
Defective sodium channel leading to muscle hyperexcitability
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Excessive calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle

The primary ionic abnormality caused by mutation in the RyR1 receptor is excessive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle.

Malignant hyperthermia is a genetic condition in which mutated RyR1 receptors are present in the skeletal muscles. In the presence of certain triggers, this mutated RyR1 causes severe dysfunction in the RyR1 channels. This causes abnormal calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to excessive cytoplasmic calcium concentration, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, rigidity, increased heat production, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, and increased end-tidal CO₂. Patients with positive family histories and patients with congenital myopathies are at increased risk for the development of this condition.

The process of sequestering excess Ca²⁺ consumes large amounts of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and generates excess heat (hyperthermia). The muscle cell is damaged by ATP depletion and high temperatures, and cellular constituents "leak" into the circulation, including potassium, myoglobin, creatine, phosphate, and creatine kinase.

The key clinical features are

* Succinylcholine-induced masseter muscle rigidity (causing trismus) or generalized muscle rigidity

* Tachycardia

* Hypercarbia (increased CO₂ production) and reduced oxygen saturation

* Hyperthermia (rise of 1° Celsius can occur every 5 minutes)

* Arrhythmia

* Hypertension

* Myoglobinuria and myoglobinaemia indicate muscle damage

* Metabolic derangements like hyperkalemia and mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis

When volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine are used, malignant hyperthermia should be suspected in case of an unexpected rise in end-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂). This is considered to be one of the earliest and most sensitive indicators of malignant hyperthermia. It can be supported by taking arterial blood gas reports with metabolic acidosis.

Treatment is to discontinue the triggering agents, i.e., succinylcholine, followed by administration of 100% oxygen. Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice. It is given rapidly at a dose of 2.5 mg/kg intravenously and can be repeated every 5-10 minutes till the attack subsides. Metabolic acidosis and hyperkalaemia need to be corrected. Hyperthermia must be controlled by cooling the patient. Continuous monitoring in intensive care is required for 24 to 48 hours.

Dantrolene is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant that acts on the RyR1 (ryanodine receptor) calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscles and inhibits calcium-induced calcium release. This results in the uncoupling of membrane depolarisation and muscle contraction, thus inhibiting muscle contraction.

Drugs triggering malignant hyperthermia:

* Succinylcholine

* Halothane

* Isoflurane

* Sevoflurane

Pearl PF1601: Malignant hyperthermia key features

Pathophysiology:

* Prolonged opening of functionally altered ryanodine receptors, leading to uncontrolled release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum resulting in sustained muscle contraction.

Drugs known to trigger malignant hyperthermia:

* Inhaled anesthetics: Halothane, Isoflurane, Sevoflurane, Desflurane, Ether, Methoxyflurane

* Depolarising muscle relaxant: Succinylcholine

Clinical signs:

* Increased metabolism: Increased EtCO2, decreased SpO2, metabolic acidosis

* Increased sympathetic activity: Tachycardia, hypertension, arrythmia

* Muscle damage: Masseter spasm, generalised rigidity, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria

* Hyperthermia: Fever, sweating

Treatment:

* Discontinuation of all anesthetic agents

* Hyperventilation with 100% O2

* Dantrolene: 2.5 mg/kg intravenously every 5 min until the episode is terminated (upper limit - 10 mg/kg).

* Correction of acid-base, electrolyte abnormality

* Cooling the patient
questions.learning: Excessive calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle The primary ionic abnormality caused by mutation in the RyR1 receptor is excessive calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Given below is an illustration of a transverse section of the heart. Identify the marked structure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sub-aortic curtain

The marked structure is the sub-aortic curtain. It is also called the trigonum fibrosum sinistrum.

The fibrous skeleton of the heart is formed by fibrous tissue that is continuous between the atrio-ventricular and arterial orifices. They exist to keep the valves competent, allow attachment of cardiac musculature, and act as an insulating layer for the conducting system of the heart. The fibrous rings of importance are:

• The atrioventricular fibrous rings - existing in a figure of 8 configuration, connecting the atria, ventricles and the membranous part of the interventricular septum.
• The trigonum fibrosum dextrum - between the atrioventricular rings and the aortic ring.
• The trigonum fibrosum sinistrum - between the mitral valve and the aortic valve.
questions.learning: Sub-aortic curtain — The marked structure is the sub-aortic curtain. It is also called the trigonum fibrosum sinistrum.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman presents with decreased fetal movements, and her newborn shows respiratory distress. On examination, the neonate is cyanotic with increased work of breathing, and bowel sounds are auscultated in the left hemithorax. A chest X-ray is provided. Which congenital anomaly is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical finding of bowel sounds in the left hemithorax combined with severe neonatal respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen is diagnostic for Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH). The X-ray confirms this by showing multiple loops of air-filled bowel occupying the left chest and a contralateral shift of the mediastinum. CDH results from a failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close (Bochdalek hernia). The presence of abdominal contents in the chest prevents normal lung development, leading to life-threatening pulmonary hypoplasia and hypertension. Tetralogy of Fallot (Option B) and Transposition (Option C) are cyanotic heart diseases that would show normal lung fields and no bowel in the thorax. Tracheoesophageal fistula (Option D) typically presents with excessive salivation and choking during feeds. Management of CDH involves immediate stabilization with intubation (avoiding bag-mask to prevent bowel distension), gentle ventilation, and eventual surgical repair of the diaphragm once pulmonary pressures are controlled
questions.learning: The clinical finding of bowel sounds in the left hemithorax combined with severe neonatal respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen is diagnostic for Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended work area per worker in a factory, assuming that any height above a certain limit is disregarded in the calculation?
questions.explanation: The Factories Act in India establishes strict guidelines to prevent overcrowding and ensure worker safety and ventilation. Every workroom must provide at least 500 cubic feet of space for every individual worker employed therein. When calculating this volume, the Act specifies that any height above 14 feet (approximately 4.25 meters) from the floor is not taken into account. This rule ensures that employers provide sufficient horizontal floor area rather than meeting the requirement through very high ceilings in cramped rooms. Options A, C, and D (100, 300, and 400) are below the legal safety threshold. Maintaining this standard is essential for reducing the spread of airborne infections, minimizing heat stress, and ensuring that workers have enough room to operate machinery without accidental collisions. Compliance with these spacing requirements is a critical part of regular occupational health and safety inspections

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl is admitted for evaluation for recurrent seizures. She has a large port-wine stain on the right side of her face as shown below. The MRI of the head shows a leptomeningeal angioma. What is the most common ocular manifestation of the underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glaucoma

The given clinical picture of a young child presenting with unilateral port wine stain in the region of trigeminal nerve supply and leptomeningeal angioma as seen on MRI is indicative of Sturge-Webber syndrome (SWS). Glaucoma is the most common ocular manifestation of SWS.

Sturge weber syndrome is a neurocutaneous disorder(phakomatoses) that is characterized by unilateral capillary malformation at the region of trigeminal supply known as port wine stain or nevus flammeus, ipsilateral diffuse cavernous hemangioma of the choroid and ipsilateral leptomeningeal hemangiomatosis, which causes seizures and mental retardation.

Ocular manifestation of SWS include:

• Glaucoma - most common ocular manifestation. It develops anywhere between infancy to adulthood. When developed in infancy it presents as buphthalmos.
• Diffuse choroidal hemangioma
• Serous retinal detachment
• Visual field defects- homonymous hemianopia due to the leptomeningeal hemangiomas affecting the optic tract or occipital lobe.
• Heterochromia of the iris
• Episcleral and conjunctival lesions

Option A: Uveitis is the inflammation of the uveal tissue of the eyes. It can be associated with a number of systemic conditions such as sarcoidosis, behcet's disease, ankylosing spondylitis, reiter's syndrome,Toxoplasmosis and Posner–Schlossman syndrome (PSS).

Option B: Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited or acquired pigmentatory retinal dystrophy affecting the rods more. The earliest manifestation is worsening of night blindness which gradually progresses to tunnel vision and ultimately loss of central vision. The classic triad of findings in RP comprises bone-spicule retinal pigmentation, arteriolar attenuation and waxy disc pallor.

Systemic Associations of RP include:

• Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome
• Cockayne's syndrome
• Refsum's syndrome
• Usher's syndrome
• Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome

The below given image shows the classical triad findings of Retinitis pigmentosa.

Option C:Keratitis is the inflammation of cornea which is characterised by corneal edema, cellular infiltration and ciliary congestion. It can be either infectious or non-infectious in nature which includes allergic keratitis, neurotrophic keratitis, exposure keratitis and peripheral ulcerative keratopathies such as Rosacea keratitis and Mooren's ulcer.
questions.learning: Glaucoma — The given clinical picture of a young child presenting with unilateral port wine stain in the region of trigeminal nerve supply and leptomeningeal angioma as seen on MRI is indicative of Sturge-Webber syndrome (SWS).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When assessing Polycystic Ovary Disease/ Syndrome (PCOD/PCOS), which is associated with multiple clinical features and hormonal abnormalities, which of the following parameters or findings is typically evaluated in this condition?
questions.explanation: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS/PCOD) is a complex endocrine disorder defined by the Rotterdam criteria, which include ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism. Consequently, measuring serum testosterone levels is a fundamental biochemical study used to document the hyperandrogenism characteristic of the condition. While women with PCOS have a higher incidence of obstructive sleep apnea (making a sleep study, Option B, occasionally relevant) and may have metabolic issues (urine study, Option A, for glucose), these are not the primary diagnostic studies for the syndrome itself. Elevated free or total testosterone supports the diagnosis in patients presenting with hirsutism, acne, and irregular periods. Other relevant studies include the LH:FSH ratio (often increased) and fasting insulin levels to assess insulin resistance. Therefore, among the options provided, serum testosterone is the most direct and standard laboratory investigation used to characterize the hormonal derangement in PCOD, aiding in the differentiation from other causes of virilization

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant presents with hypotonia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and acid maltase deficiency. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pompe's disease

Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid α-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency (GAA gene mutation), resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation. The infantile form classically presents with hypotonia (“floppy baby”), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, feeding difficulties, respiratory insufficiency, and markedly elevated CK levels. Enzyme replacement therapy (alglucosidase alfa) is the treatment of choice and significantly improves survival when initiated early.

Why not the other options?

• B. Cori disease (GSD III): Debranching enzyme deficiency; hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, and myopathy; cardiomyopathy may occur but acid maltase deficiency is absent.
• C. McArdle disease (GSD V): Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency; presents with exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, and myoglobinuria, not infantile cardiomyopathy.
• D. Andersen disease (GSD IV): Branching enzyme deficiency; causes progressive liver cirrhosis and hepatosplenomegaly, not acid maltase deficiency.
questions.learning: Pompe's disease Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid α-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency (GAA gene mutation), resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: How is a 'Case' of tuberculosis defined according to standard medical guidelines?
questions.explanation: This question is a duplicate from the source, re-emphasizing the definition of a TB case. A definitive diagnosis of tuberculosis requires the detection of the pathogen. Sputum positive status (Option B) (either by smear, culture, or molecular test) is the gold standard for defining a "microbiologically confirmed case." This is the highest priority for public health because these patients are actively shedding the bacteria. X-ray (Option A) is a screening tool used to identify lung damage. Mantoux (Option C) is an immunological test for exposure. A history of cough (Option D) for more than two weeks is the primary trigger for investigation but does not constitute a diagnosis . Modern guidelines have shifted to include "clinically diagnosed cases" where microbiology is negative but symptoms and imaging are highly suggestive, but the classic epidemiological definition for reporting still prioritizes the sputum-positive status to ensure accurate disease tracking and transmission control

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with Prinzmetal angina is administered isosorbide mononitrate and is noticed to have symptomatic relief. What is the mechanism of action of nitrate in this case?
options: Increased left ventricular end diastolic volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endothelium independent coronary vasodilation

The mechanism of action of nitrates in prinzmetal angina is endothelium-independent coronary vasodilatation.

Prinzmetal angina occurs due to vasospasm of the coronary arteries. Nitrates relax the smooth muscles of epicardial coronary arteries and relieve coronary artery spasm.

In the case of stable angina, the primary mechanism of action of nitrates is preferential dilatation of veins (by increasing cGMP). Venous dilatation leads to a decrease in the venous return to the heart (preload). This decreases the ventricular end-diastolic volume and thereby a decrease in myocardial oxygen consumption. The diastolic perfusion pressure (aortic blood pressure in diastole - left ventricular pressure in diastole) is increased.
questions.learning: Endothelium independent coronary vasodilation — The mechanism of action of nitrates in prinzmetal angina is endothelium-independent coronary vasodilatation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old primigravida in labor is being augmented with oxytocin. On abdominal examination, the fetal head is 5/5 palpable. Following artificial rupture of membranes (ARM), there is a sudden onset of fetal bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cord prolapse

Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency that should be suspected when artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is followed by sudden fetal bradycardia, particularly if the presenting part is high and unengaged (5/5 palpable abdominally). The unengaged fetal head allows the umbilical cord to slip below the presenting part, resulting in cord compression and acute fetal hypoxia.

Why not the other options?

• B. Uterine rupture: Presents with severe abdominal pain, cessation of contractions, maternal instability, and fetal distress, usually in women with a previous uterine scar.
• C. Abruptio placentae: Characterized by painful vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and fetal distress; not classically precipitated by ARM.
• D. Precipitate labor: Refers to labor lasting <3 hours and is not associated with sudden fetal bradycardia immediately after membrane rupture.
questions.learning: Cord prolapse Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency that should be suspected when artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is followed by sudden fetal bradycardia, particularly if the presenting part is high and unengaged (5/5 palpable abdominally).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: OCPs can be given in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are safe for use in women with HIV infection. While clinicians must monitor for potential drug-drug interactions with certain antiretroviral therapies, HIV itself is not a contraindication to their use. In contrast, moderate to severe Hypertension (HTN) (Option A) is a contraindication because estrogen increases the risk of stroke and myocardial infarction. Diabetes Mellitus (DM) (Option B) with vascular complications or a duration of >20 years is a contraindication due to heightened cardiovascular risk. Hyperlipidemia (Option D) is also a contraindication as OCPs can further alter lipid profiles and increase the risk of arterial thrombosis. Therefore, among the choices provided, HIV is the only condition where OCP use is generally acceptable

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Which of the following is true regarding CORADS?

CORADS- COVID-19 Reporting and Data System
options: Pleural thickening is typical of COVID-19
Lobar consolidation is typical of COVID-19
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19

Among the given options, CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 is the true statement.

COVID-19 Reporting and Data System (CO-RADS) is a categorical assessment for pulmonary involvement of COVID-19 on chest CT.

CO-RADS Category
Summary

CO-RADS 0
Scans are incomplete or of inferior quality

CO-RADS 1
Normal or non-infectious

CO-RADS 2
Typical features of other infections but not of COVID-19

CO-RADS 3
Features compatible with COVID-19 but also with other diseases

CO-RADS 4
Suspicious for COVID-19

CO-RADS 5
Typical for COVID-19

CO-RADS 6
Proven COVID-19 by positive RT-PCR test

CO-RADS categories:

• CO-RADS 0: Not interpretable - Technically insufficient to assign a score: Scans are incomplete or of inferior quality.
• CO-RADS 1: Very low level of suspicion for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Mild or severe emphysema, perifissural nodules, lung tumors, or fibrosis.
• CO-RADS 2: Low level of suspicion for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Includes infectious etiology that is not compatible with COVID-19 such as bronchitis, bronchiolitis, bronchopneumonia, lobar pneumonia, abscess.
• CO-RADS 3: Equivocal findings for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Findings overlap with other viral or infectious etiologies. Could include perihilar ground-glass, homogenous extensive ground-glass with or without sparing of secondary pulmonary lobules.
• CO-RADS 4: High level of suspicion for pulmonary involvement by COVID-19. Findings are similar to CO-RADS 5 but are not present in the typical locations. Findings may also be superimposed on severe pre-existing pulmonary abnormalities.
• CO-RADS 5 based on typical CT findings. It requires the presence of at least one confirmatory pattern (mentioned below).
• CO-RADS 6: Proven COVID-19 by positive RT-PCR test.

CT features typical of pulmonary involvement in COVID-19 include:

• Obligatory features

• Ground glass opacities, with or without consolidation in areas close to the visceral pleural surface, including the fissures.

• Confirmatory features

• Ground glass regions
• Crazy paving pattern
• Organizing pneumonia compatible patterns
• Thickened vessels with parenchymal abnormalities
questions.learning: CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 Among the given options, CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 is the true statement. COVID-19 Reporting and Data System (CO-RADS) is a categorical assessment for pulmonary involvement of COVID-19 on chest CT.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man develops headache, nausea, and breathlessness while trekking at high altitude. To relieve his symptoms, the physician prescribes a medication. This drug primarily acts on which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from acute mountain sickness (AMS) due to high-altitude hypoxia. The standard pharmacological intervention is acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that primarily acts on the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron. By inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the PCT, the drug prevents bicarbonate reabsorption, leading to mild metabolic acidosis. This acidosis stimulates the central respiratory centers, prompting compensatory hyperventilation which increases blood oxygenation and alleviates AMS symptoms. Regarding the distractors, loop diuretics (Option B), thiazides (Option C), and potassium-sparing diuretics (Option D) act on different segments of the nephron and do not address the physiological causes of altitude sickness. Therefore, the PCT is the specific site where acetazolamide exerts its therapeutic effect for mountain climbers
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from acute mountain sickness (AMS) due to high-altitude hypoxia. The standard pharmacological intervention is acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that primarily acts on the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the nephron.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is responsible for ear pain after a tonsillectomy surgery ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glossopharyngeal nerve

The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia after a tonsillectomy.

The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal nerve and the styloid process lie in relation to the lower part of the tonsillar fossa. Therefore, any irritation or pain can be referred to the ear along the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal (Jacobson's) nerve.

Image below shows the anatomic relations of tonsil and tonsillar bed.

The ear receives an extensive sensory innervation via four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) and two spinal segments (C2 and C3).

Jacobson's nerve, along with branches from the sympathetic plexus forms the tympanic plexus. This plexus provides sensation to the middle ear, upper eustachian tube, and medial surface of the tympanic membrane. Referred otalgia transmitted by the glossopharyngeal nerve may be secondary to lesions and/or inflammatory processes of the nasopharynx, palatine tonsil, soft palate, or posterior one-third of the tongue.

Causes of referred otalgia via glossopharyngeal nerve:

* Acute pharyngitis

* Tonsillitis

* Peritonsillitis

* Peritonsillar abscess

* Post-tonsillectomy

* Foreign bodies embedded in the base of the tongue or tonsillar area

* Elongated styloid process
