questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which action of a midwife is considered harmful to a newborn baby in the immediate postnatal period?
options: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab
Giving a bath immediately after birth
Helping to initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour
Placing the baby on the mother’s chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Giving a bath immediately after birth

The harmful practice in the immediate postnatal period is giving a bath immediately after birth. Newborn infants are highly prone to heat loss because their body surface area is relatively large, subcutaneous fat is thin, and heat production mechanisms are limited.

Bathing immediately after birth increases evaporative and conductive heat loss, which can cause hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, and respiratory stress in the newborn. Thus, delaying the first bath is essential to avoid cold stress and to allow skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding, which help in maintaining warmth.

Heat loss occurs by four mechanisms:

* convection of heat energy to the cooler surrounding air

* conduction of heat to the colder materials touching the infant,

* heat radiation from the infant to other nearby cooler objects

* evaporation from skin and lungs.

Other options:

Option A: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab is a routine hygienic practice in newborn care.

Option C: Initiating breastfeeding within 1 hour is strongly recommended, since it provides colostrum, enhances immunity, and strengthens mother-infant bonding.

Option D: Skin-to-skin contact on the mother’s chest is a recommended practice for thermal regulation, bonding, and successful initiation of breastfeeding.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient has multiple blood clots in the urine following a TURP procedure. Which catheter should be used for irrigation in this patient? Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 22 French Foley's 3-Way catheter

22 French Foley's 3-Way Catheter is the most appropriate choice for this patient with blood clots after a TURP procedure.

The 3-way Foley catheter includes an additional channel for continuous bladder irrigation, making it essential for managing gross hematuria, post-prostate surgery care, and clot evacuation; this third channel allows for simultaneous inflow of irrigation fluid while maintaining continuous drainage.

Three-way Foley catheter, shown below, is used for irrigation and helps in preventing clot retention following surgeries like TURP.

Other options:

Option B: A 22 French 2-way Foley catheter, the most commonly used type, has two channels - one for urine drainage and one for balloon inflation, making it suitable for routine bladder drainage and post-operative care.

Option C: A 22 French 4-way Foley catheter, less commonly used, has an extra channel typically used for pressure monitoring or additional irrigation capabilities, particularly useful in complex urological procedures or when precise pressure monitoring is required.

Option D: The McKonly catheter, distinct from the Foley types, is specifically designed for suprapubic placement and features a curved tip and specialized drainage system; it's particularly useful for long-term bladder drainage in patients who cannot have urethral catheterization or require extended catheterization periods, though it requires surgical placement through the abdominal wall.

Pearl PF1865: Foley's catheter

A Foley catheter is a thin, sterile tube inserted into the bladder to drain urine. Because it can be left in place in the bladder for a period of time, it is also called an indwelling catheter.

French scale corresponds to the external circumference in millimetres. French size divided by 3 will give the outer diameter of the catheter.

Fr. size = 3 x d, where d is the outer diameter in mm.

A 3 Fr. catheter will have a circumference of approximately 3 mm and a diameter of 1 mm.

Note:

Colour of the foleys is the colour at the baloon port as shown in the figure below

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In ectopic pregnancy, where is the most frequent site of implantation?
questions.explanation: Ectopic pregnancy most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, which is labeled as A in the image. The ampulla is the widest and longest part of the tube and is the usual site of fertilization. Because fertilization occurs here, any delay in the movement of the fertilized ovum toward the uterus can lead to implantation at this site. Approximately 70% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the ampullary region. Its relatively thin wall and rich blood supply make it prone to distension and rupture if implantation occurs. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Ovary: Ovarian pregnancy is rare (C) Cervix: Very rare site of ectopic implantation (D) Uterus: This is the normal site for implantation, not ectopic

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 65-year-old treated leprosy patient came with complaints of a well-demarcated, non-tender ulcer on his foot with hyperkeratotic borders as given below for the last 3 months. What should be the appropriate next step?
options: Rest the limb, non weight bearing splints and foot care
Admit the patient and aggressive debridement and antibiotics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rest the limb, non weight bearing splints and foot care

The given scenario and the image indicate a neuropathic ulcer. This can be managed by limb rest, utilising non-weight-bearing splints, and administering foot care.

Leprosy, a condition affecting the skin and peripheral nerves, results in peripheral neuropathy and subsequent loss of sensation. This can lead to the development of chronic trophic or neuropathic ulcers characterised by punched-out appearance, regular margins, and calluses due to repeated trauma in the presence of anaesthesia of feet.
Management primarily focuses on relieving pressure through the application of non-weight bearing splints for even pressure distribution across the entire foot, limb elevation to mitigate swelling, and regular foot inspection to promptly identify trauma, in addition to the use of microcellular rubber footwear.

Other options:

Option A: Trophic ulcers are not an indication for restarting MDT in an already treated leprosy patient.
Option C: Due to the absence of debris or signs of infection in the ulcer, aggressive debridement and antibiotics are not indicated.
Option D: As there are no signs of vascular compromise or gangrene, amputation of the limb is not required.

questions.text: Identify the test shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schirmer test

The image shows a tear strip placed in the lower lid of the eye. This is the Schirmer test which is used to check for dry eye.

Treatment of dry eye include medical treatment (lubricating eyedrops, most commonly methylcellulose derivatives) or surgical treatment (lacrimal punctum occlusion using silicone plugs)

Option B: To measure tear film break-up time(TBUT), fluorescein is instilled into the patient's tear film and the patient is asked not to blink while the tear film is observed under a broad beam of cobalt blue illumination. The TBUT is recorded as the number of seconds that elapse between the last blink and the appearance of the first dry spot in the tear film.

Option C: In rose Bengal staining, the eye is stained using the rose Bengal stain.

Option D: A tear osmolarity test is performed using a handheld sampler that collects a very small sample of tear fluid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with blurred vision, dizziness, and a severe headache after consuming an unknown amount of homemade alcohol earlier the same day. He is disoriented on examination, and laboratory investigations show a high–anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which metabolite is primarily responsible for the toxicity in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of blurred ("snowfield") vision, dizziness, and metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap after consuming homemade alcohol are classic for methanol poisoning. Methanol (Option A) itself is not directly toxic. It is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde (Option C), which is then rapidly converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase into formic acid. Formic acid is the primary metabolite responsible for the toxicity; it inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia, optic neuropathy, and severe metabolic acidosis. Acetic acid (Option D) is the non-toxic product of ethanol metabolism. Formaldehyde is an intermediate but is too short-lived to be the primary driver of systemic toxicity. Treatment involves ethanol or fomepizole to block the formation of these toxic metabolites
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of blurred ("snowfield") vision, dizziness, and metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap after consuming homemade alcohol are classic for methanol poisoning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident is assessed and found to have a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10. Based on this score, how would the severity of the head injury be classified?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the universal clinical tool used to categorize the severity of traumatic brain injuries (TBI). Head injuries are classified based on the following total GCS scores: 1. GCS 13–15: Mild TBI (Option D) or Minor TBI (Option C) 2. GCS 9–12: Moderate TBI (Option A) 3. GCS 3–8: Severe TBI (Option B) A score of 10 falls clearly within the intermediate range. Patients with a moderate TBI are typically conscious but often confused or lethargic and may have significant neurological deficits. They require urgent CT imaging and close monitoring, as they are at risk for secondary brain injury or deterioration into the "severe" category. Therefore, based on the standardized GCS-severity scale, a patient with a score of 10 is definitively classified as having a moderate traumatic brain injury
questions.learning: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the universal clinical tool used to categorize the severity of traumatic brain injuries (TBI). Head injuries are classified based on the following total GCS scores: 1.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding pathological findings of placenta accreta? 1. Absence of decidua basalis 2. Absence of Nitabuch’s fibrinoid layer 3. Loss of normal hypoechoic retroplacental myometrial zone in ultrasonography Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is characterized by abnormal adherence of the placenta to the uterine wall due to defective decidualization. It occurs because of absence or deficiency of the decidua basalis and Nitabuch’s fibrinoid layer, allowing chorionic villi to attach directly to or invade the myometrium. Ultrasound is the primary modality for antenatal diagnosis.

• 1. Absence of decidua basalis ✓

• The fundamental pathological defect in placenta accreta is the absence or deficiency of the decidua basalis, permitting abnormal placental attachment.

• 2. Absence of Nitabuch’s fibrinoid layer ✓

• Nitabuch’s layer normally separates the placenta from the myometrium. Its absence facilitates abnormal trophoblastic invasion.

• 3. Loss of normal hypoechoic retroplacental myometrial zone on ultrasonography ✓

• One of the characteristic ultrasound findings is loss of the retroplacental clear (hypoechoic) zone, suggesting placental invasion into the myometrium.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is characterized by abnormal adherence of the placenta to the uterine wall due to defective decidualization.

questions.text: Quadruple testing is done during:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 15-20 weeks

The quadruple screening test is ideally done in the second trimester, during 15-20 weeks of gestation. The most accurate values are seen during 16-18 weeks of gestation.

It is the measurement of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP), unconjugated estriol, hCG, and inhibin-A.

In Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) or Edward's syndrome (trisomy 18), quadruple-marker screenings do not provide any added benefit over first-trimester screenings. It is generally used as a stand-alone test if screening is done for the first time in the second trimester or if first-trimester screening is not available.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is used as an abortive treatment for cluster headache?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sumatriptan

For aborting an acute attack of cluster headache, subcutaneous sumatriptan (6 mg), a selective 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor agonist, is most effective.

High-flow oxygen is also effective in the management of an acute attack. 100% oxygen at 10–12 L/min for 15–20 min is required as treatment. If injectable sumatriptan is unavailable, then high-flow oxygen is the next best treatment option.

Verapamil is the best prophylactic treatment for cluster headaches to reduce the frequency and severity of cluster headaches. Verapamil, which is a calcium channel blocker, is the drug of choice for the long-term prophylaxis of cluster headaches.

Cluster headache is characterised by severe, one-sided headaches that occur in clusters, often associated with autonomic symptoms, such as tearing, redness of the eye, runny nose and unilateral headache that typically lasts between 15 to 180 minutes. The important feature of this headache is periodicity. At least one of the daily attacks of pain recurs at the same hour each day. It is also associated with autonomic features, such as unilateral lacrimation and rhinorrhoea. Occasionally, features of Horner's syndrome may be seen.

The typical cluster headache patient has daily bouts of one to two attacks of relatively short-duration unilateral pain for 8–10 weeks a year; this is usually followed by a pain-free interval that averages a little less than 1 year.

The acute (abortive) management relies on therapies that terminate the attack quickly, whereas prophylactic treatment prevents recurrence during cluster periods.

The treatment includes:

Abortive treatment:

* Sumatriptan (subcutaneous or intranasal) is the first-line abortive therapy, highly effective in rapidly terminating attacks.

* High-flow oxygen inhalation (100% O₂, 7–10 L/min for 15 min) is safe, fast-acting, and commonly used.

* Non-invasive vagal nerve stimulation (nVNS) has also been shown to abort attacks in some patients and is FDA-approved.

Prophylactic treatment: Depends on the length of bouts and whether the patient suffers from chronic cluster headaches (period of remission less than 3 months while not medicated)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the instrument shown below that is used to create a pneumoperitoneum ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Veress needle

The given image showing a long, slender laparoscopic instrument is Veress Needle. It is used in direct puncture laparoscopy to produce a pneumoperitoneum.

Direct puncture laparoscopy (closed method):

1. The abdominal wall is grasped with towel clips or fingers to elevate the abdominal wall away from the underlying structures.
2. A small incision is made in the umbilicus and the Veress needle is introduced into the abdomen. Two distinct pops can be felt as the needle pierces the abdominal wall fascia and the peritoneum.

The umbilicus is the preferred location for introducing a Vereess needle because the abdominal wall is thin at this location.

Carbon dioxide (CO2) gas is usually used and the maximum pressure is in the range of 14-15 mmHg. But N2O is used if the procedure is done under local anesthesia. Insufflation with N2O is stopped at a pressure of 10 mmHg or when 2L of gas is insufflated.

The Hasson Trocar is used to gain access to the peritoneal cavity and generate pneumoperitoneum by the open direct peritoneal access technique (option C). This is known as the Hasson technique and is done only occasionally. It is preferred for patients who have undergone previous abdominal surgeries as the small bowel may be adherent to the undersurface of the abdominal wound in such cases.

Other options:

Option B: Salah's needle is a type of reusable bone marrow biopsy needle that has a guard situated 2 cm from the tip and a side screw.

Option D: Von Graefe needle (also known as Graefe's knife) is primarily used in ophthalmic surgery.
questions.learning: Veress needle — The given image showing a long, slender laparoscopic instrument is Veress Needle. It is used in direct puncture laparoscopy to produce a pneumoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In a case where an Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive infant and the newborn has a positive Coombs test, what is the underlying mechanism responsible for this hypersensitivity reaction?:
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes Erythroblastosis Fetalis (Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn), which is a classic Type II hypersensitivity reaction. In this condition, maternal IgG antibodies against the Rh antigen cross the placenta and bind to the baby's Rh-positive red blood cells. These antibody-coated cells are then recognized and destroyed by the fetal splenic macrophages through the process of Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC). Option A is a non-standard term. Option C refers to Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex diseases like SLE). Option D refers to Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity (like the TB skin test). The positive Coombs test confirms that antibodies are already bound to the fetal RBC surface. Therefore, the direct destruction of cells mediated by specific antibodies identifies ADCC as the definitive immunological mechanism in Rh incompatibility

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Name the location of the nucleus supplying the muscle marked by the arrow in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superior colliculus

The muscle marked is the medial rectus. The medial rectus is supplied by the oculomotor nerve, the nucleus of which is situated at the level of the superior colliculus in the posterior midbrain.

The oculomotor (3rd cranial) nerve nucleus consists of

• Single central nuclei for the levator palpebrae muscle of both the eyes
• Bilateral subnuclei with crossed projections supplying the contralateral superior rectus
• Bilateral subnuclei with uncrossed projections supplying the ipsilateral inferior rectus, inferior oblique, medial rectus in the dorso-ventral order.
• Bilateral subnuclei known as the Edinger-Westphal nucleus which provides parasympathetic input to the ciliary body and the iris sphincter.

Option A: Superior olivary nucleus is an important relay station in the auditory pathway, it is responsible for detection of direction and localization of sound.

Option B: Inferior colliculus- The trochlear(4th cranial) nerve nucleus lies in the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. The trochlear nerves leave the midbrain from its posterior surface and decussate before supplying the contralateral superior oblique muscle of the eyeball.

Option D: Facial colliculus- the facial colliculus is located in the cranial part of the pons. It is produced by the facial nerve(7th cranial nerve) winding around the nucleus of the abducens nerve (6th cranial nerve).
questions.learning: Superior colliculus — The muscle marked is the medial rectus. The medial rectus is supplied by the oculomotor nerve, the nucleus of which is situated at the level of the superior colliculus in the posterior midbrain.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following options is false in a patient with advanced liver disease?
options: Increased synthesis of glutamine and glutamate from alpha-ketoglutarate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto glutarate

Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate is not seen in a patient with advanced liver disease. Option C is false.

Normally, ammonia, a toxic by-product of protein catabolism, is excreted as urea upon being metabolised in the urea cycle, which takes place in the liver. In advanced liver disease, impaired ammonia metabolism leads to hyperammonemia. Ammonia withdraws α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate and glutamine. This leads to lowered concentrations of all citric acid cycle intermediates, and hence reduced generation of ATP.

The Krebs cycle involves a sequence of reactions occurring in mitochondria that oxidize the acetyl moiety of acetyl-CoA to CO2 and reduces the coenzymes that are reoxidized through the electron transport chain. It is the final common pathway for the oxidation of carbohydrates, lipids, and protein also has a central role in gluconeogenesis, lipogenesis, and interconversion of amino acids. Although processes occur in many tissues, the liver is the only tissue in which all occur to a significant extent.

The reactions that occur in Kreb's cycle are shown in the image below.

One of the steps of the Krebs cycle involves α-ketoglutarate undergoing oxidative decarboxylation in a reaction catalyzed by α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, resulting in the formation of succinyl-CoA. High concentrations of ammonia inhibit α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, thereby preventing its oxidative decarboxylation.
questions.learning: Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto glutarate Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate is not seen in a patient with advanced liver disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following milestones would you generally expect a 3 year old child to display?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spoon handling

The ability to handle a spoon well and feed self is usually developed by 24 months (2 years) and would be expected in a 3 year old child.

Other options:

Option A: The ability to hop on one foot usually develops by 48 months (4 years).

Options C and D: The ability to draw a triangle from copy and repeating a sentence of 10 syllables usually develops at around 60 months (5 years) of age.

Some key milestones of children from 15 months of age are listed below:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident with a head injury. He is conscious, but when questioned about the incident, his responses are irrelevant despite fluent speech. Which area of the brain is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of fluent but irrelevant speech characterizes Wernicke's aphasia, also known as receptive aphasia. This condition results from a lesion in Wernicke's area, located in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. These patients can produce speech with normal rate and rhythm, but they lack comprehension of language, leading to "word salad" answers. A lesion in the pre-central gyrus (Option A) would cause motor weakness or paralysis on the contralateral side rather than a language disorder. Damage to the inferior frontal gyrus (Option B) causes Broca's aphasia, where speech is non-fluent and effortful, though comprehension is relatively preserved. Brain stem injuries (Option D) would typically involve severe motor/sensory deficits or altered consciousness rather than an isolated fluent aphasia. Thus, the disconnect between speech production and meaningful content localizes the injury to the superior temporal gyrus
questions.learning: The patient's presentation of fluent but irrelevant speech characterizes Wernicke's aphasia, also known as receptive aphasia. This condition results from a lesion in Wernicke's area, located in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mode of transmission of abdominal TB includes all except
options: Direct spread from mesenteric lymph nodes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Feco-oral route

Abdominal tuberculosis (TB) is not transmitted by feco-oral route.

The terminal ileum and the cecum are the sites most commonly involved in abdominal TB. It causes abdominal pain (at times similar to that associated with appendicitis) and obstruction, hematochezia, palpable mass in the abdomen along with fever, weight loss, anorexia, and night sweats.

Modes of spread:

• By ingestion of infected food or milk (primary intestinal TB) or infected sputum (secondary intestinal TB)
• Contagious spread from infected adjacent foci
• Hematogenous spread from distant TB focus
• Through lymphatic channels
• Direct contact with an infected animal (Mycobacterium bovis)

There is no evidence of spread of TB through the feco-oral route.
questions.learning: Feco-oral route Abdominal tuberculosis (TB) is not transmitted by feco-oral route. The terminal ileum and the cecum are the sites most commonly involved in abdominal TB.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a facility offered by Ayushman AROGYA mandirs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Essential drugs

Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health & Wellness Centres) are mandated to provide free and essential medicines as part of comprehensive primary healthcare services.

Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are envisaged to deliver an expanded range of services that go beyond Maternal and child health care services to include care for non-communicable diseases, palliative and rehabilitative care, Oral, Eye and ENT care, mental health and first-level care for emergencies and trauma, including free essential drugs and diagnostic services.

Ayushman Arogya Mandir represents a shift from a selective model of healthcare to one that offers a comprehensive package of services, including preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care. The scheme has two complementary components. The first aims to establish 1,50,000 Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to provide universal, free, and comprehensive primary health care, with an emphasis on wellness and expanded services delivered closer to communities. The second component is the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), which offers health insurance coverage of ₹5 lakhs per year to more than poor and vulnerable families for secondary and tertiary level treatments.
questions.learning: Essential drugs Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly Health & Wellness Centres) are mandated to provide free and essential medicines as part of comprehensive primary healthcare services.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple nodulocystic lesions on the face. Which among the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isotretinoin

The likely diagnosis in this patient is nodular acne and the drug of choice for this condition is oral isotretinoin.

Isotretinoin is an orally administered systemic retinoid that is used in the management of severe acne.

Commonly seen adverse effects of isotretinoin are cheilitis (dry lips), xerosis (dry skin), xerostomia (dry mouth), dry nose, and increased sun sensitivity.

Oral isotretinoin is contraindicated in pregnant patients and patients who may be pregnant.

Other Options:

Option A: Steroids are not indicated in cases of acne as they can exacerbate the condition due to increased sebum production and skin cell turnover disruption.

Options B and C: Nodulocystic acne is a severe form of acne that often requires more aggressive treatment options, such as isotretinoin. While antibiotics may be used in some cases of nodulocystic acne, they are not the first-line treatment option.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An elderly woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer develops marked hair loss. What is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-induced hair loss is typically classified as anagen effluvium. This occurs because chemotherapeutic agents target rapidly dividing cells, which include the hair matrix cells during their active growth (anagen) phase. The damage causes the hair shaft to narrow and eventually break or fall out suddenly and diffusely within weeks of starting treatment. Regarding the distractors, telogen effluvium (Option A) is a delayed shedding triggered by stress or illness that pushes hairs into the resting phase prematurely. Trichotillomania (Option B) is a behavioral disorder involving compulsive hair pulling resulting in irregular patches. Alopecia areata (Option D) is an autoimmune condition causing well-defined circular patches of hair loss. Because chemotherapy specifically interrupts the mitotic activity of the hair bulb during the growth cycle, anagen effluvium is the correct pathological diagnosis
questions.learning: Chemotherapy-induced hair loss is typically classified as anagen effluvium. This occurs because chemotherapeutic agents target rapidly dividing cells, which include the hair matrix cells during their active growth (anagen) phase.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Dehydration is more severe in infants compared to adults. Which of the following is a true statement about infants?
options: Extracellular fluid (ECF) is more than intracellular fluid (ICF)
Intracellular fluid (ICF) is more than extracellular fluid (ECF)
Total body water in infants is more than in adults
questions.explanation: Infants have a significantly higher percentage of total body water (TBW) compared to adults, which contributes to their increased susceptibility to severe dehydration. At birth, TBW accounts for approximately 75–80% of an infant's body weight, whereas it is only about 55–60% in adults. In the early neonatal period, the extracellular fluid (ECF) volume actually exceeds the intracellular fluid (ICF) volume (supporting Option A at birth, but not as a general lifelong rule). As the infant grows, the ICF eventually becomes the dominant compartment. Option B is incorrect for neonates but true for older children and adults. ECF and ICF are never equal (Option D). Because infants have higher metabolic rates and higher water turnover, any fluid loss represents a larger proportion of their TBW, making dehydration a pediatric emergency
questions.learning: Infants have a significantly higher percentage of total body water (TBW) compared to adults, which contributes to their increased susceptibility to severe dehydration.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A person was brought to the emergency department with facial swelling, itching, and hypotension following a bee sting. The mentioned clinical features are due to the increase in which immunoglobulin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgE

The given clinical features suggest type 1 hypersensitivity reaction and are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE).

Immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity reactions refer to allergic reactions or allergies.

It is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It occurs in a previously sensitized individual. These reactions are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals.

Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils. IgE coats mast cells by binding to the FcεRI receptor. Re-exposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI which in turn causes activation of mast cells releasing powerful mediators. The principal mediators are:

• Histamine
• Proteases
• Prostaglandins
• Leukotrienes
• Cytokines like TNF, IL-1, and chemokines.

The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

It occurs in two phases:

• The immediate phase is characterized by vasodilation, vascular leakage, smooth muscle spasm (in asthma), or glandular secretions. These changes occur within minutes after exposure to an allergen and subside in a few hours.
• Late-phase reaction is characterized by infiltration of tissues with eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, monocytes, and CD4+ T cells. Late-phase reaction sets in 2 to 24 hours later and may last for several days.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate (type 1) hypersensitivity.
questions.learning: IgE — The given clinical features suggest type 1 hypersensitivity reaction and are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE). Immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity reactions refer to allergic reactions or allergies.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following parasites directly invade the skin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schistosoma mansoni

The parasite that directly invades the skin is Schistosoma mansoni.

Adult worms of S. mansoni live in the inferior mesenteric vein and their infective form is fork-tailed cercaria. Following skin penetration by cercariae, a pruritic rash termed cercarial dermatitis or swimmers itch develops locally which is self-limiting.

After 4- 8 weeks of the cercarial invasion, high worm load, and egg antigen stimuli lead to the formation of immune complexes which result in a serum sickness-like illness termed Katayama fever. They present with high-grade fever, rash, arthralgia, and hepatosplenomegaly.

When eggs get deposited in the small intestine, patients develop abdominal pain and blood dysentery for a long time called intestinal bilharziasis. The drug of choice is praziquantel 40mg/kg single oral dose. Oxamniquine 15mg/kg single oral dose is also an effective dose.

A yellowish-brown egg with a lateral spine near the rounded posterior end is suggestive of Schistosoma mansoni. In Schistosoma hematobium, the egg has a terminal spine. In Schistosoma japonicum, the egg has no spine but shows a lateral small rudimentary knob.

The life cycle of schistosomes is represented below:

Other options:

Option B: Dracunculiasis/Guinea worm disease is a vector-borne parasitic disease caused by Dracunculus medinenesis. Transmission occurs by consumption of water containing cyclops harboring infective stages of the parasite. This disease is totally a water-based disease and has no alternate way of transmission.

Option C: Wuchereria bancrofti causes filariasis. The adult worms block the lymphatic vessels leading to inflammation and granuloma formation. This causes hard pitting or brawny edema. It can present as lymphadenitis, lymphedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis. The disease spreads from person to person through mosquito bites.

Option D: Onchocerca volvulus is a tissue nematode. The life cycle of Onchocerca volvulus is completed partly in humans, the definitive host, and partly in female blackflies, the intermediate host. During a blood meal, the female blackfly ingests the microfilariae from the skin and lymphatics of an infected person. Within the vector, the microfilariae develop into the infective stage. When the infected black fly bites another person, it introduces third-stage filarial larvae into the skin of the human host.

Pearl PF1690: Eggs in parasitology
questions.learning: Schistosoma mansoni — The parasite that directly invades the skin is Schistosoma mansoni. Adult worms of S. mansoni live in the inferior mesenteric vein and their infective form is fork-tailed cercaria.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of pterygium?
options: The parts of a pterygium are head, neck and body
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rate of recurrence is 95%

The recurrence rate of 95% is not a feature of pterygium. The recurrence rate of pterygium is around 80% after simple surgical excision.

Pterygium is a wing-shaped, triangular fibrovascular ingrowth (Option B) of degenerative conjunctival tissue that can encroach onto the cornea. It is a response to prolonged exposure to ultraviolet rays, dry heat, etc. It has 3 parts mainly, a head (apical part on the cornea), a body (the region between the limbus and canthus), and a cap(semilunar white infiltrate in front of the head)(Option C).. Some authors mention the neck as the constricted part near the limbal area.

Patients may complain of itching and grittiness due to Dellen (localized drying effect). If the pterygium encroaches onto the pupillary area, it may interfere with vision and also induce astigmatism. Stocker's line may be associated with a pterygium. It is a linear deposition of iron seen in the corneal epithelium, anterior to the head of a pterygium. Pterygium is of 2 types (Option D):

• Progressive which is thick, fleshy, and vascular.
• Regressive which is thin, atrophic, and attenuated.

This condition can be treated symptomatically with tear substitutes for dry eye symptoms and patients are advised to avoid ultraviolet rays. Surgical excision with free conjunctival limbal autograft is the preferred treatment to avoid recurrence.

The recurrence rate of pterygium is around 80% after simple surgical excision. Excision together with adjunctive therapies such as mitomycin C or 5-fluorouracil can reduce the risk of recurrence to approximately 10%

The image below shows a pterygium.
questions.learning: Rate of recurrence is 95% — The recurrence rate of 95% is not a feature of pterygium. The recurrence rate of pterygium is around 80% after simple surgical excision.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person reported to OPD alongside his 32-year-old brother working in a factory. The brother was recently subjected to a test – Coproporphyrin in urine. The physician should suspect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lead poisoning

Detection of coproporphyrin in urine is a characteristic finding in lead poisoning, due to inhibition of enzymes involved in heme synthesis.

Lead interferes with ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, causing accumulation of porphyrin precursors that are excreted in urine.

In contrast, silicosis, byssinosis, and bagassosis are occupational lung diseases and are not associated with porphyrin metabolism abnormalities.
questions.learning: Lead poisoning Detection of coproporphyrin in urine is a characteristic finding in lead poisoning, due to inhibition of enzymes involved in heme synthesis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with headache, vomiting, amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, acromegaly, and infertility. On examination, she has bitemporal hemianopia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mammosomatotrope adenoma

The symptoms of headache, vomiting, galactorrhea, infertility, decreased libido, acromegaly is suggestive of excess prolactin and growth hormone along with features of raised intra-cranial tension. The most likely diagnosis is a mammosomatotrope adenoma of the pituitary.

Prolactinomas are the most frequent type of hyperfunctioning pituitary adenomas. They are usually found in adults. They may be functioning or non-functioning. Based on the size, they can be called microadenomas if <1 cm in diameter and macroadenomas if ≥1 cm in diameter.

The symptoms include

* Headache and vomiting

* Bitemporal hemianopia suggestive of a local mass effect

* Increased intracranial pressure due to a pituitary tumour

* In females- amenorrhea, galactorrhea, loss of libido, and infertility

* In males- impotence, loss of libido, and gynecomastia

The diagnosis of prolactinoma is most likely to be associated with a prolactin level >200 μg/L.

Treatment is only required in symptomatic cases as microadenomas rarely progress to macroadenomas. Dopamine and dopamine agonists are used and they act as inhibitory signals to prolactin secretion in the pituitary. Cabergoline is a long-acting dopamine receptor agonist with high D2 receptor affinity and is the preferred drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia

Excessive GH secreted before puberty results in gigantism. Acromegaly occurs when excessive GH is secreted after puberty (after fusion of long bone epiphysis).

Increased secretion of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor- 1 (IGF-1) results in acral bone overgrowth. Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, and widened space between the lower incisor teeth. Soft tissue swelling results in increased heel pad thickness, increased shoe size, ring tightening, characteristic coarse facial features, and a large fleshy nose. Other manifestations seen in GH excess are cardiomyopathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes mellitus, etc.

Serum IGF-1 levels and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load. GH-secreting adenomas are managed with surgery. Transsphenoidal resection is the preferred surgery.

Other options:

Option A: Corticotroph adenoma secrete ACTH. They present with features of Cushing's disease.

Option B: Gonadotroph adenoma secrete FSH and LH. They can present with  polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), infertility, menstrual irregularities, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in women, and testicular hypertrophy and sexual dysfunction in men.

Option D: Gliomas are neoplasms that originates from glial cells. They present with headaches, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and in more advanced cases weakness or altered mental status.

Also known as Wermer’s syndrome

Characteristic tumors seen in:

* Parathyroid adenoma – 90 % - Most common overall

* Entero pancreatic tumors - Most common functioning tumor is gastrinoma (most common site is duodenum)

* Pituitary adenoma – Most common is prolactinoma

* Mnemonic – Par Pan Pit – in decreasing order of frequency

Associated tumors are:

* Angiofibroma

* Collagenomas

* Adrenal cortical tumors

* Lipoma

* Neuroendocrine tumors - gastric, thymic, lungs

* Meningioma

* Pheochromocytoma

* Carcinoid tumors, usually of the foregut

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient is admitted with tachycardia and arrhythmias. On examination, multiple scratch marks are noted on the body. Which drug of abuse is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of tachycardia, arrhythmias, and multiple scratch marks on the body is highly suggestive of Cocaine abuse. The scratch marks are a result of Magnan's sign (formication), a specific type of tactile hallucination where the user feels like insects are crawling under their skin ("cocaine bugs"). This leads to frantic, compulsive scratching. Cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that also causes severe cardiovascular effects, including hypertension, tachycardia, and potentially fatal arrhythmias. Morphine (Option B) is an opioid that typically causes bradycardia, respiratory depression, and "pinpoint" pupils. Datura (Option C) causes an anticholinergic syndrome ("mad as a hatter, red as a beet"). Cannabis (Option D) usually causes relaxation and reddened eyes (conjunctival injection). Understanding these specific "behavioral clues" is essential for emergency physicians and psychiatrists to identify the hidden drug of abuse when a patient presents with non-specific systemic symptoms

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents for an antenatal check-up and is currently on lithium for her bipolar disorder. This drug must be stopped, due to the risk of development of which of the following conditions in the fetus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ebstein anomaly

Lithium should be stopped as it can cause an Ebstein anomaly in the newborn.

Ebstein anomaly is characterized by the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which results in a thin-walled, low-pressure, “atrialized” segment of the right ventricle due to the anomalous attachment of the tricuspid leaflets.

Lithium can also cause macrocephaly as a teratogenic effect.

Lithium use in early pregnancy causes Ebstein anomaly in the fetus. Fetal lithium exposure is associated with neonatal goiter, CNS depression, hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), and cardiac murmur.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. His left leg is shortened, internally rotated, and adducted, with absent femoral artery pulsation. A plain radiograph is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
options: Fracture neck of femur with injury to femoral vessels
Anterior dislocation of hip with femoral artery injury
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of a shortened, internally rotated, and adducted limb following high-energy trauma is pathognomonic for a Posterior Dislocation of the Hip (Option D) . This position is the classic "orthopedic posture" for this injury. The provided radiograph confirms the diagnosis, showing the femoral head out of its socket, typically appearing smaller and more superior than the contralateral side. In an anterior dislocation (Option C), the leg would instead be externally rotated and abducted. Fractures of the femur (Options A and B) typically result in an externally rotated limb. While vascular injury can occur, the characteristic "adducted and internally rotated" deformity is the definitive hallmark of a posterior dislocation. This is a medical emergency requiring urgent reduction to prevent avascular necrosis of the femoral head and sciatic nerve injury. Therefore, Option D is the accurate clinical and radiological diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical triad of a shortened, internally rotated, and adducted limb following high-energy trauma is pathognomonic for a Posterior Dislocation of the Hip (Option D) .

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following should a cotton swab with pus be discarded?
questions.explanation: According to Biomedical Waste Management rules, a cotton swab contaminated with pus is classified as soiled waste. Soiled waste, which includes items contaminated with blood or body fluids, must be disposed of in yellow category bags. These bags are made of non-chlorinated plastic because the contents are typically destined for incineration or plasma pyrolysis. Biodegradable materials like cotton and gauze are never chlorinated before incineration to prevent the release of toxic gases. The Red category (Options C and D) is strictly reserved for contaminated but recyclable plastic waste, such as tubing, catheters, and syringes without needles. Yellow chlorination bags (Option A) are not standard since yellow waste is already sterilized by high-heat methods. Therefore, the yellow non-chlorination bag is the only appropriate choice for pus-soaked cotton
questions.learning: According to Biomedical Waste Management rules, a cotton swab contaminated with pus is classified as soiled waste. Soiled waste, which includes items contaminated with blood or body fluids, must be disposed of in yellow category bags.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following symptoms is least likely to be associated with a panic attack?
questions.explanation: A panic attack is a sudden episode of intense fear that triggers severe physical reactions when there is no real danger. Common physiological symptoms include "palpitations" (Option A), "chest discomfort" (Option C), sweating, and shortness of breath. Cognitive symptoms often include an intense "fear of losing control or dying" (Option B). While patients with chronic panic disorder may be at a higher risk for depression and suicidal ideation over time, a "suicide attempt" (Option D) is "least likely" to be a symptom of an acute panic attack itself. An attack is characteristically short-lived, usually peaking within 10 minutes, and the patient is typically paralyzed by the immediate somatic sensations of terror rather than engaging in deliberate self-harm during the event. Understanding these symptoms is vital because panic attacks often mimic medical emergencies, such as a myocardial infarction. Management includes reassurance, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), and occasionally short-term benzodiazepines or long-term SSRIs to reduce the frequency of attacks
questions.learning: A panic attack is a sudden episode of intense fear that triggers severe physical reactions when there is no real danger. Common physiological symptoms include "palpitations" (Option A), "chest discomfort" (Option C), sweating, and shortness of breath.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and dull chest pain. Examination reveals a high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border. Chest X-ray shows widening of the mediastinum. CT angiography demonstrates a dilated ascending aorta with aortic regurgitation. Serology is positive for treponemal antibodies. The underlying pathological process responsible for this patient’s condition primarily involves:
options: Immune-complex deposition in the aortic media
Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
Lipid deposition in the intima with foam cell formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum

Treponemal-positive patient with ascending aortic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation suggests tertiary syphilis. The key pathology is obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, causing ischemia of the aortic media → medial degeneration, scarring (“tree-barking”), aneurysmal dilation, and AR.

A Immune-complex deposition → vasculitides like SLE, not syphilitic aortitis.

C Lipid/foam cells → atherosclerosis (intimal), usually abdominal aorta.

D Caseating granulomas → TB; doesn’t classically cause syphilitic AR/aneurysm.
questions.learning: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum Treponemal-positive patient with ascending aortic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation suggests tertiary syphilis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old man presented with the following lesion in his eye. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bitot's spots

The image depicts Bitot's spot, a pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia.

Bitot's spot is a triangular, silvery-white, foamy patch on the bulbar conjunctiva which is usually bilateral. The most common site is temporal.

Ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency include loss of sensitivity to green light (earliest to appear), nyctalopia (night blindness), and xerophthalmia.

Xerophthalmia includes conjunctival xerosis (dryness) with Bitot’s spots (white patches of keratinized epithelium appearing on the sclera), corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia (softening of the cornea) that leads to corneal scarring and ultimately, blindness.

Pearl PF0046: WHO grading of Vitamin A deficiency

The term xerophthalmia is reserved to cover all the ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency.

The first symptom of xerophthalmia is nyctalopia.

The first sign of xerophthalmia is conjunctival xerosis.

The pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia is the appearance of Bitot's spots.

Note:

Up to the level of Stage 2, the manifestations are reversible if treated with vitamin A supplements.

However, active conjunctival xerosis and Bitot’s spots begin to resolve within 2—5 days after supplementation. Most will disappear within 2 weeks, although a significant proportion of temporal lesions may persist in shrunken form and may therefore not be completely reversible.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the true statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve.
options: At point E, the nerve is more excitable
Point C to D is due to opening of Na+ and closure of K+ channels
Point B to D is refractory period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Point B to D is refractory period

The correct statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve is point B to D is the refractory period.

The sequence of events occurring during an action potential is shown below

• Point A represents the resting state where both channels are closed.
• Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus and sodium enters the cell. The initiation of action potential occurs only after a certain potential is reached, which is called the threshold potential represented by point B. (Option A)
• After this, the sodium influx causes the opening of more Na+ channels through a positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs to reach point C.
• At point C, Na+ channels close and K+ channels open, causing repolarization due to K+ efflux. (Option C)
• Point D represents continued repolarization due to potassium efflux.
• At point E, Na+ channels are reset and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus. During this phase, the K+ channels remain open and slowly return to the closed state, causing after-hyperpolarization. As a stronger stimulus is required to reach the threshold potential, the excitability of nerve fiber is reduced at point E. (Option B)
• As both channels close, the membrane returns to resting membrane potential back to point A.

Point B-D is a part of the refractory period. During this period, the application of even a stronger stimulus will not elicit an action potential.

The refractory period is divided into an absolute refractory period and a relative refractory period. During the absolute refractory period, the nerve will not be excited no matter how strong a stimulus is given. However, during the relative refractory period, stronger than normal stimuli can cause excitation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which of the following is a component of trotter's triad?
options: Conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporopa- rietal neuralgia, Palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, contralateral tempo- roparietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, ipsilateral temporo- parietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis
Conductive hearing loss, contralateral temporo- parietal neuralgia, palatal paralysis
questions.explanation: Conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia, Palatal paralysis. Trotter's triad is a specific constellation of clinical findings indicating deep invasion of a nasopharyngeal carcinoma into the skull base. The three definitive components are: 1. Conductive hearing loss: Due to the tumor blocking the Eustachian tube, leading to middle ear effusion. 2. Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia: Caused by the invasion of the maxillary nerve (CN V2). 3. Palatal paralysis : Resulting from the involvement of the levator veli palatini muscle or its nerve supply. Option A correctly lists these three features. All other options are incorrect as they mention sensorineural loss (Option B and C) or contralateral neuralgia (Option B and D). Trotter's triad is a classic board examination topic because it represents a late-stage, anatomical presentation of NPC. Therefore, because it describes the specific mechanical and neurological impacts of local tumor spread, Option A is the only accurate description of this clinical triad. .
questions.learning: Conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia, Palatal paralysis. Trotter's triad is a specific constellation of clinical findings indicating deep invasion of a nasopharyngeal carcinoma into the skull base.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old with a history of swimming in a freshwater stagnant pond presents with neurological manifestations. CSF should be cultured on which medium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Non-nutrient agar with Escherichia coli

A young adult who develops acute neurological symptoms after swimming in warm freshwater is highly suggestive of Primary Amebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) caused by Naegleria fowleri. The organism enters through the nasal mucosa, traverses the cribriform plate, and invades the brain. CSF can be cultured on non-nutrient agar overlaid with Escherichia coli, where the amoebae feed on the bacteria.

Why not the other options?

• B. Diamond medium: Used for Trichomonas vaginalis culture.
• C. Blood agar: Used for routine bacterial culture, not free-living amoebae.
• D. Lowenstein–Jensen medium: Used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A clinical trial was done between two groups to measure their blood pressure after treatment. Which of the following tests would be appropriate to use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Unpaired t test

In the given scenario, two groups are being compared independent of each other. Hence, students t test/ unpaired t test should be used.

T tests are used if 2 groups are being compared. If the same group is compared before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which is the most common benign tumour of the ovary in the reproductive age group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Benign teratoma

A benign teratoma or dermoid cyst is the most common benign tumor of the ovary in the reproductive age group. It is also the:

* Most common benign tumor of ovary diagnosed in pregnancy

* Most common germ cell tumor (overall)

* Most typical tumor to undergo torsion.

* Bilateral in 10-15% cases.

It consists of a Rokitansky’s protuberance, which is a projection covered by skin, sebaceous glands, sweat glands along with teeth & bones can be seen. Sometimes thyroid tissue can be seen on histopathological study – known as Struma Ovarii. The most common tissue elements found are ectodermal derivatives.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old male patient came to the outpatient department with complaints of hematuria. On examination, a 2x2 cm bladder mass is noted. The gross specimen image is given below. Which among the following is the ideal management?
options: Intravesical instillations of Bacille Calmette Guerin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transurethral resection of the tumour

The given image of the specimen shows a large, fungating growth from the bladder wall involving the entire bladder with the two lobes of the prostate not being much affected. He is likely to have bladder carcinoma and should undergo transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) for accurate staging purposes.

Given the patient's age, the presence of a bladder mass, and the need to address potential malignancy, the ideal management in this scenario would be Transurethral resection of the tumor (TURBT):

* This procedure allows for both diagnosis and treatment of the bladder mass.

* It is a less invasive approach, suitable for cases where the tumor is localized and hasn't invaded deeply into the bladder wall.

* TURBT is considered the ideal management in this case because the tumor is of a size that is amenable to this approach. It is less invasive compared to radical surgery and is suitable for localized, non-invasive or early-stage bladder cancer.

* If the tumor is found to be more aggressive or invasive after TURBT, additional treatment options can be considered.

Other options:

Intravesical instillations of Bacille Calmette Guerin:

* Intravesical BCG therapy is typically used for treating superficial (non-invasive) bladder cancer.

* In this case, there's a noted 2x2 cm bladder mass, which suggests a localized tumor. However, the size of the tumor is significant, making it less suitable for BCG therapy, which is usually effective for smaller tumors.

* BCG therapy is often used as a preventive measure or for smaller tumors that haven't invaded deeply into the bladder wall.

Cystoscopy with removal of tumor:

* Cystoscopy with tumor removal can be effective for small, non-invasive tumors. However, the size of the bladder mass (2x2 cm) suggests a larger lesion.

* If the tumor is large or invasive, a more comprehensive approach might be necessary.

Radical cystectomy:

* Radical cystectomy involves the complete removal of the bladder and nearby structures. It is typically considered for cases of advanced bladder cancer, invasive tumors, or aggressive cancers.

* While radical cystectomy is an effective treatment for certain situations, it is a major surgery with significant implications for the patient's quality of life. It's generally reserved for cases where the tumor has invaded deeply or is not amenable to less invasive treatments.
questions.learning: Transurethral resection of the tumour — The given image of the specimen shows a large, fungating growth from the bladder wall involving the entire bladder with the two lobes of the prostate not being much affected.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with a history of approximately 18 episodes of watery diarrhea and two episodes of vomiting in a single day. The child appears irritable but is still able to take fluids orally. Based on this clinical presentation and hydration status, which treatment option would be the most appropriate for management?
options: Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids
questions.explanation: Based on the WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines, this child is classified as having "some dehydration" because they are irritable and still able to drink. For children in this category, the first-line treatment is Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) using Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution (Plan B). Intravenous fluids (Options A and C) are reserved for children with "severe dehydration" (Plan C), characterized by lethargy, unconsciousness, or inability to drink. Plain water with lithium (Option D) is medically incorrect and potentially toxic. ORS is highly effective because the glucose-sodium co-transport system in the gut remains intact even during most diarrheal illnesses, allowing for efficient fluid absorption. The child should be monitored for four hours while being given ORS, and then reassessed. Continued feeding and breastfeeding are also essential components of the diarrheal management protocol to prevent malnutrition and promote mucosal recovery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Purkinje cells of cerebellum relay into _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dentate nucleus

Purkinje cells of the cerebellum relay into the dentate nucleus which is one of the deep cerebellar nuclei.

The input to the Purkinje cells come from the climbing fibres. The output of Purkinje cells is inhibitory to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

Options A and B: Caudate and lentiform nuclei are part of the basal ganglia.

Option D: Red nucleus receives afferents from the cerebellum and plays a role in modulating signals to the upper motor neurons of the cerebral cortex.
questions.learning: Dentate nucleus Purkinje cells of the cerebellum relay into the dentate nucleus which is one of the deep cerebellar nuclei. The input to the Purkinje cells come from the climbing fibres.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident with acute respiratory distress and distended neck veins. Imaging shows a large collection of air on the left side of the chest. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of trauma, respiratory distress, dilated neck veins (elevated JVP), and an X-ray showing a large volume of air in the hemithorax is pathognomonic for a Tension Pneumothorax. This is a life-threatening emergency where air under pressure compresses the heart and the opposite lung. The most appropriate immediate management is needle decompression. According to modern ATLS guidelines, this is performed by inserting a wide-bore needle into the 5th intercostal space in the mid-axillary line (or the 2nd space mid-clavicular line). This converts the tension pneumothorax into a simple one, stabilizing the patient until a chest tube can be placed. Intubation (Option B) and tracheostomy (Option C) address airway obstruction, not pleural air. Pericardiocentesis (Option D) is for cardiac tamponade. Therefore, immediate decompression is the life-saving next step
questions.learning: The clinical combination of trauma, respiratory distress, dilated neck veins (elevated JVP), and an X-ray showing a large volume of air in the hemithorax is pathognomonic for a Tension Pneumothorax.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: On the day of delivery, a newborn baby is undergoing a screening test for hearing. Which of the following tests is likely to be performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Otoacoustic emissions (OAE)

A newborn baby on the same day of delivery will undergo the Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) test as a screening test for hearing.

Universal Newborn Hearing Screening (UNHS) has become a standard practice in most developed countries. The identification of all newborns with hearing loss before 6 months has become an attainable and realistic goal. The goal is to screen newborn babies before 1 month of age, diagnose hearing loss before 3 months of age and start intervention as early as possible, or latest by 6 months of age.

In India, a two-stage screening protocol is followed according to which infants are screened first with otoacoustic emissions (OAE). Infants who fail the OAE are screened with auditory brainstem response (ABR) or Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA), which is also the definitive test. All babies kept in NICU must be screened by BERA test as per the protocol.

The first screening is usually conducted at birth or before discharge. Conducting the first screening before discharge is preferred to ensure better coverage and reduce loss to follow-up. A second screening is scheduled anytime between 1–3 weeks or during the next scheduled visit at 6 weeks.
All babies with abnormal BERA should undergo detailed ENT evaluation and hearing-aid fitting (cochlear implants) and auditory rehabilitation must be done before 6 months of age.

Pearl PF1979: OAEs - Otoacoustic emissions

It is an objective test that records the low-intensity sounds produced by the outer hair cells of a normal cochlea.

It is of two types:

* Spontaneous type- it is generated spontaneously and is present in 50% of normal individuals.

* Evoked types- also called Kemp echoes or cochlear echoes, are generated in response to sound stimulus and found in all individuals with normal hearing. The two subtypes are transient evoked and distortion product.

The applications are as follows:

* Best audiometric test for screening in neonates, infants, and small children for deafness due to inner ear causes.

* Helps to differentiate cochlear and retrocochlear hearing loss- normal OAE indicates normal cochlea and hence retrocochlear pathology in a patient with sensorineural deafness.

* Early detection of noise-induced hearing loss- since it is generated by outer hair cells that are prone to damage by noise trauma.

Pearl PF1553: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response)

It is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway.

Normally, 7 waves are produced in the first 10ms.

* Wave I – distal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave II –proximal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave III – cochlear nucleus

* Wave IV – superior olivary complex

* Wave V – lateral lemniscus

* Wave VI – inferior colliculus

* Wave VII - medial geniculate body

Findings:

* Conductive or cochlear pathology- delayed wave-I but inter-peak latency of I-V is normal

* Retrocochlear pathology- wave-I present, rest of the waves absent

* Acoustic neuroma or vestibular schwannoma- increased inter-peak latency of wave I-V and increased inter-aural latency of wave V > 0.2ms.

Uses:

* To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA

* Best audiometric test for:

* Confirming hearing loss in infants

* Diagnosing acoustic neuroma

*

* Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss

* Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:

Disease
Findings in PTA audiogram

Conductive hearing loss
AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

Sensorineural hearing loss
Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap

Mixed hearing loss
Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first)
Downsloping or descending audiogram

Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first)
Upsloping or ascending audiogram

Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss)
U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram

Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

Otosclerosis
Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Whipple's procedure

The image shows the Whipple procedure which is a complex surgery done for carcinomas involving the head of the pancreas.

It is done only in cases when:

* The entire duodenum has to be removed e.g. in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

* Tumor encroaches in the first part of the duodenum, or stomach

* A clear resection margin is not achieved by PPPD

The following structures are removed during Whipple’s procedure:

* Distal stomach

* Duodenum

* Proximal jejunum

* Head of the pancreas

* Gallbladder

* Common bile duct (CBD)

* Regional lymphatics

The reconstruction following Whipple’s procedure or pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy involves anastomosis in the following order:

Pancreaticojejunostomy

↓

Choledochojejunostomy

↓

Gastrojejunostomy

This is controversial since there is a difference in the reconstruction procedures mentioned in standard textbooks:

Bailey and Love, 27th edition (Pg no: 1236) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy

Schwatrz, 11th edition (Pg no: 1493) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy + gastrojejunostomy/duodenojejunostomy

Sabiston, 20th edition (Pg no: 1546) - Pancreaticojejunostomy + hepaticojejunostomy + duodenojejunostomy

Pearl PF0333: Resection and Hybrid Surgical Procedures for Chronic Pancreatitis

Beger’s procedure: Duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR)

* The completed resection after transection of the pancreatic neck and subtotal removal of the pancreatic head, with preservation of the distal common bile duct and duodenum (Marked A).

* Completion of the reconstruction of the anastomosis to the distal pancreas and to the proximal pancreatic rim by the same Roux limb of the jejunum.

Frey’s procedure:

* The local resection of the pancreatic head with longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (LR-LPJ) provides complete decompression of the entire pancreatic ductal system. Reconstruction is performed with a side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy.

Warren’s modification of Beger’s procedure:

Berne modification (Beger + Frey) involves excavation of the central portion of the head without formal division of the neck.

(image below)

Hamburg modification of Frey’s procedure

Note:

Surgical treatments for chronic pancreatitis

* Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Kausch–Whipple procedure)

* Pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (Traverso–Longmire)

* Beger procedure

* Near-total or total pancreatectomy

Decompression/Drainage

* Duval procedure

* Puestow–Gillesby procedure

* Partington–Rochelle procedure (Puestow)

* Izbicki procedure

questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a crush injury on his hand. He says that he received his last dose of TT vaccination at the age of 23. What is the treatment of choice in this patient?

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the composition of lactulose?
questions.explanation: Lactulose is a synthetic, non-absorbable disaccharide widely used as an osmotic laxative and in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It is composed of the monosaccharides galactose and fructose. 1. Glucose + Galactose (Option A) forms lactose, the natural milk sugar. 2. Glucose + Fructose (Option B) forms sucrose (table sugar). 3. Fructose + Ribulose (Option D) is not a physiologically relevant disaccharide. Humans lack the intestinal enzyme (lactulase) required to digest lactulose, so it reaches the colon unchanged. Colonic bacteria ferment lactulose into short-chain organic acids (e.g., lactic and acetic acids), which acidify the colonic lumen. This acidic environment converts ammonia (NH₃) into ammonium (NH₄⁺), a non-absorbable form, thereby reducing systemic ammonia levels—the key mechanism in treating hepatic encephalopathy. Additionally, its osmotic effect draws water into the colon, producing a laxative action
questions.learning: Lactulose is a synthetic, non-absorbable disaccharide widely used as an osmotic laxative and in the management of hepatic encephalopathy. It is composed of the monosaccharides galactose and fructose.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following nerves are involved in the movement of the eyeball except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

The nerve marked as 'A' is the optic nerve (II CN), and is not involved in the movement of the eyeball.

The nerves marked in the image are:

1. Optic nerve (II CN)
2. Oculomotor nerve (III CN)
3. Abducens nerve (VI CN)
4. Trochlear nerve (IV CN)

Extraocular muscles involved in the movement of the eyeball:

• Superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris muscles - supplied by the oculomotor (III) nerve.
• Lateral rectus - supplied by abducens (VI) nerve.
• Superior oblique - supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is able to roll over, babble ‘mama’ and ‘dada,’ and exhibits stranger anxiety but is unable to sit without support. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reassurance

Developmental milestones can show normal variation, and a single mildly delayed milestone in the presence of otherwise appropriate development does not necessarily indicate pathology.

• At 9 months, expected milestones include babbling (“mama/dada”), stranger anxiety, and rolling over, all of which are present in this child
• Sitting without support typically develops around 8–9 months, but slight delay can still fall within normal variation
• Absence of red flag signs (loss of milestones, global delay, abnormal tone) supports reassurance

Clinical approach:

• If development is normal in other domains (social, language, fine motor), isolated borderline delay can be observed
• Regular follow-up is important to ensure progression
questions.learning: Reassurance Developmental milestones can show normal variation, and a single mildly delayed milestone in the presence of otherwise appropriate development does not necessarily indicate pathology. • At 9 months, expected milestones include babbling…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is caused by exposure to cotton dust?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Byssinosis

Byssinosis is caused by exposure to cotton dust.

Byssinosis is an occupational disease due to chronic exposure to cotton dust as in textile and rope-making industries. Chest X-ray shows hyperlucency, diaphragmatic flattening, and emphysema. A chest CT demonstrates ground glass opacities largely distributed in the basal regions with centrilobular nodules.

Other options :

Option A: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially, it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Option B: Silicosis is a form of pneumoconiosis which is a cause of permanent disability and mortality. It occurs in people working in sandblasting, pottery, and ceramics industry, mining, and construction work. It occurs due to the inhalation of silica dust. The patient presents with a cough, exertional dyspnea, and chest pain.

Option D: Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of bagasse or sugarcane dust. A thermophilic actinomycete, Thermoactinomyces sacchari is the causative organism. The symptoms are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and fever. Initially, it can result in acute diffuse bronchiolitis, If left untreated it can progress to diffuse fibrosis, emphysema, and bronchiectasis.
